lineShape.example: 2026-08-16 15:28:55 · COMP/1 · the assistant was ready after 1.8s
lineShape.why: Local time to the second, then the course and section when the line is about one, then a sentence in the words a teacher would use. Not a function name and not a level: the trail is read by a person deciding what went wrong, months later, and 'started preview.sh COMP 1' beats 'DEBUG runScript(preview.sh)'.

mustRecord.carries: app version, build number, process id, bundle path
mustRecord.why: The bundle path and process id are not decoration. Two copies of the app can run at once, and when they do they take turns rewriting the same working folder; two process ids in one trail is the fastest way to see it. The bundle path answers 'is this build the one I think it is' without asking.

mustRecord.carries: OS version, OS build, architecture, core count, memory
mustRecord.why: The assistant runs natively on one architecture and not the other, and the whole toolchain emulates on the wrong one. Memory decides which model tier a teacher gets. OS build number and kernel release isolate virtualization, Metal, and WinUI/WSL2 platform issues.

mustRecord.carries: the bundled assistant engine's build, and the helper programs as FOUND on this machine: on macOS each one's version measured by asking it (Colima, Lima, Docker CLI, Buildx) and where it came from (Plantoir's own copy, Homebrew, or the folder it was found in), or 'not found' with the version that would be installed; on Windows the runtime kind, read from disk
mustRecord.why: The assistant flags and chat template handling depend on the engine build. The helper versions isolate whether a machine is running what Plantoir expects - but only if they are MEASURED: the launchers use whatever copy is already installed and download only what is missing, so a line naming the pinned versions described a machine that did not exist, and on a Mac with Homebrew's tools it once sent a diagnosis the wrong way (issue #222). On macOS the line is written a moment after the other two launch lines, once the programs have answered.

mustRecord.carries: the folder path, redacted
mustRecord.why: Almost every question about a course begins with which folder it is in - and a folder outside the home directory bind-mounts as an EMPTY folder inside the container, which is a whole class of report explained by this line alone.

mustRecord.carries: the course code; which sidebar items this save hid or showed (names only, compared with the file as it was before the save); which settings it kept or replaced because another window or a build had changed the file since this window read it, and — when the sidebar list was one it replaced — that the teacher was told so (specialNames.settingsSaveReplacedSidebarChange); and whether a preview or a publish of the course was running, so it could not see the save
mustRecord.why: 'It broke after I changed something' is the commonest report there is, and this is the line that dates the change. Issue #265 (2026-09-24) widened it: two windows on one working folder each held their own copy of a course's settings, a Save in the stale one put back its older sidebar list, and a Save made while a preview was open never reached that preview. Every one of those looks, from the teacher's chair, like switches with 'no correlation' to the site; the line naming what the save hid, what it kept from elsewhere and what was running settles it in one read.

mustRecord.carries: the course code and the reason
mustRecord.why: A save that failed leaves the teacher believing it succeeded. Recording only successes would hide exactly the case worth seeing.

mustRecord.carries: the course code and the section
mustRecord.why: A preview reads the SAVED settings file, while Course Settings keeps unsaved edits in memory and goes on showing them after the teacher leaves the form. A preview started in that state disagrees with the switches on screen for a reason nothing on screen explains, so the teacher is told (specialNames.previewUsesSavedSettings) and the trail says it happened (issue #265).

mustRecord.carries: the course code and the sections whose preview was built again — or, when none was still open at the moment of the press, that nothing was
mustRecord.why: The button beside specialNames.settingsSavedWhilePreviewing. It stops and restarts a preview that may be in another window, so the trail says it was the Settings button that did it rather than a press in that window (issue #265).

mustRecord.carries: the launcher and its arguments, redacted
mustRecord.why: What was actually asked for, as against what the teacher believes they asked for.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, and WHICH of the three starting points the course began from: the ready-made pages written for its code, the subject's skeleton (named — "from the computer studies skeleton"), or empty folders. A skeleton course also says whether the curriculum pages written for its code came with it — "from the computer studies skeleton with the ICS4U curriculum pages" — and only when they did. A club (#267: `class_page_scheme` "numbered" in the file just written) says so instead, with its page word and class folder — "created CODING as a club, with pages named “Week 1” in “All Meetings”" — and every other course's line is byte-identical to before. Nothing else: not the course name the teacher typed, not where it publishes, not its folder lists.
mustRecord.why:
"My new course came out empty" is the report this event exists to answer, and until 2026-09-21 the trail could not answer it at all. Creating a course recorded ONE line — "started setup.sh" — whose arguments are empty for a creation, so the trail carried neither the code nor what the course was meant to start as. Adding a single folder to a list recorded more ("folder created" carries the course and the list). That asymmetry is how GitHub issue #248 stayed invisible for five weeks: a teacher declined the ready-made pages for a code that had some, got empty folders instead of the subject's skeleton, and nothing written down said which of those two things the app had done.

The skeleton clause was added for GitHub issue #251 (2026-09-22), and it is rule 5's "a changed behaviour changes its line too" rather than noise: a skeleton course now comes out TWO ways, and they differ by fifty-nine pages and by whether the curriculum coverage map works at all. A line that could not tell them apart could not answer the report it was added for. Read from include_curriculum_pages in the file the wizard has just written, so it says what was actually asked for. The other two sentences are untouched — the ready-made pages have always carried their own curriculum, and an empty course has none to speak of.

It is one line per creation, written BEFORE the launcher starts, so a creation that fails part-way still says what was asked for. Both platforms create courses, so this carries no appliesOn — a course made on Windows leaves the same line.

WHICH creators write THIS event, so nobody adds a duplicate: the New Course wizard, and the "Add Example Course" button — which writes it AFTER the run and from the run's own output, because the example installs under another code when EXC2O is taken, so its code is not known until the script says it. Three other things that produce a course folder deliberately write their OWN event instead, each answering a different question: "course kept for reference" and "course imported for reference" (a frozen copy of a course that already exists, carrying the school year and the folder it was given), and "section started a new website" (a rollover, which re-points a course rather than starting one). A teacher reading the trail should see one line per thing they did, not two for the same act.

The club clause was added for #267 (2026-09-24), rule 5's "a changed behaviour changes its line too": a club starts from none of the three starting points — empty folders plus one first page, its pages named with ONE number in a folder it names itself — and the report it will be looked up for is "my club's pages are not being seen", which only the word and the folder can answer. Read from the configuration the wizard has just written, never from the interface, so it says what was actually asked for. The page word and folder are settings the teacher chose, not page content.

mustRecord.carries: the launcher, the outcome, and how long it took
mustRecord.why: The outcome distinguishes a failure from a task stopped on purpose and from one backed out of at a question - all three exit non-zero, and only one is a fault.

mustRecord.carries: which credential was asked for, never the answer
mustRecord.why: The first publish of a section stops behind a dialog asking for a Netlify or Cloudflare token, and a teacher who does not notice it reports a publish that 'never finished'. This line is the difference between reading that as a hang and reading it as a question waiting. The answer is a live credential and is never written down - only the name of the thing asked for.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and which assistant - except that an OUTSIDE door (app-rules.json -> outsideAgents: 'Revise with Claude…', 'Revise with Codex…') is course-wide and so carries the course and the assistant's name with no section. Naming the assistant is the load-bearing half once there is more than one door: 'assistant opened' on its own cannot answer the first question anybody asks about a report.
mustRecord.why: Which tier is running decides what routing accuracy to expect, and it is the first thing to establish about any report of the assistant misunderstanding something.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and how long the engine took
mustRecord.why: A slow start and a failed start read identically to a teacher ('it just sat there'). The seconds tell them apart.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and the reason
mustRecord.why: The one assistant failure that leaves nothing else behind - no turn, no tool, no output.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and one line the engine itself printed - shortened, and redacted like every other line on the trail
mustRecord.why: Until this existed a report from a teacher whose assistant was misbehaving could carry nothing the engine had said, because both its streams went to the null device. That was not laziness: a redirected pipe nobody drains fills up and blocks the engine mid-request, which is exactly what wedged the Windows server, so the output must never be read on the engine's timetable. It goes to a FILE, and a bounded tail of it is sampled onto the trail - never the firehose. What is sampled is deliberately narrow, and the narrowness was measured against a real engine: a healthy start prints six warnings that are pure noise here (a CORS block that cannot matter on a loopback-only server, and a token-type quirk in the weights), so warnings are NOT recorded. Errors are, along with any line naming an error or an exception - which is the shape of the two lines worth having, 'request (20030 tokens) exceeds the available context size' and 'got exception'. When the engine never becomes ready at all, the tail is taken whatever it says, because then every line is the diagnosis.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and the sentence the teacher typed, on its own marked line
mustRecord.why: Recorded the moment the teacher's words are ACCEPTED, above every branch below it - not when the message goes to the model, and not when an answer comes back. Two different bugs came from placing it lower: a sentence matching a fixed shape returns early and never reaches the model, so a whole class of input left no trace at all; and an engine that failed, or one still thinking when the teacher gave up, lost the sentence that caused the trouble. It is also what the report's checkbox keys off, so recording it late made the checkbox vanish for somebody who had plainly just used the assistant. The general rule: record what the teacher did where they did it, above every branch, never at a later point that can be skipped.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, the tool it ran, and - when the phrasing named a time and the app settled it onto a day - the whole moment it settled on; or, for a time with no am or pm ('deploy at 6:30'), that it asked whether the time was morning or evening and set nothing; or, for a time written a way the app can read but does not set ('deploy at 6.30 pm', 'deploy at 6:30 tonight'), that it gave the spelling to use and set nothing
mustRecord.why: Some phrasings are matched in code and never reach the model at all. Without this line, 'why did it not think about what I said?' is unanswerable - the trail would show a tool running with nothing between it and the teacher's sentence. The moment joined it with the deploy-at-a-time family (issue #168): 'deploy at 6:30 am' names no day, so the app chooses one - the next such time, counting today while it is still to come - and a teacher writing in to say 'it went out on Saturday, I meant Friday' would otherwise leave a trail carrying their sentence and the tool but not the day that was chosen. The conversation is not on the trail, so this is the only place that choice is recoverable. A WHOLE moment only, never a half-settled word and never anything a teacher wrote. Since issue #194 the same event also records a time ASKED about rather than scheduled: 'deploy at 6:30' is morning or evening, the app asks which in code and nothing is set, and without a line the trail would show the teacher's sentence followed by nothing - which reads exactly like a model that failed to answer. The line carries no clock, because the clock is something the teacher wrote. Since issue #277 it also records a time answered with the spelling to use (AssistAgent.askedToSayTheTimeAsLine): the same reasoning, the same absence of a clock, and 'nothing was set' because the line sits where a scheduled deploy's would.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, the tool name, the ARGUMENT NAMES, the seconds, the completion-token count, and whether it waited for the approval button
mustRecord.why: Routing has no automated gate anywhere in this product, so the field is the only place a routing regression shows. Argument NAMES rather than values: which tool with which arguments filled in answers the routing question completely, while the values are the teacher's page titles. The token count is the honest check on thinking having been switched back on - the engine parses the thinking OUT of the content, so a bad reply looks clean and is merely slow.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and the reason
mustRecord.why: The failure that leaves nothing else behind: no tool, no turn, no output. Without this line 'I asked it something and nothing happened' is unfalsifiable.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, which tool the model had BEGUN to name when there was one, and WHICH of the three things happened - an answer the engine stopped part way, a finished answer whose arguments could not be read, or (since issue #198) a finished answer that wrote nothing for a tool that needs more than the section window supplies. Never what it had begun to write.
mustRecord.why: A model can write until it is stopped, and what it has half-written is not an instruction: the app throws it away, runs nothing and says so. Without this line the teacher's side of that - a long wait and then the assistant declining - is indistinguishable from a misroute, so a report of 'it thought for ages and then said no' has nothing to look at. Separate from 'assistant could not answer', which is for an engine that FAILED; here the engine answered perfectly and the app refused the answer. The tool it had begun to name is carried because 'it ran away trying to publish' and 'it ran away trying to deploy' are different reports; what it had begun to WRITE is not carried, because that is the teacher's page titles. The two causes share one event and one sentence to the teacher - from their side both are mended by asking again - but the LINE distinguishes them, because whoever reads the report cannot: an answer stopped at the cap is a question about how much the model was asked to write, and a finished answer whose arguments will not parse is a question about the model itself. Since issue #198 (2026-09-23) there is a third: a finished answer that wrote NOTHING for a tool that needs more than the section window supplies, which the line says in those words ("wrote nothing for") - it is neither a cap nor garbled JSON, and a report reader could not otherwise tell it from either.

mustRecord.carries: this window's course and section, that nothing was run, and that the turn was taken back out of the conversation. Never the sentence - 'assistant asked' already carries it, on its own marked line - and never any page content.
mustRecord.why: The assistant's whole reply was the teacher's own sentence, handed back. Measured on 2026-09-19 (issue #215): "hide unit 4, day 20" came back word for word, date line and all, with no tool chosen - and that echo was then kept in the conversation, so the model copied the pattern it could see and the NEXT request echoed too, including one the same model answers correctly every time in a fresh window. One unrecognised phrase made the window useless until it was closed and reopened. The app now refuses that turn, says so plainly, and winds the turn back out of the conversation - and this line is what says it happened: a teacher's side of it is the assistant saying it did not follow, which is indistinguishable from an ordinary misroute, so a report of "it stopped understanding me" would otherwise have nothing to look at. Separate from 'assistant answer was cut off', whose NAME would be false here - that answer never finished and this one did - and a line describing something other than what happened is worse than no line, because it will be believed. Separate from 'assistant could not answer', which is for an engine that FAILED; here the engine answered perfectly and the app refused the answer. The WIND-BACK is as much of the fact as the refusal: the conversation after this turn is not the one before it, and nothing else on the trail would say so.

mustRecord.carries: this window's course and section, the course the model named instead - AS THE MODEL SPELT IT - and the tool it had chosen. Never the teacher's sentence and never the argument values, which are their page titles. Since issue #167 the same event is written, with no model involved, when a 'what does <page> link to?' question matched in code names another course ('... in SPH3U section 1 link to?' in an ICS3U window): the line then carries both codes - the other one as the TEACHER typed it - and says it was matched in code, not sent to the model, and that nothing was read (AssistAgent.linksQuestionNamedAnotherCourseLine). Never the page title.
mustRecord.event: assistant was asked about another course
mustRecord.why: An assistant window is opened for one section of one course. The SECTION is simply taken back from whatever the model answered, but the COURSE is not: taking it back too means 'publish MCV4U's class', typed in an ICS3U window, quietly succeeding on ICS3U - a failure that reports success, which is the one kind a teacher cannot catch. So the turn is refused and nothing runs, and this line is what says so. The pair of course codes IS the evidence: a teacher's side of this is the assistant declining something they thought they had asked plainly, which is indistinguishable from a misroute, and only the pair tells the guard doing its job apart from a model slip being refused at the teacher's expense. Any differing code is refused, including one naming no course in the folder - binding a typo to this window is the very fault being fixed - and the teacher is told which of the two happened, because one of them can be opened in the sidebar and the other cannot. Separate from 'assistant chose a tool', which carries argument NAMES and never values, so it cannot say WHICH course was named; and from 'assistant answer was cut off', where the answer never finished. Here the answer was perfect and the app refused it. One deliberate divergence, and it is a rule rather than an oversight: the SENTENCE a teacher reads names the other course the way the working folder spells it (a teacher told to open 'mcv4u' is sent looking for something their sidebar does not show), while this LINE keeps the spelling the model actually wrote. The trail is evidence about the MODEL, so a code it spelt oddly is worth keeping as it spelt it; normalising the line would throw away the only record that it did.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant the teacher is set to use
mustRecord.why: The settings panel is where a teacher changes how much of their Mac the assistant may take, and 'it got slow last week' is a report about a change nobody else can date. Recording the state on the way IN also means a trail shows what the setting was even when the teacher looked and changed nothing.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant was chosen, and which one that lands on for this Mac
mustRecord.why: The choice is the single biggest lever a teacher has over the assistant's accuracy AND over the machine's memory, so almost every later report about either is explained by this line. Both halves are recorded because 'chose automatic' does not answer the question anybody is asking months later - the resolved answer depends on the Mac and on a rule that can change.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant, and how big the download is
mustRecord.why: Gigabytes over a school connection, and the commonest failure is that it never finished. A start with no matching finish is the whole diagnosis, and it cannot be seen without recording the start.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant, and how big the download was
mustRecord.why: The other half of the pair above. It also dates when a Mac gained several gigabytes, which is the answer to a disk-space question that otherwise looks like it has nothing to do with Plantoir.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant, and the reason it failed
mustRecord.why: Same reasoning as 'settings could not be saved': recording only the successes hides exactly the case worth seeing. A captive portal answers 200 with something that is not a model, so the failure here is a wrong-size file rather than a network error, and that sentence is worth having verbatim.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant, and how much space it freed
mustRecord.why: Removing one is allowed even when it is the one in use - the next time the assistant is opened it offers to download it again. Without this line that re-download looks like the app losing a file on its own, which is a report about a bug that is not there.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant
mustRecord.why: A start with no ending line reads as a stall, and a stall is what somebody would go looking for. Recording the stop is what makes the absence of a stop mean something - it turns 'started, nothing after' from ambiguous into a genuine finding.

mustRecord.carries: whether the assistant now asks before changing anything
mustRecord.why: Turning off the confirmation step changes what every later request DOES - it goes straight through instead of stopping for a button. A report that says 'it just did it without asking' is explained entirely by this line, and without it the behaviour looks like a bug in the gate rather than a setting somebody chose.

mustRecord.carries: which course, the section when the repair is about one, and what was put back — "put the front page back"
mustRecord.why: A different event from finding the problem, deliberately: one records that something is wrong, the other that somebody acted on it, and a trail that could not tell them apart leaves "did they ever fix it?" unanswerable. Only the two genuinely repairable cases can produce it — a missing Media folder and a missing section front page.

mustRecord.carries: which course and section, and what was in the way — never anything from inside it. The one line written today is "found a folder called index.md where the front page belongs, and left it alone"
mustRecord.why: A repair the teacher ASKED for that did not happen. Without it the trail shows the problem being found and then nothing at all, which reads exactly like a teacher who never pressed the button — and the thing in the way is a folder they will very likely have moved or deleted by the time they report it, so it cannot be looked for afterwards. Named for the OUTCOME rather than for its one cause: today only the "a folder is sitting where the front page belongs" refusal writes it, and a repair that simply failed (a read-only volume, a permissions problem) still records nothing. That gap is deliberate rather than forgotten, and this is the line it joins when it is closed, without a rename on either platform. See siteHealth.repair.refusedWhenSomethingIsInTheWay.

mustRecord.carries: which course and section, and WHICH of the two things stopped the copy — the page it would have become still held a lesson, or the copy could not be made certainly hidden — in both cases saying that other classes may already have moved. NOT the titles of either page: the assistant's own "assistant chose a tool" leaves argument values out for the same reason, and the line answers the report without them. Two lines share the event on purpose; see why
mustRecord.why: Duplicating a class makes the room for the copy FIRST — every later class renamed and re-dated — and only then discovers that the page the copy was meant to become is still somebody's real lesson. The copy is refused rather than written over it, so the teacher sees their classes move and no new page appear. "I duplicated a class, my classes moved, and nothing was copied" is then a report nothing else on the trail can answer: the tool that ran is recorded and its conclusion is not. The OTHER refusals on that path deliberately record nothing — a page that is not there, a page with no numbers in its name, a timetable with no class dates left — because they answer before anything has been touched, so there is nothing to explain afterwards. Named for the outcome rather than for today's single cause, the way "folder problem not repaired" is: a second reason a copy is not made joins this line instead of earning a rename on both platforms.

mustRecord.carries: which course and section, and the file name of the copy it was put back from — never a page
mustRecord.why: A teacher put a section back to how it was when an assistant conversation started ("Restore Section N…"). The one line that explains a section whose pages are older than the conversation that changed them: without it the trail shows the changes and then nothing, which reads as a teacher who never pressed the button. Windows recorded it first and proposed it on 2026-09-07 as appliesOn: ["windows"], because the mac had the same button and wrote nothing; the mac adopted it the same day and the appliesOn is gone, so it is pinned on both sides now. One gap is deliberate rather than forgotten, and is the same on both platforms: a restore that fails PART WAY (a permissions problem, a full disk) has already emptied the section folder, so the section is damaged, the teacher is told "Nothing was put back" — which is not true — and no line is written. Recording a restore there would be worse, since the restore did not happen; what is missing is a THIRD outcome both apps lack, and until one exists the trail is silent about the one case where its silence misleads.

mustRecord.carries: which course and section, how many pages shared by every section were given a date and a published-or-hidden setting for the new section, and how many of those were kept hidden because the setting they would copy cannot be read - its value runs onto the next line, it is not complete on its own line, or it is a legacy draft value the reader cannot tell - never which pages
mustRecord.why: Adding a section writes into pages the teacher never opened: every course-level page with per-section keys gains a pair for the new section, copied from the lowest existing one. When that went wrong it went wrong silently - a page hidden in section 1, fenced in a way the old finder missed, was PUBLISHED in the new section (GitHub #175) - and until then the trail had no line about a section being added at all, so 'why is this page showing in section 2?' had nowhere to start.

mustRecord.carries: which course and section, and a sentence naming what happened with the stable check NAME in brackets — 'found a problem with this course’s folders (curriculumCoverageFoundNothing)'. Never the product wording, which changes, and never anything written on a page
mustRecord.why: A teacher who reports 'it stopped showing my curriculum map last month' leaves nothing to look at otherwise: the finding is printed into a build console that is gone by then, and the condition itself is invisible on disk — a renamed folder looks exactly like a folder that was always called that. Recording the check NAME rather than the sentence is deliberate: the sentence is product wording and will be reworded, while the name is what a person searching the trail six months later can match against the contract. A scheduled publish's findings are recorded too, dated to the RUN rather than to when somebody next opened the section - or a problem found at half six is filed under the morning somebody looked, and a teacher who never opens that section gets no line at all (the reasoning of scheduledPublishStopped.trail; #153). Who writes it is platform-local: the mac's scheduled run is Plantoir itself and writes the line at the end of the run, from its own log; Windows writes it when the app reads the run's record, dated to that record's write time. Since #246 it also covers a PAGE whose settings the build could not read (pageSettingsUnreadable), not only a folder: the name is kept because the event is the site-health family and renaming it would cost both platforms, and the line still carries the check's name only - never which pages, which are the teacher's own names.

mustRecord.carries: which section, and which destinations it was published to
mustRecord.why: Why a section stopped saying " — Edited". The marker is DERIVED - its presence and its absence look identical on disk - so a teacher reporting 'it still says Edited after I published' leaves nothing to look at without this line. It is also the only record that a publish succeeded at EVERY destination rather than merely at one.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the scope ('shared' or 'per-section'), and the item name
mustRecord.why: A teacher removed a folder or file in Course Settings, excluding it from previews and deploys. Without this line, 'why is my folder not showing on the site' cannot be answered from the trail alone.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the scope ('shared' or 'per-section'), and the item name
mustRecord.why: A teacher added back a previously excluded folder or file in Course Settings, returning it to previews and deploys.

mustRecord.carries: the item name, which list it is in, and the reason sentence the teacher was shown (a specialNames sentence, never page content)
mustRecord.why: A teacher tried to remove or untick a folder or file a feature depends on (Course Settings or the New Course Wizard) and was shown why it cannot go. 'I could not remove the folder' is a report support will receive; the line says which rule refused.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the old folder name, the new one, which list it was in, and how many folders on disk were moved
mustRecord.why: A rename leaves nothing behind to look at: a folder called 'Class Pages' is indistinguishable from one that was always called that, and every key that named the old one has been rewritten. Without this line, 'when did this course stop having a Tasks folder?' — the first question asked when a curriculum map goes wrong — has no answer at all. The folder NAME is recorded; nothing from inside the folder ever is.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the old word and the new one, how many class pages were renamed, how many links were updated, and the backup's file name — never anything from inside a page
mustRecord.why: Afterwards a course whose pages say 'Module 2, Day 3' looks exactly like one that always did, and every link has been rewritten to match. 'When did these pages stop being Units?' — the first question when the next-class button or the curriculum map starts counting the wrong pages — has no other answer. The same event records a rename that stopped part way (how many pages had moved, and why it stopped) and one whose pages moved but whose settings could not be written, because those are the two states somebody will be asked to explain.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the folder name, and which list it was added to
mustRecord.why: Adding a name in Course Settings now creates the folder on disk, so a folder appears in the teacher's vault that they did not make in Obsidian. Separate from the rename because it answers a different question, and unexplained new folders are exactly what a teacher reports as 'Plantoir did something to my notes'.

mustRecord.carries: the service's name and the folder path, redacted — recorded by a WINDOW only, never by the assistant's or the MCP server's own reading of a folder, since those show nothing
mustRecord.why: The working folder just opened is kept in sync by a cloud service and the teacher had not yet been told about THIS folder. The effects of a synced folder — a slow build, a rename that takes minutes, a move that failed once — arrive weeks later as unrelated reports, and this one line is what connects them. See cloudSyncedFolders.

mustRecord.carries: whether it was the picker's choice or the window's notice, and the service's name
mustRecord.why: The teacher read the note and went ahead. Separate from 'synced folder noticed' because it is a different fact: one says Plantoir saw it, the other says the teacher did — and 'nobody warned me' is answered by the second, not the first.

mustRecord.carries: the course code. Or, written by a launcher, that a second copy of the working folder's workspace and built websites, left under another spelling of the folder's name, was cleared away - with the course and section the launcher was run for, or the word setup (GitHub #189, launcherLineWhenASecondCopyIsClearedAway)
mustRecord.event: built site moved out of the working folder
mustRecord.line: moved {course}'s built website out of the working folder, so it is no longer copied, synced or backed up with the course
mustRecord.launcherLineWhenASecondCopyIsClearedAway: {course}/{section} · cleared away {what}, left under another spelling of its name

GitHub #189. Written by setup.sh, preview.sh and deploy.sh alike, from the function they share in the PREVIEW PORT BLOCK, when buildOutputLocation.aSecondSpellingIsClearedAway removed something — a stopped workspace, a builds folder, or both; {what} is buildOutputLocation.aSecondSpellingIsClearedAway.whatWasCleared for whichever it was. Filed under THIS event rather than a new one, as #280 filed its launcher line: the app never writes it (the Swift sweeps nothing), a new event would need an app call site that does not exist, and it is the same subject — where a folder's built websites are kept, changed once, by the launchers, and visible to a teacher as a folder that got smaller. {course}/{section} is the literal word setup when setup.sh does it. Never a path: the folder is the one the line is filed from. scripts/test_folder_spelling.py checks the launchers against this field.
mustRecord.lineWhy: The one line in this list whose WORDS are pinned, because it has two authors: the app writes it when a folder is opened, and the launchers write it when the move is done by a build at the command line or by a publish launchd ran overnight. A sentence typed in two places is a sentence that stops matching, and a trail whose lines differ by who wrote them is one nobody can search.
mustRecord.why: A one-off change a teacher can SEE. Their working folder suddenly weighs much less, a folder they may have looked at in Finder is a shortcut afterwards, and a folder they sync stops uploading builds. Each of those arrives separately — 'where has my website gone?', 'did something delete my files?', 'why did my folder shrink?' — and this line, dated and per course, answers all three. Recorded ONCE per course, at the moment the move happens, and never again: a line on every launch would say nothing and bury the one that does.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: Windows has always built into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Plantoir\builds\<id> (PLANTOIR_BUILD_ROOT, row 290), so there is nothing to move there and no moment to record. If Windows ever migrates a folder that predates that, the event is here to use.

mustRecord.carries: which course and section, and HOW MANY website-builder processes were ended
mustRecord.why: The count is the point. Stopping a preview, closing a window or cancelling a publish asks the launcher to end whatever that section still has running, and nothing else on the trail can tell “there was nothing left to stop” from “a build was still going and was ended” — which are the two competing explanations when a teacher reports that their publish stopped halfway. Recorded from 2026-09-05, when the sweep began ending a mid-flight BUILD and its driver rather than only a preview server: that is a change in what a teacher can lose, and it had no line describing it. The launcher prints the number and the app used to discard it.

mustRecord.carries: which course and section, how long the preview had been saying nothing, and WHICH of the THREE things was true - the website builder was serving the site and this Mac could not reach it, nothing was serving it at all, or the builder could not be asked and Plantoir does not know. Or, with no silence waited out and nobody asked, that its website started and no address for it was ever announced, so there was nothing to open (GitHub #235 - the line that replaced trying a guessed address). Or, written by a launcher before anything was built, that every address Plantoir can use for a preview was taken, so no workspace could be made for the folder - with the course and section when the launcher has them (preview and publish) and the word setup when it does not (GitHub #280, launcherLineWhenEveryAddressIsTaken). Or, written by preview.sh before anything was built, that this Mac could not reach the website builder, so the preview was stopped rather than built into an address nobody could open (GitHub #234, launcherLineWhenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder)
mustRecord.launcherLine: {course}/{section} · the preview stopped before building — Plantoir could not find out where it would be
mustRecord.launcherLineWhenEveryAddressIsTaken: {course}/{section} · stopped before starting — every address Plantoir can use for a preview was taken
mustRecord.launcherLineWhenEveryAddressIsTakenWhy: GitHub #280. Written by setup.sh, preview.sh and deploy.sh alike, from the one function they share (the PREVIEW PORT BLOCK), when all forty blocks in contracts/app-rules.json -> previewPorts are taken; the console says previewPorts.whenNoBlockIsFree.sentence. Filed under THIS event rather than a new one by the director's ruling: it is the same outcome for a teacher - a preview (or a publish) that never appeared - and a new event would be one more name for Windows to implement with nothing new to say. {course}/{section} is the literal word setup when setup.sh makes the workspace, because it has no course yet. A walk that FOUND a block beyond the first six writes nothing: the announced address already carries the port. scripts/test_port_blocks.py checks the launchers against this field.
mustRecord.launcherLineWhenThisMacCannotReachTheBui: {course}/{section} · the preview stopped before building — this Mac could not reach the website builder

GitHub #234. Written by preview.sh alone, before the build, when a connection to the address it was about to announce is refused on every try (contracts/app-rules.json -> previewPorts.whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder); the console says that key's sentence. The same fault #225's thisMacCannotReachIt names after a build, found two minutes sooner, so it is filed under THIS event, like #280's line, rather than a new one. It names no port (a review asked for 'address' over 'port', and the port is in the console transcript already; the sibling lines name none). A preview that reached the builder on a later try writes nothing here - the console says how many tries it took. scripts/test_preview_reach.py checks the launcher against this field.
mustRecord.launcherLineWhy: GitHub #235's review. The ending a teacher will actually meet when no address can be found is preview.sh's refusal (it asks for the published port twice and stops before building), not the app's no-address stop, which is a defence that is practically unreachable while the two ship together. Without its own line the trail said only that preview.sh failed. Written by the launcher through note_on_the_trail, with the course/section prefix the app's own lines for this event carry, so one search finds both; the words are pinned here because the app never writes this one and scripts/test_preview_address.py checks the launcher against this field.
mustRecord.why: The failure that left NOTHING behind, which is exactly the report that arrived on 2026-09-19 (GitHub issue #225). A teacher pressed Preview three times in four minutes on a Mac that had stopped passing new addresses through from the builder; the website was built and served every time and never appeared; and the trail recorded only that a task started and was stopped on purpose - so an evening of a broken Mac reads, months later, as somebody changing their mind three times. WHICH of them it was is the whole value of the line, because the first two are one sentence apart when a teacher describes it ("the preview never came up") and a world apart in what to do: one is their pages, one is their Mac. The seconds are recorded rather than the total run because the run is not the fault - a first preview legitimately takes minutes, and what cannot be explained is a run that announced its server and then said nothing. DELIBERATELY WITHOUT `appliesOn`, and the red Windows suite that follows is the request rather than damage: Windows has its own wait for a preview to appear and owes the same line, so this is an obligation and not a permanent platform difference - the two cases appliesOn exists for. The `windows` issue opened with this work says so, and the choice on that side is theirs: record it, or hold it open by name in NamedGapLedger with the issue and milestone that own it. What Windows is NOT exposed to is the CAUSE - there is no container in their preview path, so the question this line's second half answers (can the builder see its own site?) has no counterpart there and they should not build one. What they owe is the bounded quiet time and the line.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the section number, and — when there was a website to move away from — where last year's details were kept
mustRecord.why: A rollover that cuts a section loose is the moment its published address changes, and nothing else on the trail records it. The same act turns off any publish that was set to happen on its own — a section with no agreed website and a scheduled run with nobody to ask would otherwise create a website nobody named — so a teacher whose overnight publish stops happening has one line explaining both.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the section number, and where it published
mustRecord.why: The positive case, and it is here for the same reason the two failures are, read the other way round: a scheduled publish that leaves NO trace cannot be told from one that never happened. Without this line the trail can answer “why did my site not update?” and cannot answer “did it?” — and a teacher wondering whether last night's publish went out has nowhere to look. Added 2026-09-09 on Russell's instruction, after a real scheduled run showed the failures recorded and the successes silent.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: Owed on both platforms for the same reason as the other two, and RECORDED on both as of 2026-09-09: the mac when Russell asked for it, Windows the same day (GitHub issue #130). This said "Windows records neither today" until that landed; nothing reads appliesOnWhy, so only a reader would have been misled, which is the quiet way a contract stops being true. scheduledPublishStopped.platformDifferences is where the two are compared.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the section number, and which destination stopped — or, when the BUILD failed before any destination was reached, that the pages could not be built, because no destination was (widened 2026-09-25, #137)
mustRecord.why: The same silence as “needed an answer”, from a different cause — a revoked token, a network that was down, a build that failed. It is a SEPARATE event because the other one's own wording says a question went unasked, and filing a revoked token under it would make the trail say something untrue about the one run a teacher is trying to understand. Both matter for the same reason: a scheduled publish that did not happen is invisible unless something writes it down.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: Added on the mac 2026-09-09, when Russell widened the readout to ANY failed scheduled publish rather than only an unanswered question, and adopted by Windows the same day (GitHub issue #130) — so nothing is owed and neither suite is red on this list. The earlier wording said Windows records only the question case and that its suite was red until it caught up; that was true for about six hours and is kept here only as the reason this sentence changed.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the section number, and which destination stopped — or, when the BUILD stopped for a question, that it stopped before any destination was reached, because none was
mustRecord.why: The one thing that can happen to a scheduled publish that a teacher will otherwise never find out about. It runs at half six with the app closed, so a question it could not ask is asked of nobody and seen by nobody; before --non-interactive it either waited for ever (measured at 45 minutes) or took a default and published the site to an address nobody chose. The trail is where "my site did not update on Tuesday and I do not know why" gets answered, and without this line the run is indistinguishable from one that was never scheduled. The DESTINATION is carried because a course can publish to several and only one of them may have needed anything — "it published to the folder and not to Netlify" is the shape of the report. Dated to when the RUN wrote its record, never to when the app read it, or an overnight problem is filed under the wrong night. Never the question's TEXT: that comes from a launcher's console, and a line naming a credential prompt would put a teacher's own words on the trail.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: DELIBERATELY not scoped to one platform. The mac's launchd wrapper has the identical problem and the identical fix available — deploy.sh takes --non-interactive as of the same change — so this is owed on both. Proposed from Windows 2026-09-08; GitHub issue #126 carries what the mac owes and why.

mustRecord.carries: the course code and the section number
mustRecord.why: The OTHER answer, and the one a problem report is more likely to be about: a teacher writing in weeks later to say last year's class site was replaced is describing this branch. A trail recording only the cut-loose could not answer the question it would actually be read for. Both answers are recorded because the question is asked every time and neither answer is a default.

mustRecord.carries: the working folder's NAME - never its path - and which of the two occasions it was; or, for the setup shared by every folder, nothing but the fact that it stopped
mustRecord.why: Until 2026-09-19 this never happened. The app asked for it at every quit and asked programs it had never told itself where to find, with the answer sent to the null device: a fault that reported nothing, and a teacher whose Mac stayed slow all day had nothing to show anybody (issue #220). The line is what turns 'quitting does not seem to free anything' from a feeling into a report. Written by the detached script rather than by the app, because the app is gone before the answer is known - the same arrangement the launchers already use for their own trail lines. TWO occasions file here and the event name says neither, on purpose: quitting, and the last window on a folder closing. They are the same act on the same builder under the same conditions, and the SENTENCE says which one it was; an event called "...at quit" would be a lie on every window close, which is the commoner of the two. A builder that was not running at all records NOTHING - a line every time saying there was nothing to stop would bury the one time something happened.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: PERMANENT and deliberate, which is what appliesOn is for - the same case as "built site moved out of the working folder" above, and NOT the softening that contracts/README.md rejects. Windows ships a native toolchain: no image, no container, no virtual machine, nothing for the app to stop when it quits. Their FolderContainers.StopContainer and .ReleaseEverythingAtQuit both open with `if (Scripting.NativeRuntime.Directory is not null) return;`, and documentation/12-windows-app.md says the WSL2 engine path they guard "is gone; do not build toward it". An event cannot be recorded where the moment it describes does not exist. If that ever changes - a Windows build with no native runtime, falling back to WSL - drop the appliesOn rather than adding a windows twin.

mustRecord.carries: which folder was left alone and WHY - a publish or preview for that folder still going, this folder's own builder still running when the shared setup was asked about - whether it was left alone deliberately or refused to stop, or other software on this Mac sharing the same setup
mustRecord.why: The companion line, and the one support will read more often, because 'quitting did not free anything' is the report and this is the only thing that can answer it. Three different deliberate refusals file here. One: a publish or preview for that folder is still running, on the host or inside the builder, so stopping it would break work the teacher cannot see - a scheduled publish, an assistant working over a connection, a second window. Two: the shared setup was asked about and THIS teacher's own builder is the thing still in it, either because it was deliberately left alone or because it REFUSED to stop - both reach this line, because either way our container is in the emptiness check's answer - which must be said in those words, because a builder just left running is itself in the emptiness check's answer, and calling it "other software" on a Mac that has no other software in there would be false every time. Three: other software on this Mac genuinely does share the same setup, which is never stopped out from under anybody. Without the line, a deliberate refusal is indistinguishable from the fault it replaced.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: Permanent for the same reason as its companion above: a native Windows toolchain has no builder to leave running and no shared machine to leave alone.

mustRecord.carries: that nothing was stopped, and which of the FOUR ways it failed - the programs could not be found, the shared setup could not be asked what was running in it, the stop was asked for and refused, or the whole attempt ran out of time
mustRecord.event: website builder could not be stopped
mustRecord.why: Issue #220 was a fault that REPORTED NOTHING: the quit path could not find the programs it needed, exited 0, and left no evidence anywhere. This is the line that makes the same failure visible the next time it happens rather than a year later. The two that matter most are the ones that would otherwise be written down as SUCCESSES: a `stop` that was asked for and refused looks identical to one that worked unless somebody checks the answer, and an attempt killed at its own deadline says nothing at all unless the deadline writes a line before it fires. Deliberately SEPARATE from 'website builder left running': that one says a choice was made and names it, and a choice nobody was able to make is a different fact - filing them together would make the trail say a refusal was deliberate when nothing was refused at all.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: Permanent for the same reason as the two above: there is no stop to fail where there is nothing to stop.

mustRecord.carries: what was under way - a publish, or since issue #232 a preview being built - in the words the teacher was shown, and which of the two buttons they pressed
mustRecord.event: quit asked about work under way
mustRecord.why: BOTH answers are recorded, and 'keep working' is the one that matters most: a teacher who says 'I pressed Quit and it would not quit' is describing that branch and nothing else would explain it. Since issue #232 the line also names a preview being BUILT when that is what was under way (a publish, when there is one, is still what is named), so 'it would not quit while my preview was loading' has the same answer on the trail. The other branch explains a publish that stopped part way with no error anywhere - the teacher was told and went ahead, which is a completely different report from a publish that died on its own. Never asked, and so never recorded, when the Mac is logging out, restarting or shutting down: a question put up there holds up the whole log out.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: NOT permanent, and this one is an acknowledged exception rather than the ordinary use - read contracts/README.md's "Four ways out" passage, which rejects exactly this move, and its Named gaps section, which records why it was taken here anyway. Windows could ask the same question: it has publishes and it has a quit. The honest alternative reddens their ContractTests with a failure only they can mend (a NamedGapLedger entry is theirs to write), on a release where nobody is on that side. The cost is real and is stated rather than hidden: appliesOn has NO mend-check, so the day Windows implements this, nothing anywhere goes red to say the contract is now lying. What points at it instead is this sentence, the README's Named-gaps entry, and the windows issue that carries the work. Adopt the rule (quittingWhileWorkIsUnderWay, below) and this line together, or neither - a line saying a teacher was asked, in an app that asks nothing, would be worse than no line - and delete both appliesOn keys when you do.

mustRecord.carries: the course, the section, and WHY - which of the things that turn one off without being asked did it; for a replacement that failed (since issue #195), when the deploy that was lost had been set for
mustRecord.why: A deploy the teacher set to happen on its own was turned off by something other than them asking for it: the course was removed, the section was removed, the day it was set for had gone by, or - since issue #195 - a new deploy for the same section was set in its place and macOS then refused it - or, since #156, another program was still building the course after a publish set for later had waited ten minutes for it (the old one is booted out and its plist overwritten before macOS is asked, so that refusal leaves neither, and the refusal the teacher reads speaks only of the new one). A failed WRITE is NOT one of these: the old plist is still on disk, it is handed back to macOS, and 'scheduled deploy could not be set' says it still stands. Without this line a teacher whose site stopped updating has nothing anywhere explaining it - the alarm simply is not there any more, which reads exactly like one that was never set, and that is the same silence 'scheduled publish needed an answer' exists to break, one step further back. ONE event with several reasons rather than one event each (three when it was written; a fourth since a course could be kept for reference; a fifth since issue #195, a replacement macOS refused): somebody reading the trail wants to know their overnight deploy was turned off and by what, and the difference between two ways of removing something means nothing to them. It says DEPLOY where its three neighbours say publish, because a site is deployed and a page is published (Russell, 2026-09-20); the shipped names are left alone rather than renamed here, since a NEW name carrying the old vocabulary is the expensive mistake - this list pins it on both platforms. NOT written by the teacher's own Cancel item, nor by the assistant's cancel_scheduled_deploy: those are the teacher asking, and the trail already carries what they asked for. No appliesOn, deliberately - Windows cancels on removing a SECTION and not on removing a COURSE (Plantoir.Core/Models/CourseArchiver.cs), so two of the three reasons are theirs whatever they decide about the third.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the section number, when the deploy that was replaced had been set for, and when the new one is set for
mustRecord.why: Scheduling a section that already has a scheduled deploy removes the old one - deliberately, since a section has one per Mac - and until issue #195 (2026-09-23) nothing said so, before or after. The old job leaves nothing behind once it is replaced, so a teacher who set Friday and then Saturday and asks why it went on Saturday has no answer anywhere unless this line exists. The approval card and the schedule sheet now say it BEFORE anything is written (wording.scheduleReplaces); this is the record AFTERWARDS. Written where the replacement happens, in the one function every way of scheduling reaches, so it cannot be missing from one of them. Not written when the old deploy was set for the same minute, or had already gone by: neither is a promise being broken. The old deploy may belong to ANOTHER working folder, because a section's scheduled deploy is one per Mac, and that is the case this line matters most for.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the section number, the moment asked for, and - when the section already had a scheduled deploy - whether that one still stands
mustRecord.event: scheduled deploy could not be set
mustRecord.why: Added 2026-09-24 with issue #195's fix review. 'I set it for Friday and it never went' is otherwise answered only by the refusal that was on screen at the time, which nobody quotes a week later. The two ways it fails leave DIFFERENT things behind, and the line has to say which: when the new deploy's files could not be WRITTEN, the old deploy's plist is still on disk (the failed write is atomic and everything before it writes elsewhere), so it is handed back to macOS and the line says it still stands - saying 'turned off' there would be false, because the old job would still fire; when macOS REFUSED the new one after its plist was written, the old one's plist has been overwritten, so it is gone, and 'scheduled deploy turned off' says so beside this line - including when the old one was set for the same minute, which the card rightly leaves unsaid but whose loss is still a loss.

mustRecord.carries: the folder it was given, the code and school year it shows, how many sections came across, and which course it was copied from - and, only when the copy was made without any (#255), the Obsidian add-ons left behind by FOLDER name, or that the add-ons folder or the settings folder was a link or could not be read, or that Obsidian Publish's site setting stayed behind (referenceCourses.obsidianAddOns). A course with none leaves a line byte-identical to before. Never anything read from inside an add-on
mustRecord.why: A reference course is a course that appeared in the sidebar without the teacher creating one, and which can never be deployed. Without this line a report of 'where did ICS3U-2025 come from' or 'why will this one not publish' has nothing anywhere behind it. It names the FOLDER and the displayed code separately because they deliberately differ, and that difference is the first thing somebody reading a report will want to check. The source path never appears raw - a course is named, not a path - and the contents of a page never appear at all. A copy that was NOT made writes 'course could not be kept for reference' instead (#287), never both.

mustRecord.carries: which course it was copied from, the folder it was to be given, and why - being made in another window or another copy of Plantoir (#245), a folder of that name already there, or the copy could not be made (the system's reason, which may name a file; never a page's contents). The reason is the sentence the sheet showed the teacher
mustRecord.event: course could not be kept for reference
mustRecord.why: Added 2026-09-25 for issue #287. Keep a Copy for Reference is a button a teacher pressed and saw refused, and until then no failure of it wrote anything: the trail showed nothing had happened, so 'it said no' had nothing behind it. Written once, around the whole act, so a way to fail added later is covered without anyone remembering. Its OWN event rather than 'course could not be imported for reference', because nothing was imported and that line names a source folder this act does not have - a failure line carrying the other act's name misleads whoever reads it back. Not written for the sheet's own refusals of a name or a school year: those grey the Keep a Copy button out with a sentence, and a disabled button is not a press.

mustRecord.carries: the code the teacher reads, the folder it lives in, and the school year before and after
mustRecord.why: The ONE thing a frozen course still lets a teacher change, so rule 5 applies to it like any other feature. It names both the code and the folder because those two deliberately differ on a reference course, and a report saying 'ICS3U moved' would not say WHICH of the three ICS3Us on the shelf did. Not written when the sheet is cancelled, and not written when the write fails - the teacher is told about that in a sentence of its own.

mustRecord.carries: the course, how many pages had to be locked again, and how many would not stay locked
mustRecord.why: Written ONLY when a pass actually did something, so a folder in a steady state leaves no lines at all. It is the answer to the one report this feature can produce that would otherwise be unexplainable: 'my reference course let me edit a page'. A count of 37 after a restore is a backup coming back unlocked, because a zip carries the mode and not the flag; a handful that would not stay locked, over and over, is usually a folder kept in a cloud drive whose file provider clears the locked bit while a file uploads - but the LINE says only the count, deliberately, because a volume with no support for the flag at all produces the same count and naming a cause would be a confident wrong diagnosis. Neither is a failure to put in front of the teacher, and neither is retried after a delay - the next pass is the mechanism.

mustRecord.carries: the NAME of the folder it was read from, the folder it was given here, the code and school year it shows, and how many sections came across - and, for a course in the MODERN layout only and only when there were any (#255), the Obsidian add-ons left behind by FOLDER name (or that a folder was a link, could not be read, or Obsidian Publish's site setting stayed behind). The two older layouts say theirs on their own second line, so this line adds nothing for them; a course with none leaves a line byte-identical to before. Never anything read from inside an add-on
mustRecord.why: The folder it was READ from is the half a copy does not have, and it is the answer to 'where did this ICS4U come from' - a folder somewhere else on this Mac, which the teacher may have moved or deleted since. Named rather than written as a path, the same way every other line here names a course rather than a path. The contents of a page never appear.

mustRecord.carries: the class folder's NAME, the folder it was given here, the shared folder its pages and pictures came from and HOW that folder was found (by its name, chosen by hand, or none), how many of the shared folders and pages the class used were brought across out of how many and the names of any that are missing, how many of the class's links the shared folder's real entries REPLACED, how many things were left out as a LOSS with each one's path (a link below the top or inside a shared entry, a name the course uses for itself), how many Obsidian add-on entries were left behind, and whether an empty Media folder was made - names and paths only, never what is written on a page
mustRecord.event: course imported from the older layout
mustRecord.why: Written right after 'course imported for reference' for a class kept in the older folder-per-class layout (#254). The shared pictures of such a course come from a SECOND folder, found by its name or chosen by hand, and a class whose shared folder was not found still imports - so 'where are this course's pictures' is the question a report about one will ask, and only this line answers it. Names only; never what is written on a page, and never anything read from the add-ons that were left out.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: PERMANENT and deliberate - the ordinary use of appliesOn, not the softening contracts/README.md rejects. Russell decided on 2026-09-25 (GitHub issue #257) that the Windows app does not get the import of the 2023-24 folder-per-class layout: only he kept courses that way, and only on a Mac. An event cannot be recorded where the import it describes does not exist. If Windows ever builds that import, drop this appliesOn rather than adding a windows twin.

mustRecord.carries: where the pages were read from (a path from the home folder, redacted on the way in) and the Finder shortcut's name when one was followed, the section and HOW it was told (its front page's link text, its folder's name, or being the only one) with any disagreement between the front page and the name, the course pages folder the files came from (source-<code>) and how many files, the word its class pages use and how many placeholder pages (Thread 2, Day x) were set aside, then as TWO separate clauses what was LEFT BEHIND by kind with counts - the website's own program files, the folders skipped without being looked inside, the links replaced by what they showed, the editing folders and the other sections by name, anything in the course pages folder no link showed, the Obsidian add-on entries - and what was LOST, by name (a link that showed somewhere unexpected also says where it pointed, from the home folder), or 'nothing lost'; and whether an empty Media folder was made
mustRecord.event: course imported from a class website folder
mustRecord.why: Written right after 'course imported for reference' for a class kept in the 2024-25 layout, a whole website folder per class (#256). S1's and S2's copies of the pages DIFFER (335 entries, measured), so 'which copy did this come from, and what did not come' is a real question about one of these, and only this line answers it; left behind and lost are separate clauses so machinery is never read as a loss or a loss as machinery. Names and counts only, never what is written on a page.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: PERMANENT and deliberate, for the same reason as the event above: Russell decided on 2026-09-25 (GitHub issue #258) that the Windows app does not get the import of the 2024-25 layout, a whole website folder per class. That issue stays open for the OTHER half, which Windows owes regardless and which this does not excuse: Copy a Page strips the old section-2 keys (the Copy a Page rule in this file, from #256). If Windows ever builds this import, drop this appliesOn rather than adding a windows twin.

mustRecord.carries: which course did not come across, and why, as the sentence the summary showed - already kept for reference under that school year (the shelf rule, which also refuses a second course of the same code in one run) or a folder of that name already there (both #287), already being imported in another window or another copy of Plantoir (#245), what an earlier unfinished attempt left behind could not be cleared away (#245), could not be read, no room on the disk. Written for EVERY course the summary lists as not imported - refused before it starts or failed part way; never for a course the teacher stopped
mustRecord.event: course could not be imported for reference
mustRecord.why: Written per COURSE, because a run of four that imports three is the ordinary shape of this and 'the import failed' is exactly the report that cannot be looked into. Without it, a teacher who ticked four courses and found three has nothing to point at, and the one that is missing is the one they will ask about.

mustRecord.carries: which course an unfinished import was going to be
mustRecord.event: unfinished import for reference tidied away
mustRecord.why: A reference course is built under a hidden name and renamed into place last, so an import the app never finished leaves a folder nothing can see - and therefore nothing would ever remove. This is the line that says the disk space came back, and the answer to 'my import did not finish and now there is no trace of it'.

mustRecord.carries: the course the pages came FROM by its folder name, the course and folder they landed in, how many pages and pictures were created, reused, brought in under a new name and left alone, how many could not be removed and must not be deployed, and the backup's file name
mustRecord.why: A page appearing in a course a teacher did not write it in has no explanation anywhere else: on disk a copied page looks exactly like one they typed, and 'where did this come from?' is a question nothing else in this trail could answer. One line at the END of a copy, in every outcome - a copy that stopped part way says so in the same line, because the counts already show it. NEVER a page's title and never anything from inside one, the line classCopyNotMade's own entry draws for the same kind of act.

mustRecord.carries: the course that was in hand and was not kept, and the name of the folder it was coming from
mustRecord.why: Its own event rather than a failure: a teacher who presses Stop chose to, and a line calling that a failure is a line that misleads whoever reads it back. It is also what explains a folder that is NOT there - the course in hand is removed on the way out, so without this line the trail shows an import that started and nothing about how it ended.

mustRecord.carries: the course and section that was built, how many of the teacher's pages the build rewrote, and their NAMES - their place in the course folder, never anything written on them
mustRecord.why: From 2026-09-25 every preview and every publish can REWRITE the teacher's own pages: the front page takes the date of the class it shows, and a page a class links to directly takes the date of the earliest visible class that links to it (class-planning.json -> sectionIndexPointer.dateCases and datingPagesAClassBrings.atBuildTime). A change to a teacher's files that nobody asked for in so many words is exactly what a trail exists to answer - 'why did the date on this page change?' - and the build's console, where it is also said, is gone by the time anyone asks. Recorded from the build's own PLANTOIR_DATED: line (pagesDatedByTheBuild), which says nothing when nothing was rewritten, so a build whose dates were already right leaves no line. A SCHEDULED publish records it too, from that run's own part of its log once the run is done: it is often the first build after a class goes visible, so the one likeliest to rewrite files, and nobody is watching a console then.

mustRecord.carries: the course code or codes, how many were deleted, what they took together when every size is known (the LOGICAL size), each deleted file's NAME - a course code, a moment and who made it, never anything written on a page - and, when some were asked for and kept, which ones the open assistant conversation could still restore from, and how many could not be deleted
mustRecord.why: A teacher's own backups are never pruned (Russell's decision on #242, 2026-09-21: keep every backup a teacher makes, and make the space visible), so a backup that has gone was deleted by a person - and 'my backup is gone' is answered by this line and nothing else. Until #242 there was no line for deleting a backup at all, one or many. The file NAMES are recorded rather than only a count (the #242 plan review's L2): a name is a course code, a timestamp and a maker, carries no content, and answers 'which one' exactly - the same reason 'section restored from the start of an assistant conversation' records its backup's file name. Written by the single delete and the delete-several alike, because the single one is the one-item case of the same function. One line per delete, and none when nothing was deleted. No appliesOn: Windows lists backups too and owes the same line - the red suite that follows is the request, said so in the windows issue drafted from #242.

mustRecord.carries: the course, the section asked about, what was asked for (Preview, Deploy, the assistant's rebuild or deploy, an outside assistant's rebuild or deploy), what the other program holds (building, publishing or previewing) and its process id - never anything written on a page
mustRecord.why: Added with #156, when the mac began reading the work leases other programs write. The program in the way is invisible from where the teacher is: an outside assistant, another copy of Plantoir, a publish set for later. A teacher who reports 'Preview said somebody else was using it' can be answered only by the process id - on the lease file itself, and on this line; the window's own 'app opened' line names it too when the other program is a copy of the app, while the --mcp-stdio and scheduled processes write no opening line - and without a line at all a declined press reads exactly like a button that did nothing. Written by whichever program declined; the MCP process writes the same trail.

mustRecord.carries: the course, the section, how many seconds it waited, what the other program held and its process id, and whether it then went ahead or stood down
mustRecord.event: scheduled publish waited for the course
mustRecord.why: Added with #156. A publish set for later that finds another program building the course waits up to ten minutes (workLeases.declining.whyTheScheduledPublishWaits). A publish that went out ten minutes late, or not at all, looks from outside exactly like one that misfired; this line says it waited, for whom, and what it then did. A stand-down ALSO writes 'scheduled deploy turned off' (the job is cleared) and leaves the section's courseWasBusy record.

mustRecord.carries: the course and the section, and which of: told with a notification; not sent because notifications are turned off; not sent because permission was never given; could not be sent; and, when a teacher first schedules from the app, that the permission question was put and what the answer was. NEVER the notification's text.
mustRecord.why: Added with #212. 'I never got told' is answerable only if the trail says whether the notification went out, or that notifications were off for the app — from the teacher's side a notification that was blocked and one that was never sent look identical. The question's own line is written BEFORE the answer, because a question that is ignored, or arrives under a Focus, may never be answered. See scheduledPublishStopped.notification.

activityTrail.note: The breadcrumb trail: what the teacher was doing, in the order they did it, in ONE file. Task records answer 'what did that publish print'; they do not answer the question support opens with, which is 'what were you doing when it went wrong'. Two files each holding half a story force whoever reads them to interleave by timestamp in their head, and they will get it wrong - so the assistant's turns go in here too. The list below is the MINIMUM: an app may record more, but a missing event is a gap in both apps at once. Deliberately coarse - every line is something a teacher would recognise as an action they took, never a view redraw or a state change, because the failure mode of logging everything is that the one line that mattered is on page forty.

promptMarker.why: The teacher's own words go on their own line behind a fixed prefix, so leaving them out of a report is dropping lines by prefix rather than parsing anything. They are kept locally because a routing problem cannot be looked into without the sentence that caused it, and withheld from the report unless the teacher ticks the box, because their words are the one thing here unmistakably theirs to hand over.

activityTrail.rule: EVERY new feature, and every CHANGED behaviour, that a teacher can see leaves a line on this trail. Adding one means naming the event here and in both apps — not writing free text at a call site, and not deciding it is too small to bother with. The failure this prevents is the one already met in the field: a teacher builds a preview, opens the assistant, asks for a report, and is told there is nothing to report, because the two things they just did were not among the things anybody had thought to record. A feature that leaves no trace is a feature that can only be diagnosed by asking the teacher to do it again, which is the thing they came to you because they could not do.

assistantConfirmation.note: Whether the assistant describes what it is about to do and waits for a button, before anything that changes the built website.
assistantConfirmation.why: The local model is a router and routers are wrong sometimes. Showing what it understood before it acts turns a misroute from a thing that HAPPENS into a thing a teacher declines.

sameOnBothAssistants.why: The smaller assistant used to refuse to be turned off and was never told the setting existed, on the measured reasoning that one request in five going wrong is not a rate at which anybody should stop reading. That withheld a setting from exactly the machine where knowing about it matters most. The measured number is put in front of the teacher as a caution instead, which respects the measurement AND the person.

deployingAlwaysAsks.why: Deploying puts work in front of students and cannot be taken back by us, so it is gated separately and the setting does not reach it.

theImmediateDeployCardSaysItIsImmediate.why: Matched as a WHOLE WORD, case-folded, which is what mustContainIsAWholeWord says and why it is not left to each platform's `contains`: 'knows', 'known' and 'nowhere' would all satisfy a substring test, so a sentence that says nothing about time could keep this rule green. `value` being true is asserted rather than read as a switch - a rule turned off from the data is a rule that goes quiet without anybody deciding to turn it off. The two approval cards were asymmetric exactly where a misroute lands. The scheduled one names the whole moment; the immediate one named no time at all, so a teacher who asked for 6:30 tomorrow and was routed to an immediate deploy read a card that was perfectly true and said nothing to contradict them. Measured on 2026-09-18: the smaller assistant sent 'Deploy at 6:30 AM' to deploy_section 10 trials out of 10 and 3 of 3 in the app itself (research/ai-assist/metal-routing-results.txt, issue #168).
