The WORD is asserted, case-folded, and not the sentence: the sentence lives in wording.deployApproval, has been rewritten three times already and will be again, while the rule that an immediate deploy must say it is immediate should outlive every rewording. It helps every misroute of this shape, not only the one that was measured.

mentionedAfter.why: For DISCOVERABILITY, not to ask for trust: a switch nobody knows about might as well not exist. App-wide because the count used to reset with every conversation, so a teacher working in short bursts could accept a hundred plans and never be told. Once ever, because a suggestion declined is an answer and asking again is how a helpful mention becomes nagging.

aCancelDoesNotResetTheCount.why: The number measures how much of the assistant's work this teacher has READ, and a cancel is evidence of reading rather than evidence against it.

oneStoredAnswer.why: The switch in Settings and the gate in the conversation are the same value, read fresh each turn - the two windows are open at the same time, and a teacher who turns it off expects the next thing they ask to go straight through.

assistantModelChoice.note: Which assistant runs on a teacher's machine, and what they are allowed to do about it. Shared because these are rules with inputs and outputs, not pictures: the panel that holds them looks nothing alike on the two platforms and must BEHAVE identically. What is deliberately not here is the layout, the keyboard shortcut, and where the settings window lives - see documentation/10-local-ai-assistant.md.

automaticResolvesAtPointOfUse.why: The automatic choice is stored as an INTENT and resolved every time it is used, never resolved once and written into preferences. Storing the answer would mean a later change to the tier ladder reached every machine EXCEPT the ones whose teacher had opened Settings - so the people who engaged with the setting would get the stalest behaviour.

comfortFraction.why: A model is comfortable on a machine when its resident size is at most a third of physical memory. Not a new number: it is the line the automatic ladder has always been held to, which is why the automatic choice can never produce a caution and a test asserts that.

caution.appearsWhen: a hand-picked choice is not comfortable on this machine
mustName: the chosen assistant's memory while working
caution.why: A caution rather than a disabled row. A teacher who has just quit everything else knows something the operating system does not, and greying the option out with the reason beside it gives them no way to act on what they know. What they are owed is both numbers in one sentence, so the choice is informed rather than prevented.

removal.why: The refusal is about ANY open assistant, not about whether that window happens to use that rung: working out which file is genuinely mapped means tracking state neither app keeps, and getting it wrong deletes weights out from under a running engine. Removing the CHOSEN one is allowed on purpose - it is not a broken state, it is the state every machine is in before its first download, and refusing would trap a teacher who wants their disk space back behind a choice they did not want to change.

guidance.why: Two different decisions, and neither is guessable from the other: disk is what runs out on a small laptop, memory is what makes the machine feel slow while a class is being prepared and never appears as a number anywhere. On the mac the larger download is 2.2x the smaller but 2.9x the memory, because most of the difference is the conversation being held rather than the file being read. Derive both from the tier table; typing them into the interface guarantees they drift the first time a quant changes.

namesNoModel.why: Rule one, applied where it is hardest: the settings panel is the one screen genuinely ABOUT the model, so a name leaks in most naturally here. Sweep every label, detail, caution and summary the panel can produce against this list rather than spot-checking.

cases.why: The anchor is machinery and is cut.

cases.body: Compare two designs ^ and contrast them
cases.expect: Compare two designs ^ and contrast them
cases.why: Only a BARE word can be an anchor. Anything with a space after it is the teacher's own prose, and cutting there would lose wording.

expectationWording.note: What an expectation page SAYS: the body after the frontmatter, without the `^anchor` Obsidian puts on the end of a block.

cases.why: The normal case outside the example content — folders are rarely called plain 'Curriculum'.
Case-insensitive.
The FILE name is ignored — a lesson that mentions the word is not curriculum material.

isCurriculumPage.note: Matches `build_site.py`'s own rule exactly, and that is the point — the Python decides what ships, so an app that disagreed would report coverage for pages the site does not treat as curriculum. Any FOLDER segment containing 'curriculum', case-insensitive; the FILE name is ignored.

cases.why: Either case.
BC Applied Design competency code.
BC Content knowledge standard code.
A strand heading, not an expectation.
Whole-name match: anything after the code makes it not a code.
Must start with a letter.

isExpectationCode.note: A leaf expectation is coded like A1.1 or B2.3: one letter, digits, a dot, digits — the WHOLE name, not a prefix. Index and strand-heading pages sit in the same folder and must not be counted.

curriculumRules.note: What counts as a curriculum expectation. Written after checking the code rather than from memory: an expectation is not a code found in a page's TEXT, it is a PAGE named by a code inside a curriculum folder. A first draft of this contract asserted text-scanning and was wrong before it was ever run.

followingLinks.note: What publishing and unpublishing do to the pages a named page LINKS TO. The two verbs are not mirror images and each rule is written once. Shared because both apps sweep the same folders and a difference here silently changes what students can see.

publishing.why: Publishing a page whose links lead somewhere students cannot see is the one thing publishing must never do, so it always takes what it links to, and what those link to in turn. The plan names every page that will become visible, so a teacher agreeing to publish one class can see the four pages going with it. These three stay TRUE alongside stopsAtAClassPage below: the walk is still transitive and still takes what a page links to, it has ONE stop, and the plan names the classes it stopped at as well as the pages it took.

unpublishing.why: 'X still links to it' is a reason to keep a page published only when students can SEE X. Counting hidden referrers left pages visible and reachable from nothing, held up by drafts nobody had published - kept alive by a page that is not there. Safe in one direction because of the other: publishing is transitive, so a page taken down here comes back the moment anything visible needs it again. That safety argument has ONE exception since 2026-09-19 (issue #173): publishing now stops at a class page, so a CLASS this sweep takes down does not come back by republishing the page that referred to it. The exception exists because the two reaches were decided apart - publishing and date-moving stop at a class, unpublishing does not yet - and closing issue #201 removes it rather than adding a rule.

appliesTo: copying a page into another course
stopsAtAClassPage.why: A class goes up when the teacher names that class. A link that lands on another class publishes nothing and is not followed through, so material reachable only THROUGH another class belongs to that class and goes up with it. Publishing Day 4's worksheet because Day 3 links to Day 4 puts it in front of students a day early and dates it to the wrong lesson. Decided 2026-09-19 (issue #173), after the two apps were found to disagree: Windows stopped, the mac walked through. REJECTED: the middle position - do not publish the linked class, but walk past it to the material beyond - for the same two reasons. UNPUBLISHING is deliberately NOT in this list: its reach is the sibling decision, held as issue #201, and until that lands an unpublish still walks through a class page on both platforms.
stopsAtAClassPage.theNamedPagesAreNeverStopped: The rule is about pages REACHED. Naming two classes makes both of them starting points, and publishing a whole unit names every class in it, so nothing is lost by asking for more.
stopsAtAClassPage.saidToTheTeacher: The plan and the reply name the linked classes that were left alone, so a teacher is not surprised by a link students cannot follow yet - but only the ones students cannot already see, since 'publish it when you get to that class' is false about a class that is already published.

cases.name: a class linked from a class is neither published nor walked through
both classes named means both are starting points
a page both classes link to directly is unaffected

neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.kind: a page this section's Key Links points at, and the Key Links page itself
neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.why: A section cannot do without them; they are the way in to everything else.

neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.kind: a folder's landing page - index.md - which includes All Classes and every sidebar folder
neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.why: It is the way IN to a folder rather than a page anything links to, so following links must never take it down.

neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.kind: a curriculum page: any page with a folder segment containing 'curriculum'
neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.why: build_site.py's own rule, so a course whose folder is called 'Ontario Curriculum' is covered exactly as a plain one is. In a real course this is every expectation page, the folder's own index, and the page explaining them.

theOrderIsLoadBearing.why: The exclusions are checked BEFORE the referrer test, so narrowing what counts as a referrer cannot reach them. Narrowing a sweep rule makes every exclusion above it matter more than it did the day before, which is why the exclusions are the thing to re-test after any change to what gets swept.

note: The rule sets both apps need and neither platform owns. The MECHANISMS behind several of them differ completely - launchd against Task Scheduler, AppKit against WinUI, ~/Library/Logs against %LOCALAPPDATA% - which is exactly why the rules are written here instead: what must be refused, matched, stripped, or taken out of a problem report does not change with the machinery that does it.

pageNaming.note: What a page is CALLED when the assistant talks about it, which is not what its file is called. Shared because it is a rule with inputs and outputs and because both apps read the same folders: a teacher told that 'index' still links to a page has been told nothing, since every folder in a course has an index.md. Reported from a real course (ADA1O Section 1).
theRule: the frontmatter title, unless it is literally 'index'
for a file called index.md, the name of its FOLDER
pageNaming.why: Copied from Quartz's own fileTrie.ts displayName rather than invented, so what the assistant says and what the site's sidebar shows cannot drift: `const nonIndexTitle = data?.title === 'index' ? undefined : data?.title; return displayNameOverride ?? nonIndexTitle ?? fileSegmentHint ?? slugSegment`. If Quartz's rule changes, follow it.

identityIsSeparateFromLabel.why: A page's FILE NAME stays the identity, because wikilinks resolve by file name and every lookup in the page graph goes through it. Only the label changes. The trap is what happens in between: a referrer remembered by NAME and looked back up resolves 'index' to whichever folder's landing page came first in the walk, which was invisible while the answer printed as 'index' and becomes a confidently WRONG folder name the moment it does not. Carry the page, not its name.

wording.rule: The title and the caption below, word for word, on ALL FOUR surfaces that ask this question — Course Settings and the New Course Wizard, on both platforms. The caption goes BELOW its list on every one of them: “a page in one of these” points at the list, and Windows used to put the caption above, where “these” had the section header “Marks” in front of it and nothing to refer to. One string rather than a per-surface variant, because the caption names no switch and no platform.
wording.listTitle: Folders whose work counts for marks
wording.caption: Tick the folders holding work that counts for marks. The curriculum coverage map shows an expectation as evaluated when a page in one of these addresses it. Most courses keep “Tasks”; tick “Tests” or anything else you mark.
wording.why: Proposed from Windows 2026-09-08, resolving the second Course Settings divergence after specialNames.contentStructureTip: the two apps had worded this title and caption differently since the control was built, and nothing pinned either. The TITLE is the mac's, Russell's choice — it is also the closer match to specialFoldersHelp's already-pinned “Work that counts for marks”, so it cost the mac nothing. The CAPTION is a union of the two apps' and its middle sentence is the specialFoldersHelp marks row’s with ONE word changed — the map’s name. It is not identical to that row, and this why claimed it was until 2026-09-08: the help sheet still says “the curriculum map”, deliberately, as recorded below. Three decisions inside it, each of which was argued the other way first. THE MAP'S NAME: “the curriculum coverage map”, Russell's choice 2026-09-08, because both spellings are already pinned and this is the one shown on THIS control — specialNames.lastGradedFolderBlocked says “while the curriculum coverage map is enabled” in the flyout raised from this very list, and the switch beside it is labelled “Publish the curriculum coverage map”, so the caption now makes three matching names on one screen. specialFoldersHelp's “the curriculum map” is knowingly left as the outlier on a different surface; that is a recorded mixed state, not drift to be tidied up. Windows' capital-C “the Curriculum Coverage map” WAS drift and is gone: that is the built page's title, not a common noun. THE VERBS: “tick”, not the mac's “add … and remove”. This list is a tick list with no Add button, so the mac's caption named two actions the control does not offer, and “remove what you don't” invited the one thing lastGradedFolderBlocked refuses — unticking the last graded folder while the coverage map is on. THE OPENING CLAUSE was kept rather than dropped as a restatement of the title above it: the title is a noun phrase and this is where the teacher is told what to DO, and it is what makes the sentence survive if any surface ever puts the caption back above its list. WHAT THE CAPTION DELIBERATELY DOES NOT SAY: it is a summary, and the full conditions are stricter. _coverage_counts in build_site.py also requires the page to be published rather than a draft, and to be one the course actually TEACHES — reachable from a class page directly or through one hop — and the map itself is absent when include_curriculum_coverage is off, or when the course has no curriculum folder or no expectations, which is the normal state of a from-scratch wizard course. Those conditions are spelled out to the teacher on the coverage page itself (COVERAGE_NOTES) and were left out here on purpose: this sentence has been shown in specialFoldersHelp in exactly this form since that sheet was written, and lengthening a caption to carry three exceptions would bury the one thing it is for. WHAT THE CAPTION GIVES UP, so it is not rediscovered later as a bug: the mac’s “add “Tests”” was wrong about the control but loosely right about something this sentence does not say — that a folder must EXIST before it can be ticked. The pool offered is the declared lists plus a disk walk (gradedFolders.choices), so a teacher who marks tests and has no Tests folder has nothing to tick here and is told nothing about making one. Judged the lesser fault, because naming a button the control has not got is a dead end while a missing folder is visible in the very list they are looking at. One inherited imprecision is flagged rather than fixed: the map's own word is “assessed”, while this sentence says “evaluated”. Changing it means changing the specialFoldersHelp row too, which is a separate piece on both platforms.

gradedFolders.note: Which folders hold work that COUNTS FOR MARKS. An expectation is "assessed" — the ring on a cell in the Curriculum Coverage map, and Ontario's requirement that every overall expectation be evaluated at least once — when a page addressing it lives in one of these. It used to be hardcoded: any folder whose name CONTAINED "task". A teacher who called theirs "Tests", or renamed "Tasks", silently lost every assessed mark on the map with nothing said.

absentIsNotEmpty.rule: An ABSENT `graded_folders` key means the teacher has never been asked, and the HISTORICAL rule applies: any folder segment containing "task", case-insensitive. An EMPTY list means they were asked and cleared it, which is a real answer and is honoured.
absentIsNotEmpty.why: This is the whole migration, and conflating the two breaks courses both ways. The exact-name rule is NARROWER than the substring one — `support/skeletons` ships a family whose folder is "Thinking Tasks", which the old rule counted and a pool of ["Tasks"] does not — so seeding every existing course with ["Tasks"] would have quietly taken the assessed marks off that course's map. Nothing is written back from a build either: the apps serialise course_config.json wholesale from their own in-memory copy, so a key a build wrote is dropped the next time a teacher saves anything in Settings.

matching.rule: A FOLDER segment — never the file name — equals a pooled name, case-insensitively, at ANY depth.
matching.why: At any depth so a teacher who files by unit inside `Tasks` does not lose credit. Never the file name, because a page is not assessed work on account of what it is called.

choices.rule: The folders the Marks checklist OFFERS: the course's `shared_folders`, then its `per_section_folders`, then every folder found inside the course folder itself — in that order, de-duplicated by exact name.
choices.why: `matching` counts a folder at ANY depth, but a checklist built from the two top-level lists offers depth 1, and `absentIsNotEmpty` means the FIRST TICK FREEZES THE POOL. So anything the build counts today and this list omits loses its marks from that tick onwards, silently and permanently: a teacher who files assessed work in `Portfolios/Tasks` cannot tick it, and every expectation that folder addresses reads as never evaluated on the coverage map. The pool the first tick materialises must be built from this SAME list — a checklist that shows the walked names while the materialised value is inferred from the top-level lists alone loses the marks just as quietly, and a test covering only the visible list would not catch it.

walk.maxDepthWhy: The course folder's immediate children are level 1, so levels 1 to 4 are offered and level 5 is not. An affordability judgement rather than completeness, and it is honest about that: a graded folder five levels down is still absent. It must be the same number on both platforms — a different cap would mean the two apps offer different pools for the same course, so a teacher's tick would freeze a different answer depending on which app they were sitting at.
walk.skippedWhy: Build output, Plantoir's own bookkeeping, and `Media`. Skipped at ANY depth, and never walked INTO. `Media` is defensible either way — a teacher grading video portfolios might want it — and stays out because media is not assessed work in either app today, and differing here would change what the coverage map says. The two build-output names are skipped even where built websites are kept outside the course folder, so a folder left behind from before that move cannot turn up in the list.
walk.skippedMatching: EXACT, case included. A teacher's own folder called `media` is offered.
walk.hidden: A folder whose name begins with a dot, or which the platform marks hidden, is never offered and never walked into.
walk.links: A symbolic link or junction is not followed — but a folder is only treated as one when it genuinely has a LINK TARGET, rather than merely carrying a reparse point. The distinction is a Windows caution: the Cloud Files API documents a sync provider's unmaterialised placeholders as reparse points, so an attribute test could skip every folder in a cloud-synced working folder and put that course straight back on the top-level-only list this rule exists to fix. NOT reproduced on the machine this was written on — probing its OneDrive with Files On-Demand on found no reparse-point directories at all — so read it as a hazard the narrower test costs nothing to avoid, rather than as a measured fault.
walk.sectionFolders: A `sectionN` folder is NOT offered, at any depth, and its children ARE walked — with the PER-SECTION exclusion scope, wherever the section folder was found. Its contents are merged into the site and its own name never appears in a page's path there, so ticking it would count nothing — while a graded folder inside it certainly does count.
walk.excludedItems: A name in `excluded_items` is not offered and is not walked into. Filtered at the two levels the build's preflight scan actually discovers: the course folder's own children against `excluded_items.shared`, and a section folder's children against `excluded_items.per_section`. Matched EXACTLY, case included, the same way preflight matches. Without it, removing a folder from a course breaks the promise the removal confirmation makes — 'Removing it will take it out of your course's marks pool' — on the very next redraw, because the folder is still sitting on disk; ticking it again then writes a `graded_folders` naming a folder `excluded_items` tells the build to skip, so nothing counts for marks while the settings claim something does. (It does NOT suppress the `noGradedFolders` warning, whatever an older comment on this side said: `_has_graded_folders` walks the MERGED tree, so a pool matching nothing published raises the finding exactly as an empty pool would.)
walk.order: Declared names first, in list order; then the walked names DEPTH-FIRST: each folder's children in ORDINAL case-insensitive name order — upper-cased and compared by character, the way C#'s `OrdinalIgnoreCase` does it, NOT the way Finder or a locale would — and a folder's children before its own next sibling. NOT shallowest-first — `Alpha/Middle` comes before a top-level `Zebra`. Directory enumeration order is the filesystem's business and is promised by neither platform, so children are sorted, to give a teacher the same list every time and to let these cases pin an order at all.
walk.duplicates: By exact name, so a folder name appearing in two places is offered once — at the position the walk FIRST reaches it, which, the walk being depth-first, may be the deeper of the two.

cases.name: a graded folder nested inside another is offered
cases.why: The case the whole rule is for. `Portfolios/Tasks` counts for marks today under the historical rule, and a top-level-only list drops it at the first tick.

cases.name: a section folder is not offered, but its children are
the folders Plantoir looks after itself are never offered, at any depth
cases.why: `Tasks/Media` pins that the skip list applies below the top level too, and `Media/Portfolios` that a skipped folder's contents are not walked.

cases.name: the walk stops four levels down
declared folders first, then what is on disk
cases.why: Pins the ORDER, and that it is depth-first: breadth-first would put Zebra before Middle. `Alpha` sorts before `section1` before `Zebra` case-insensitively.

cases.name: a folder on disk that is in neither list is still offered
cases.why: The next build's preflight scan adds a folder like this to `shared_folders`, after which it counts for marks — so offering it is right rather than premature. It is also what a teacher is promised, in the sentence pinned as `specialNames.contentStructureTip`: that a folder made in Obsidian is added to the site by itself. Named rather than quoted, because a quoted copy is the one that keeps passing after the product's words change.

cases.name: nothing on disk: the declared lists stand alone
cases.why: A guard rather than a new rule: a course folder that cannot be read must still offer what the course declares.

cases.name: hidden folders are never offered
the same folder name in two places is offered once
numbered folders sort by character, not the way a person counts
cases.why: Pins WHICH case-insensitive comparison. Ordinal puts `Unit 10` before `Unit 2`; a locale-aware or Finder-style comparison puts `Unit 2` first, and that is the comparison each platform reaches for by default. Without a case carrying a run of digits, both implementations pass and still show a teacher two different lists. Ordinal is what shipped rather than what is nicest to read — changing it to natural order would be a shared decision, and this case is where that argument has to be had.

cases.name: a folder the teacher removed from the course is not offered back
cases.why: Proposed FROM Windows 2026-09-06 and implemented on the mac 2026-09-09 (issue #79), so both suites run it. Walking the course folder is what makes this case exist at all: before it, a folder removed from a list simply left the checklist with it. Now the folder is still on disk, so without this it comes back unticked one redraw after the app told the teacher 'Removing it will take it out of your course's marks pool'. Its children go with it: nothing under a removed folder reaches the site either. The cost, recorded rather than hidden: a pooled name found ONLY inside the removed folder then has no row to untick until the folder is put back. It is not silent — the build's health check walks the MERGED tree, so a pool naming nothing the site publishes still reports that no folder counts for marks — and nothing is lost, because a pooled name with no row is preserved rather than dropped.

cases.name: a folder named with a symbol sorts where Windows puts it
cases.why: Pins WHICH WAY the case fold goes, which the numbered case does not. `OrdinalIgnoreCase` upper-cases, so the six ASCII characters between `Z` and `a` — [ \ ] ^ _ ` — sort AFTER the letters; the natural macOS call folds to lower case and puts them BEFORE. Measured on a Mac 2026-09-09 while adopting this rule: `[.caseInsensitive, .literal]` gave ["_Archive", "Alpha", "zeta", "~Old"] where C# gives the order above. `_Archive` is an ordinary name for a folder a teacher wants at one end of their list, so this is not a corner case — and without a case for it both suites stay green while the two apps show different lists. What is deliberately NOT pinned: an ACCENTED name. macOS hands back decomposed spellings and Windows precomposed ones, so the two agree only as far as each app precomposes before comparing, and a case would pin a promise neither platform can keep on the other's files.

cases.name: a section folder found deeper down still filters its children
cases.why: A `sectionN` folder hands the PER-SECTION scope to its children wherever it is found, not only directly inside the course. Both apps have always done it — it falls out of a recursive walk that passes the scope down — and nothing said so, which is how the two would eventually stop agreeing. `Tasks` is excluded in the SHARED list and `Handouts` in the per-section one, so the case says WHICH list was consulted down there: an implementation that read the shared list would drop `Tasks` and offer `Handouts`, which is the reverse of what is expected here. (It named the same folder in both lists until 2026-09-09 and so pinned nothing of the kind — found by adversarial review the day it was written.) The narrower reading is defensible: `discover_section_items` in `build_site.py` only ever scans top-level section folders, so a folder nested this way is not what the build discovers. It is pinned the broad way because that is what both apps already do and because the case needs a teacher to have BOTH a section folder inside another folder and an exclusion of that name, which is rare enough that neither app should carry a special case for it.

cases.name: a removed name reaches only the level the build discovers it at
cases.why: The other half of `excludedItems`, and until 2026-09-09 nothing pinned it: a filter that took the UNION of the two lists, or applied either at every depth, passed every case in this list. Three things at once. A top-level `Handouts` is OFFERED, because the per-section list is not consulted against the course's own children. `Portfolios/Tasks` is OFFERED, because the shared list is not consulted below the top level — which is #79's own words, `a nested Portfolios/Tasks still counts when a top-level Tasks has been removed, because those are different folders and only one of them was removed`. And `section1/Handouts` is not offered while `section1/Tasks` is. The `Tasks` in the answer is the one inside `Portfolios`, reached before the top-level `Tasks` is refused — which is also what makes the ORDER here worth reading.

removingAFolder.rule: When a teacher removes a FOLDER from a course, its name leaves the marks pool with it — EXCEPT in two cases, and both exceptions exist to stop a removal quietly taking marks off the coverage map. (1) A course that has NEVER been asked is left unasked: `graded_folders` stays ABSENT rather than being frozen to the historical rule's answer minus the removed folder. (2) A name the checklist STILL OFFERS keeps its place: the pool is a list of NAMES, so if `Portfolios/Tasks` remains after a top-level `Tasks` is removed, `Tasks` is still on the list and still names work the build publishes. Said as "still offered" rather than "still counts anywhere in the course", because those are different questions — the checklist sees four levels and the build counts at any depth, so a `Tasks` five levels down is dropped from the pool and goes on counting. Both fall out of one rule an implementation can follow: recompute what the checklist offers AFTER the removal has been recorded, and drop the name only if it is no longer among them — asked the way the BUILD asks it, case ignored — AND the course had already been asked.
removingAFolder.why: The promise being kept is the removal confirmation's — 'Removing it will take it out of your course's marks pool' — and the failure being avoided is the one the whole `graded_folders` feature exists for: a pool that silently stops counting a folder the build still publishes. FREEZING A NEVER-ASKED COURSE is the trap, and it is not theoretical: on the ordinary course whose only marked folder is `Tasks`, materialising the historical rule's answer and then removing the name writes `[]` — asked and answered, nothing counts for marks, permanently, from a gesture the teacher was told only would take one folder out of the pool. An absent key keeps the historical substring rule running, so a `Thinking Tasks` still counts and putting the folder back restores what it had. THE SECOND EXCEPTION is the same failure by another route: dropping `Tasks` while `Portfolios/Tasks` is still there leaves the pool naming less than the course counts, and every expectation that nested folder addresses reads as never evaluated. It is in slight tension with the dialog's literal words — the FOLDER left the course, and a folder of that name did not — and that is the trade: a pool entry that still names published work is worth more than a sentence read to the letter. SETTLED 2026-09-09, RUSSELL'S CALL: Windows adopts this rule, so the difference below is work in progress rather than a choice either app gets to keep. The argument that decided it is that this is WINDOWS' OWN STATED INTENT — its `DropFromMarksPool` comment says a legacy course must not 'get one CREATED as an empty list by a removal', which is what this rule delivers — supported by the fact that a removal is not an answer to the marks question, and that recovery differs: an absent key plus putting the folder back restores the marks, while a frozen `[]` needs a teacher to notice a site-health finding they may never look at. REJECTED: freezing except where the result would be empty, which fixes only the worst course, still turns never-asked into asked on every other one, and is the kind of special case whose reason gets simplified away by the next reader. WHAT THE TWO APPS DO, as of 2026-09-18: BOTH follow this rule. Windows adopted it on 2026-09-18 (issue #142), and the whole gesture is one Core method there — `FolderRemoval.RemoveFolderFromCourse`: off the copy list, onto `excluded_items`, THEN the walk, then the pool decision. It lives in Core rather than in the view because the ORDER is the rule and `Plantoir.Tests` references Core alone, so a test calling a pure pool function while the order lived in `CourseSettingsView` would have stayed green through the very reordering that causes the bug. The cases below run there as `GradedFolderChoicesTests.WhatARemovalDoesToTheMarksPoolMatchesTheContract`, and the pre-fix body — `DropFromMarksPool` materialising over `_nestedFolderNames`, a walk CACHED by the previous `BuildForm` pass and so taken BEFORE the exclusion was written — turns cases 1, 2, 5 and 6 red when put back, the four this paragraph used to record as failing. NO COURSE IS REPAIRED, decided 2026-09-18: a course frozen by the old behaviour keeps its pool until the teacher ticks or unticks something, and neither app goes looking. Nobody can have been damaged by a version they were given — the freezing code (`a3c581fb`, 2026-08-25) is in no release tag and not on `main`, and `git grep -l graded_folders v1.1.0` comes back empty, so the whole key is unreleased — and a repair could not tell what it was repairing anyway: a pool written as `[]` by a removal is byte-identical to the deliberate empty pool case 4 calls a legitimate answer, and correlating it with `excluded_items` collides with exactly that case. REJECTED, so neither is proposed again: DETECT-AND-OFFER, which would have to ask a teacher about a state it cannot identify and would put that question in front of courses that had simply answered 'nothing counts'; and SILENT AUTO-REPAIR, which would rewrite a deliberate answer without asking — this rule's own failure arriving from the other direction. A genuinely damaged course still gets the one signal there is: `site_health.py` raises `noGradedFolders` for an empty pool. WHAT IS NOW PINNED, AND WHAT IS STILL NOT: the STILL-OFFERED half is pinned as CASE-INSENSITIVE by the seventh case below, added 2026-09-19 from issue #172, which was raised from Windows — it has asked with `OrdinalIgnoreCase` since 2026-09-18, and the mac asked exactly until this case landed, which turned the mac suite red until it changed (the other six cases all use one spelling and cannot see the difference, measured on both platforms). The reason it had to be pinned is that the walk returns names as they are spelled ON DISK: a surviving `Portfolios/tasks` is offered as `tasks`, an exact test reads that as 'no longer offered' and drops the pooled `Tasks`, and the build goes on counting the folder — marks off the coverage map because of a capital letter. Measured against the build itself (2026-09-19): `_is_graded_path('Portfolios/tasks/Quiz.md', ['Tasks'], True)` is true. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT PINNED HERE is the DROP's own comparison — the mac takes the name out of the pool exactly, Windows with `OrdinalIgnoreCase` — which shows only on a course whose pool and whose folder spell one name two ways: the mac then KEEPS a pool entry whose folder has gone (and `site_health.py` raises `noGradedFolders` for a pool matching nothing published, on a course whose coverage map is on AND whose site has curriculum expectations — `coverage_wanted and curriculum_found and not graded_folders_found`), while Windows removes it. Left unpinned because both answers err safely, but the two halves are not free of each other: the STILL-OFFERED test must be at least as PERMISSIVE as the drop, or a name can be judged absent and then removed anyway — which takes marks off an ASKED course, and, where the never-asked guard has been tidied away as well, brings the #142 freeze back with it (measured on Windows 2026-09-18, on code whose drop is `OrdinalIgnoreCase`; the mac's exact drop stops that same mutation one line LOWER, at its `!currentGraded.contains(name)`, so the course is left unasked instead). And what a RENAME does, which rewrites `graded_folders` as though the pool named folders rather than names, so a renamed `Tasks` stops counting a `Portfolios/Tasks` that a removal would have kept.

cases.name: a course that has never been asked is left unasked
the only folder that counts: still unasked, never an empty pool
cases.why: The case the rule is FOR. Freezing writes `[]` here, and `[]` is a real answer that switches the course off the historical rule for good.

cases.name: a course that was asked loses the name and keeps the rest
a per-section folder is dropped the same way, and may empty an explicit pool
cases.why: An EXPLICIT pool may legitimately end up empty: the teacher was asked, and this is their answer. Only a never-asked course is protected from that.

cases.name: a name that still counts elsewhere keeps its place in the pool
cases.why: `Portfolios/Tasks` is still published and still counts under the pooled name, and the checklist still shows a `Tasks` row for it. Dropping the name here would stop counting a folder nobody removed.

cases.name: and does not freeze a never-asked course either
cases.why: The two exceptions meeting. Read it as the SECOND one — the name is still offered, so nothing is dropped and the question of freezing never arises. The never-asked guard itself is pinned by the first two cases, where the name is gone from the list entirely.

cases.name: a name still offered in ANOTHER capitalisation keeps its place too
cases.why: The walk returns names as they are spelled ON DISK, so `Portfolios/tasks` is offered as `tasks`. An exact 'still offered' test reads that as 'no longer offered' and drops `Tasks` from the pool, while `build_site.py` lowercases both sides and goes on counting that folder — marks off the coverage map because of a capital letter. The DROP's own comparison stays unpinned; what this case pins is that the STILL-OFFERED question is asked the way the build asks it.

rerunningSetup.rule: A run of course setup that finds a saved `graded_folders` writes it back AS IT WAS: a list keeps the same names, in the same spelling and the same order, whatever the folder lists the run ends with and whatever is on disk. A saved null is written as an empty list, and a course that never had the key still has none. Entries that cannot name a folder — null, a blank string, a non-string, an exact repeat — are still removed from a saved list; nothing else is. Only a NEW course — no saved configuration at all — has its pool worked out from the payload or skeleton and reconciled against its folder lists. Each case is a saved `course_config.json` fragment (`saved`; `{}` means the key is absent), the folder lists the run ENDS with, what is on disk, and the `graded_folders` fragment written back (`expect`; `{}` means absent), with every prompt accepted as it stood.
rerunningSetup.why:
GitHub issue #192. A re-run of `./setup.sh` / `setup.ps1` on an existing course used to pass a saved pool back through the new-course reconciliation, which keeps only names on the TOP-LEVEL copy lists. That rule dates from 2026-08-24, two weeks before the Marks checklist began offering folders found INSIDE other folders (`gradedFolders.choices`, 2026-09-09), and nobody changed the re-run. MEASURED by driving the real wizard with every prompt accepted and no folder removed: a pool of ["Tasks"] for `Portfolios/Tasks` or `section1/Tasks` — exactly what the checklist writes when a teacher ticks those rows — came back `[]`: asked, nothing counts, and the historical rule never applies again. The re-run does not ask the marks question and has no way to remove a folder, so it does not own the answer.

Nothing was lost by dropping the reconciliation. Counting pages with the build's own `_is_graded_path` over the same shapes, the reconciled pool counted the same pages or FEWER in every one, never more: a name that names no folder counts no page whether it is written or not, and a respelling counts the same because the build lowercases both sides. A name taken off a copy list at a prompt is not a removal either: `build_site.preflight_update_course_config` finds the folder on disk and puts it straight back on the list (measured: shared_folders ['Concepts'] became ['Concepts', 'Tasks'] in one call), so dropping it from the pool stopped counting a folder that was still published.

A name that names no folder is not invisible, though, and the 'a name that names nothing is kept' case says so rather than hiding it: the published Curriculum Coverage page lists every pooled name in its sentence about which folders count, and Course Settings' last-folder guard counts it, so the last LIVE folder can be unticked without the block. Both could already happen through the apps' own exact-match removal (`removingAFolder`'s 'DELIBERATELY NOT PINNED' paragraph), and a clean-up by existence here would make the command line disagree with both apps about the same file.

REJECTED: reconciling against the checklist's own walk (a THIRD implementation of depth, skip list, hidden folders, links and section scope, to drop only names that count nothing); reconciling against every folder at any depth (a new walk rule of its own, the same payoff); keeping the respelling while dropping unmatched names (marks-neutral, and a pool one tool rewrites and the others do not is a file two apps can disagree about); and telling an app's new-course run from a command-line re-run so the old check stayed on the app path (both apps already narrow their own pool before they write, so the check there caught only names that count nothing). The apps run no case: neither ever re-runs setup on an existing course. `scripts/test_graded_folders_rerun.py` drives the real wizard in-process for every case, on the mac host in verify.sh's first step and on Windows through PythonToolchainTests.

cases.name: a folder ticked inside another survives a re-run
cases.why: What the Marks checklist writes when a teacher ticks the Tasks row found inside Portfolios (gradedFolders.choices). The old re-run wrote [].

cases.name: a folder ticked inside a section folder survives a re-run
the name a removal kept survives a re-run
cases.why: The issue as it was reported: removing the top-level Tasks keeps the name because Portfolios/Tasks still counts under it (removingAFolder), and the next re-run took it away.

cases.name: a name taken off a copy list at a prompt stays in the pool
cases.why: Not a removal: the next build's preflight finds Tasks on disk and publishes it again, so a pool without it would stop counting a published folder.

cases.name: the teacher's own spelling is kept
cases.why: The build compares names without regard to case, so the respelling the old re-run wrote counted exactly the same pages; it only rewrote what the teacher chose.

cases.name: several names keep their order
a course never asked stays never asked
cases.why: An absent key is what keeps the historical rule (absentIsNotEmpty); a re-run that wrote one would switch the course off it for good.

cases.name: an empty pool stays empty
a saved null is written as an empty pool
cases.why: Records what the re-run has always done rather than a decision: the build reads null and [] alike as asked-and-cleared (the 'explicit null' case below), while the mac app reads a null as never asked. That disagreement belongs to the apps and is left as it was; this case only stops the re-run changing it unnoticed.

cases.name: a name that names no folder anywhere is kept
cases.why: It counts no page, but it is not invisible: the Curriculum Coverage page names it, and Course Settings' last-folder guard counts it. Pinned so that nobody adds a clean-up by existence here that the two apps, which keep such a name, would disagree with.

cases.name: entries that cannot name a folder are cleaned out, and every real name kept
cases.why: Only a hand edit writes these. The old re-run cleaned them on its way through the new-course reconciliation, and 'written back as it was' is about the teacher's NAMES, not about keeping junk: null, a blank string, a non-string and an exact repeat are dropped, while the first spelling of each real name, its order, and a name with no folder (Unit Tasks) all stay.

cases.name: not configured: the historical substring rule
not configured: a folder that merely contains the word
cases.why: Ships in a skeleton family. The old rule counted it, so an existing course must keep counting it.

cases.name: not configured: nothing task-ish
configured: an exact pooled name
configured: nested inside a pooled folder
configured: a near miss is NOT a member
cases.why: Once a teacher has chosen the list, it means what it says. This is the case that makes seeding an existing course with ["Tasks"] unsafe.

cases.name: configured: the teacher removed Tasks
cases.why: Removing a folder from the pool is the point of the feature.

cases.name: configured: cleared deliberately
the file name never counts
an explicit null is a CLEARED list, not an unset one
cases.why: `{"graded_folders": null}` reads as configured-and-empty on both platforms rather than as absent: the key is PRESENT, and the absent case is reserved for a course that has never been asked. Pinned because the two implementations agreed by accident and nothing said which answer was intended.

askAboutPromptsWhen.why: There is something to answer the question about, so the teacher gets to decide whether their own sentences travel.

A teacher who has never TYPED to the local AI assistant should not be shown a question implying they might have - the box governs their sentences, and with none recorded, ticking it would change nothing. An unanswerable choice reads as the app knowing something about them they do not recognise. This is why 'assistant asked' is recorded the moment a message is SENT: tie it to the reply instead and the box vanishes for somebody who plainly did use the assistant, which is exactly how this was first reported.

problemReportDialog.includePromptsLabel: Include what I typed to the local AI assistant
problemReportDialog.labelWhy: The LOCAL AI assistant, said in full. Plantoir will grow ways to connect a teacher's own account with a hosted assistant, and from that day an unqualified 'the assistant' is a question about the wrong thing - answered wrongly, about where their words have been. Naming it now costs three characters and saves a rewording that would have to reach both apps at once.
problemReportDialog.note: The dialog that asks a teacher what to send. The rule worth sharing is not the layout - that is per-platform - but WHEN the question about the local AI assistant appears and what the report's own note then says. The condition is the presence of PROMPT lines on the trail, not of assistant events: opening the assistant and closing it again leaves turns but nothing the teacher typed, and the box controls only the typing.

promptStates.noteSays: nothing about the local AI assistant at all
promptStates.why: Never used it, so neither an IN line nor a NOT IN line. Promising that something was left out invites the teacher to wonder what else the app thinks they did.

promptStates.noteSays: listed under NOT IN THIS REPORT
promptStates.why: They used it and left the box unticked, which is the default. Saying so is the point: it is the promise they can check by opening the file.

promptStates.noteSays: listed under IN THIS REPORT, saying they asked for it
promptStates.why: They ticked the box. The note records that it was their choice, so nobody reading it later assumes the app took the words on its own.

reportName.why: Timed to the SECOND, not just dated. Somebody chasing a problem sends two or three reports in one afternoon - before a change and after it - and a date alone leaves a pile of files that must be opened to be told apart, or that silently overwrite one another. Dots rather than colons in the time because a colon is not legal in a file name on either platform. The folder INSIDE the archive carries the SAME stamp, or two reports unzipped side by side both land in a folder of the same name and collide on the machine of whoever is trying to help.

problemReportDialog.supportEmailWhy: Taken from here rather than from a screenshot of the mac dialog, and shown as something a teacher can CLICK rather than retype. One constant feeds the dialog and the note inside the report, so the two cannot drift.

cases.why: The account name is the single most common personal detail in this output, it appears in almost every line that names a path, and it is very often the teacher's real name. The REST of the path survives, because where a course folder sits is half of most diagnoses.

The same rule in the Windows shape. BOTH apps carry BOTH forms, deliberately: a report then reads identically wherever it was made, and neither side is left with a rule the other side's tests cannot reach.
A deploy tool announces the account it is signed in as. A board email address names the teacher and often their school.

The LABEL is kept and only the value goes. A report that says a token was present and empty is far easier to read than one with a hole in it, and the label is what tells you which credential the run was using.

Both token prompts use a silent read, so a pasted token does not echo into the output today. This rule is what stands behind that: the day a prompt is written without the silent flag, or a tool prints the token back in an error, the report is still safe.
A dumped HTTP header. The word Bearer survives so the line still reads as an authorization header.
Netlify personal access tokens carry a fixed prefix, so this one is recognisable with no label beside it at all.

An account identifier is not a credential, but it names the teacher's Cloudflare account and nothing can be diagnosed with it. The flag is kept so the report still shows that an account WAS passed, which is a real failure mode of its own.

cases.expect: Paste Cloudflare Account ID: [removed: account id]
cases.why: This prompt is NOT silent, so whatever the teacher types echoes into the output. It is the one place an identifier reaches the transcript by being typed.

A run of exactly 40 token characters is the shape of a Cloudflare API token, and it goes wherever it appears, with or without a label. Exactly 40 - neither 39 nor 41 - so ordinary long words and identifiers are left alone.

THE ONE EXCEPTION, and it is worth having. A 40-character run that is entirely lowercase hexadecimal is a git commit or a SHA-1 digest, not a token, and those are exactly what a report about a build is read for. A real token being all-hex by chance is about a 1-in-10^24 event, so nothing is given up for it.

KEPT, and this is the field the report exists to carry: the image tag says which recipe the folder actually built from, and the container name says which working folder it belongs to. Redacting these would leave a report that cannot answer the first question anybody asks of it.
KEPT. A class site address is public by design - it is the thing the teacher hands to students - and it is how a report is matched to the site that went wrong.

KEPT. A sentence that merely says the word 'token' is not a secret, and turning the product's own error messages into holes would make failures unreadable. The rule needs a value after a separator before it removes anything.

problemReportRedaction.note: What is taken OUT of a problem report before it is written to disk, and - just as important - what is KEPT. Redaction happens as the file is written, never as it is sent: a report that is only safe when it leaves by the right button leaks the first time somebody opens the folder it sits in, and writing it safe is what lets a teacher open the file and see for themselves what they are about to send. The rules lean towards removing too much, because removing a build hash by mistake costs a moment of puzzlement while a surviving token costs the teacher their account - but the four KEPT cases below are load-bearing, and a redactor that swallows them produces reports nobody can diagnose from. There is no way to switch this off in a development build: a redactor that is off while it is being worked on is a redactor nobody has run.

scheduledPublishStopped.note: What a teacher is told when a publish that was set to happen on its own did not get through. It usually runs at half six with the app closed, so the LAUNCHER writes a record and the APP reads it — that handover is the feature. Without it the run is indistinguishable from one that was never scheduled, which is exactly the shape of "my site did not update on Tuesday and I do not know why". (This said the app reads the record "the next time it opens" until 2026-09-19; see whenItIsShown, which is what made that false.)
scheduledPublishStopped.whenItIsShown: On the section that is SHOWING, without the teacher navigating anywhere, as soon as the run writes its record — and the section's sentence and the sidebar's warning appear at the same moment, because both follow one counter. Waiting for the section to be reopened is the fault GitHub issue #216 closed on the mac on 2026-09-19: a teacher who stayed on the section while the run finished was told nothing until they clicked away and back. Two things make it work and both matter to whoever implements it elsewhere. The app watches the RECORD FOLDER, one watch for the whole app rather than one per view, since the folder is per user rather than per working folder. And the wrapper must land its record in ONE step: a folder watch sees an entry arrive but not a second line appended to a file already there, so a record written with two echoes arrived as one event carrying an empty file — measured on the mac, 0 of 40 — and the line that completed it produced no event at all. The mac assembles the record in a temporary file BESIDE the folder and moves it in (40 of 40), and separately watches any record that is there but cannot be read yet, which is what covers a job whose wrapper was written by an older build. And since #212 (2026-09-25), as a system notification sent by the run itself when it finishes, so a teacher who has not opened the app at all is told too — see `notification`.

kinds.neededAnAnswer: The launcher exited 3: a question was put to nobody. deploy.py's NEEDS_AN_ANSWER, distinct from 1 precisely so a caller can tell the two apart and say something useful.
kinds.buildNeededAnAnswer: The BUILD stopped for a question, before any destination was reached. PROPOSED FROM WINDOWS 2026-09-09 (GitHub issue #132) and adopted on the mac the same day; the mac's suite was red on this key until it was, which is the mechanism working rather than damage. A scheduled publish builds before it publishes, and the build launcher asks questions of its own — the 'Open' course-code guard on both platforms, plus a section-not-listed warning that only preview.ps1 has — so under --non-interactive it refuses with the same exit 3 having contacted nothing. It is a SEPARATE kind rather than neededAnAnswer with an empty destination because the sentence differs: there is no destination to name, and telling a teacher that publishing to Netlify needed an answer when Netlify was never reached sends them to look in the wrong place. REJECTED: filling the destination slot with the section's first configured destination, which reads correctly and is false.
kinds.buildDidNotFinish: The BUILD failed for any reason but a question — any non-zero exit other than 3 — before any destination was reached, so nothing was published anywhere. Decided by Russell 2026-09-23 (GitHub issue #137) and adopted on the mac 2026-09-25; WINDOWS IS RED on `kinds` and `sentences` until it adopts it, which is the mechanism working rather than damage. It is SEPARATE from didNotFinish for buildNeededAnAnswer's reason: didNotFinish's sentence names a DESTINATION that stopped, and none was contacted. Until #137 the mac filled that slot with a phrase that is not a destination at all, and Windows with every configured destination joined — so a teacher read that publishing to Netlify stopped when Netlify was never reached, which is the shape recorded as REJECTED under buildNeededAnAnswer. And the sentence sends the teacher to PREVIEW rather than Publish, because previewing is what rebuilds the pages and shows why they would not build. Which LEG and which exit code give which kind is whichKind, below. REJECTED: merging the two build kinds into one (it loses buildNeededAnAnswer's promise that answering the question once lets the section publish on its own after that); rewording didNotFinish to cover both (a sentence that fits both a revoked token and a page that would not build names neither the place nor the fix); and telling the two apart by what the record's destination line says (meaning inferred from a display string, which could then never be reworded).
kinds.didNotFinish: Any other non-zero exit from a DESTINATION — a revoked token, a network that was down. Until 2026-09-25 this also covered a build that failed, which is buildDidNotFinish now (#137). One build failure can still land here: a build that fails INSIDE a destination's own rebuild reaches the wrapper as that destination's exit 1, because the exit code is all a wrapper has. deploy.py rebuilds for production whenever the built site's baseUrl is not the destination's address (a first publish to an address, or after it changes), and deploy.py and deploy.sh both rebuild a site still carrying the preview's live-reload client — the second reachable in a scheduled run only while the wrapper's own is-the-site-stale check is narrower than the launchers' (GitHub issue #136).
kinds.succeeded: It worked. Recorded for the same reason the failures are: a scheduled publish that leaves no trace cannot be told from one that never happened, so without it the trail can answer “why did my site not update?” and cannot answer “did it?”
kinds.tooLateToRun: The day it was set for had gone by, by more than the course allows (scheduledDeployCancellation.howLateIsTooLate), so the run STOOD DOWN: it deployed nothing, cleared the job away, and said so. Added on the mac 2026-09-20 with the fix for a scheduled deploy outliving its course. It is a SEPARATE kind for the reason buildNeededAnAnswer is one, and the reason is already recorded there: didNotFinish's sentence names a DESTINATION that stopped, and here there was none, so filling that slot in would read correctly and be false. It is not a failure either - nothing was attempted and nothing went wrong - and the sentence has to say that, or a teacher goes looking for a fault there was not. WINDOWS MAY NOT NEED IT: their task is created with /SC ONCE, which has no annual recurrence to close, so this kind is owed there only if their task is set to run after a MISSED start. Say which, rather than adopting or declining it silently.
kinds.courseWasBusy: Another program on this computer was still BUILDING or PUBLISHING the course after the run had waited ten minutes for it (#156; shared-rules workLeases.declining), so the run STOOD DOWN: it deployed nothing, cleared the job away so it cannot recur, and said so. A SEPARATE kind for tooLateToRun's reason - nothing was attempted, so there is no destination for a sentence to name - and it earns the attention badge for the same reason: the site the teacher expected is not there. Added on the mac 2026-09-25. Windows owes it once its scheduled publish reads leases (it writes none today, and takes none).

sentences.neededAnAnswer: {course} Section {section} was set to publish on its own, and it stopped because publishing to {destination} needed an answer nobody was there to give. Publish this section once yourself, answer the question, and it can publish on its own after that.
sentences.buildNeededAnAnswer: {course} Section {section} was set to publish on its own, and it stopped before it started, because building the pages needed an answer nobody was there to give. Preview this section once yourself, answer the question, and it can publish on its own after that.
sentences.buildDidNotFinish: {course} Section {section} was set to publish on its own, and it stopped before it started — the pages could not be built, so nothing went up anywhere. Preview this section once yourself, and the reason will be in that section's window.
sentences.didNotFinish: {course} Section {section} was set to publish on its own, and it did not finish — publishing to {destination} stopped, so nothing went up there. Publish it yourself to see what happens.
sentences.succeeded: {course} Section {section} published on its own to {destination}. Your students have the new pages.
sentences.tooLateToRun: {course} Section {section} was set to deploy on its own, but this computer wasn’t awake at that time and too long has passed since. Plantoir left the site as it was. Deploy it yourself when you’re ready, or schedule another from the section’s menu.
sentences.courseWasBusy: {course} Section {section} was set to deploy on its own, but the course was still being built somewhere else on this computer after ten minutes of waiting, so Plantoir left the site as it was rather than build it twice at once. Deploy it yourself when that has finished, or schedule another from the section’s menu.

whichKind.note: Which LEG stopped, and with which exit code, decides the kind — the code alone does not, because the build and the destinations both use 3 for a question and anything else for a failure (#132, #137). Exit 3 is tested BEFORE the general non-zero branch, since 3 is non-zero too. A build that stopped for ANY reason publishes nothing and names nothing. How a runner plays a case: run the REAL generated scheduled wrapper, with stand-in launchers, against one configured destination. For a `build` row the build launcher exits `exitCode`; for a `destination` row the build exits 0 and the one destination exits `exitCode`; for `none` everything exits 0. A wrapper that builds only when the site looks stale (the mac's) must be given a folder that looks stale. Then read the record: its kind must be `kind`; the teacher's sentence for it must contain the record's destination exactly when `namesADestination` is true; and the run must count as published — every destination leg ran and exited 0 — exactly when `anythingPublished` is true. Added 2026-09-25 with #137, because the decision asked for a case that names the exit code and the expected kind, so that a wrapper filing a failed build against every configured destination is caught by data rather than by a teacher.

cases.why: The build's own question (#132): the build launcher refused a question under --non-interactive, so nothing was reached and there is nothing to name.
The case #137 is about: the pages could not be built. Nothing was contacted, so no destination is named, and the teacher is sent to Preview.

ANY code but 3 is this kind, not only 1: a build launcher that could not be run at all exits with a different code, and so does one stopped by a signal. A wrapper that tests for 1 rather than for not-3 records nothing here, and this case is what catches it.
The build succeeded and the destination asked a question nobody was there to answer; the destination is named, because it was reached.
The build succeeded and the destination failed for an ordinary reason; the destination is named, because it was reached.
Every leg exited 0. The destination named is where the pages WENT.

scheduledPublishStopped.firstDestinationWins: The record is per SECTION and keeps the FIRST destination that stopped. A course can publish to several places and only one may have gone wrong, so "it published to the folder and not to Netlify" is the shape of the report; overwriting would tell the teacher about the last thing that went wrong rather than the first.
scheduledPublishStopped.attention: Every FAILURE asks for the teacher's attention and gets a warning beside their section in the list as well as the sentence inside it — a teacher who does not know WHICH section failed cannot open the right one. So does a run that STOOD DOWN (tooLateToRun), which is not a failure at all: nothing was attempted and nothing went wrong, and it still deserves the badge, because the site the teacher was expecting is not there either way and silence is what this whole key exists to break. The test is not "did something break" but "is the site other than the teacher expects". A SUCCESS is news rather than a problem: it gets the sentence and no badge, because a badge on every section that published fine overnight is a badge nobody reads by Wednesday.
scheduledPublishStopped.clearedBy: A scheduled run that got ALL the way through — every destination, exit zero — OR the teacher dismissing it. Both, and the second is a decision rather than a convenience: clearing only on a successful run leaves the message standing after somebody has already fixed the problem by hand, and the next scheduled run that would clear it could be a week away.
scheduledPublishStopped.trail: One line per RUN, dated to when the RUN wrote its record rather than to when the app read it — or an overnight problem is filed under the morning somebody noticed it. There are FOUR events, and not one per kind: the three outcomes of a run that HAPPENED share three of them (activityTrail.mustRecord: scheduled publish needed an answer, did not finish, finished), and a build that stopped for a question files under the first, because a question going unasked is what happened and an event of its own would put a distinction on the trail that means nothing to the person reading it. A build that failed outright (buildDidNotFinish) files under the second, `scheduled publish did not finish`, for the same reason, with a line that names no destination because none was reached (added 2026-09-25, #137). The fourth belongs to the kind where the run did not happen at all: tooLateToRun writes `scheduled deploy turned off`, the same event and the same words a REMOVAL writes, because the same thing happened to the teacher's alarm and the reason is what differs. (This said THREE events until 2026-09-20.) The line carries the course, the section, and which destination stopped — or, for a run that got through, where it WENT. NEVER the question's own text: that comes from a launcher's console, and a line naming a credential prompt would put a teacher's own words on the trail. An earlier draft had the app note the line when a teacher opened the section and mark the record as noted; rewriting the record changed its modification date, which is what the notice shows, so the teacher saw the morning they looked rather than the half six the run stopped at — and a teacher who never opened that section, who is exactly the one who reports that their site did not update, got no line at all. WHO writes it is platform-local and cannot be otherwise: see platformDifferences.

notification.note: Added 2026-09-25 with GitHub issue #212. A publish set for half six runs with nobody looking, and until this the only places it said how it went were the section's band and the sidebar's warning — both inside an app the teacher may not open before class. So when a run finishes, WHATEVER happened, the teacher is sent ONE system notification (a macOS notification; a toast on Windows) that waits for them in the system's own list. Its text is the section's own sentence (`sentences.<kind>`, filled in exactly as the band fills it) with nothing added — no title of the app's own, since the system heads it with the app's name and every sentence already begins with the course and the section, which is also what survives a banner cut short. A SUCCESS is announced too, every time: Russell's decision, 2026-09-25 — the band carries it and `attention` gives it no badge, so without the notification a success reaches nobody who has not opened that section. One notification per SECTION, keyed so that a later run of the same section REPLACES it (a teacher is not handed last week's news beside this week's), and dismissing the section's band WITHDRAWS it, so the two never disagree about whether it is still news. The RUN never asks for permission — a question at half six is a question to nobody — and a run that may not post writes why on the trail instead. The question is put the first time a teacher schedules a publish from the app's own window or its own assistant, never from an outside assistant (which has no window to explain it) and never at launch (most teachers never schedule anything). How a runner plays the cases: with a stand-in for the system's notifications that records what it was asked, keeps what is on show by identifier (a post replaces, a withdraw removes), and never reaches the real system. A platform whose notifications need no prompt (Windows toasts) plays only the rows whose `permission` is `allowed` or `notAllowed`; the `notAskedYet` rows carry `onlyWhereThereIsAPrompt` and exist only where there is a question to ask. `trailSays` is the line after the course/section prefix the trail already puts on every line of this kind.

announcing.note: Play each row once for EVERY key of `kinds` when `record` is `everyKind` (so a kind added later is covered without touching this list), and once with no record when it is `none`. Write the record, set the stand-in's permission, run the announcement, and check: whether a notification was posted, that its text is exactly the kind's sentence, whether permission was asked (never, from a run), and the trail line.

cases.name: allowed: every kind is announced
cases.trailSays: told the teacher how a scheduled publish went, with a notification
cases.why: A success as much as a failure: the silence is the complaint whatever the outcome.

cases.name: turned off: nothing posted, and the trail says why
cases.trailSays: did not send a notification about a scheduled publish, because notifications are turned off for Plantoir
cases.why: From the teacher's side a blocked notification and one never sent look the same; the line is what tells them apart.

cases.name: never asked: the run does not ask
cases.trailSays: did not send a notification about a scheduled publish, because Plantoir has not been given permission to send them yet
cases.why: A question put by a run at half six is put to nobody, and the process is about to exit.

cases.name: the system refused the post
cases.trailSays: a notification about a scheduled publish could not be sent
cases.why: The post was attempted and did not land — including a system that never answered before the run's ceiling. Never silent, and never a reason for the run itself to fail.

cases.name: no record: nothing to say
cases.why: A run that wrote no record (a job scheduled before sections were named) has nothing the band would say, so nothing is announced and no line is written.

onShow.note: What stays on show after a sequence of posts and dismissals. Each step is `post` (a run of that section finished with that kind) or `dismiss` (the teacher dismissed that section's band). `stillShown` lists what the stand-in holds afterwards, in any order, with the kind whose sentence it carries.

cases.name: a later run of the same section replaces the earlier one
section 1 and section 11 are different sections
cases.why: Catches a key built so that one section's is the prefix of another's.

cases.name: the same section number in two courses
dismissing the band withdraws that section's notification and no other

asking.note: Where the permission question may be put. `from` is what scheduled the publish: `window` (the scheduling sheet), `appAssistant` (the app's own assistant), `outsideAssistant` (an assistant in another program, over MCP) or `scheduledRun` (the run itself, finishing). The question is put only when `permission` is `notAskedYet` — a teacher who said no is not asked again, and the switch is in the system's own settings.

trailSays: asked whether Plantoir may send a notification when a scheduled publish finishes
the teacher allowed notifications about scheduled publishes
cases.why: The first time a teacher schedules, from the one place they can see why they are being asked. The first line is written before the answer, because a question that is ignored, or arrives under a Focus, may never be answered.

trailSays: asked whether Plantoir may send a notification when a scheduled publish finishes
the teacher did not allow notifications about scheduled publishes

cases.why: Said no once; the question is not put again.

trailSays: asked whether Plantoir may send a notification when a scheduled publish finishes
the teacher allowed notifications about scheduled publishes

cases.why: KNOWN LIMIT: a teacher who only ever schedules from an outside assistant is never asked, so never notified, and every run's line says permission was not given yet. The outside assistant's process has no window, so the question would appear with nothing on screen to explain it.

trailSays: did not send a notification about a scheduled publish, because Plantoir has not been given permission to send them yet

platformDifferences.windows: Records every outcome of a run that HAPPENED — neededAnAnswer, buildNeededAnAnswer, didNotFinish and succeeded — and lets the teacher dismiss it, both since 2026-09-09 (GitHub issue #130); ScheduledPublishOutcome, plus the readout in SectionDetailView. It has NOT got the three kinds added on the mac since: tooLateToRun (2026-09-20, owed only if their task runs a missed start late — see that kind), courseWasBusy (2026-09-25, #156, owed once their scheduled publish reads leases) and buildDidNotFinish (2026-09-25, #137). A build that fails outright there is recorded as didNotFinish with every configured destination joined, which is the shape #137 replaced.
platformDifferences.mac: Every kind above, and dismissible. Russell decided on 2026-09-09 that a teacher should learn their overnight publish did not happen whatever the reason, because the SILENCE is the complaint rather than the cause, and that landed on both platforms the same day. buildDidNotFinish landed here 2026-09-25 (#137). A section scheduled BEFORE that keeps the wrapper it was given, so its one remaining run still records a failed build as didNotFinish and shows the old sentence once; that was accepted, as it was for #132.
platformDifferences.owed: By Windows: buildDidNotFinish, and whichKind.cases run against its own wrapper (#137); tooLateToRun and courseWasBusy on the conditions their kinds give. Nothing is owed by the mac. ONE difference remains and it is deliberate, because it cannot be otherwise: WHO writes the trail line. The mac's launchd agent runs Plantoir, so the RUN writes it as the trail key describes, while Windows' Task Scheduler runs plain PowerShell with no app process alive — so that side sweeps every record when the app next opens, dating each line from the record rather than from the reading. Writing it from the wrapper's own shell was REJECTED there: it would put the trail's line format in a second home, in generated PowerShell, where nothing tests it and the redaction rules do not reach. The property the contract actually asks for is kept either way — a teacher who never opens the failed section still gets the line, and that teacher is precisely the one who writes in to say their site did not update. ALSO owed by Windows since #212 (2026-09-25): the `notification` rules — every kind announced with its own sentence, one per section replaced by the next, withdrawn on dismissal, the run never asking, and `scheduled publish notification` on the trail. The rule is theirs to MATCH; the delivery is theirs to design, because their run is PowerShell under Task Scheduler with no app process, so a toast has to be attributed to Plantoir's own application identity, and a toast needs no permission prompt (so only the `allowed` and `notAllowed` rows apply there). Their trail lines for it are written the way their other scheduled-publish lines are, by the sweep when the app next opens.

scheduledPublishStopped.whereTheRecordLives: Platform-local and deliberately NOT shared: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Plantoir\scheduled\unanswered on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/Plantoir/scheduled/stopped on the mac. What is shared is the BEHAVIOUR above; a path is not a rule. The mac's folder says `stopped` rather than `unanswered` because that side records more than unanswered questions; Windows records more than that too and KEPT the old name deliberately, because a task scheduled before 2026-09-09 points at a wrapper script already on disk that writes the old path, and nothing rewrites that wrapper until the section is scheduled again — so renaming buys a better name and costs a second directory read for ever, on pain of the first overnight run after an update going silent. The record says what it is on its own first line.

scheduledDeployCancellation.note: Which acts turn a scheduled deploy off without being asked, which deliberately turn none off, and how late is too late for one to still run. The MECHANISM is not shared and never was - launchd against Task Scheduler - but which act cancels what is a rule with inputs and outputs, it is true of both products, and on 2026-09-20 the two apps disagreed about it by accident rather than by decision: Windows cancels when a SECTION is removed and does not when a COURSE is (Plantoir.Core/Models/CourseArchiver.cs), and the mac did neither. That is exactly the quiet difference this folder exists to catch.
scheduledDeployCancellation.theFault: A scheduled deploy outliving the course it was set for. The alarm lives OUTSIDE the working folder and is addressed by the course code, so removing the course left it standing, and on the mac StartCalendarInterval carries no year - so a job that never ran came due on the same date twelve months later, against whatever was in the folder by then. Which direction it errs in was MEASURED on the mac, 2026-09-20, and it is worse than it first looked: a course that publishes to NETLIFY refuses (scripts/deploy.py:1204, refuse_to_ask, exit 3) because the site marker lived inside the course folder and went with it; a course that publishes to CLOUDFLARE PAGES does NOT refuse - publish_to_cloudflare contains no refuse_to_ask at all, the teacher's surname is read from courses/.internal/profile.json which is in the WORKING folder and survives the removal, and suggest_pages_name is deterministic - so it builds the new course, creates or reuses a Pages project and reports success; and a course that publishes to a FOLDER does not refuse either, because a folder destination asks nothing ever. So the failure that REPORTS SUCCESS is not a rare edge: it is every folder and every Cloudflare course.
scheduledDeployCancellation.order: CANCEL FIRST, then archive and remove - and this is the opposite of a RENAME's order, deliberately. A rename that cancelled before a failed move would silently drop a deploy for a course still sitting there under its old name, so it archives first; a REMOVAL that archived before a failed cancel would leave the very thing this rule exists to prevent, a course that is gone with a live alarm still addressed to it.
