So: a cancel that FAILS stops the removal, and the teacher is told in a plain sentence. If the removal then fails, the deploy stays cancelled and the sentence says so.
scheduledDeployCancellation.scopedToOneWorkingFolder: Everything that cancels, lists or SHOWS a scheduled deploy asks the plist which working folder it belongs to, and leaves alone anything belonging to another. Paths compared with POSIX realpath, never Foundation's resolvingSymlinksInPath - the latter strips /private where the former keeps it, and two spellings of one folder comparing as DIFFERENT would scope every job out silently. The reason is not hypothetical: an agent's label is the course code and the section number and nothing else, so a teacher holding last year's working folder and this year's, both with ICS3U section 1, has ONE alarm between them; without this, removing the course in the folder that does not own it would cancel the other folder's live deploy and report success. That the two folders share one alarm at all is a separate fault with its own issue - a folder-scoped label would orphan every plist a teacher already holds.

cases.act: a course kept for reference is met when the working folder is read
cases.why: A reference course is never deployed, so an alarm still addressed to one is a deploy that will be refused at half six with nobody there to read the refusal. Reached when the folder is READ rather than only when a course is made one, because the marker can also arrive by hand in an editor, or from another Mac - and the course that owns the alarm is the one that was live yesterday. Scoped to THIS working folder like every other case here.

cases.act: remove one section of a course that has more than one
cases.why: The other section's deploy is still meaningful, so it stays.

Asked of the AGENTS rather than of the course's section list: a section removed on an earlier build left an alarm behind and took its number out of the settings, so a walk over the settings cannot see it.

cases.act: remove the only section of a course
cases.why: The sidebar turns that into a course removal, and it must cancel what a course removal cancels.

cases.act: remove a course whose code also exists in another working folder
cases.why: The one alarm belongs to the other folder. Cancelling it would destroy a deploy the teacher set on purpose and report success - which is worse than the fault being fixed.
Already true before this rule existed, and listed so it cannot quietly stop being true. After a rename the alarm is addressed by a code no course has any more.

cases.act: roll a section over onto a new website
cases.why: A section cut loose has no agreed website to publish to, and a run at half six has nobody to ask what to call one - it would create a name of its own and publish there while the address the students read quietly stopped updating. This case exists because the mac's rollover path was the ONE cancel left folder-blind when the rest of this rule landed on 2026-09-20: it asked only whether a file with that label exists, which is a Mac-wide question, so rolling a section over in one working folder deleted another folder's live deploy and reported it turned off. A rule asserted by prose and run by nothing is how that survived its own fix.

cases.act: restore a backup over a course
cases.why: It replaces the course's CONTENTS in place. The course and its sections are still there, its site marker comes back with it, and the schedule still means what it meant.

cases.act: restore an archived course or section
cases.why: It ADDS. A section removed - its deploy cancelled by the rule above - and later restored comes back with nothing scheduled, and the teacher sets it again if they want it. That is the safe direction.

cases.act: delete an archive, or delete a backup
cases.why: A zip is deleted; no live course changes.

scheduledDeployCancellation.howToRunACase: A case with provedBy 'run' is played through the real removal, rename or rollover with a stand-in launchctl, against agents written into a folder of the test's own - NEVER the teacher's ~/Library/LaunchAgents, and on the mac LaunchControl.run now refuses outright while that override is set, so a test that forgets the stand-in fails rather than deleting the ICS3U schedule of whoever ran the suite. A case with provedBy 'sourceHasNoCancel' is a scan of the named SOURCE FILE: it must still contain the named symbol, and it must contain no call that cancels a scheduled deploy anywhere in it. That cannot prove the act is harmless, only that nobody has since taught it to cancel, which is the regression worth catching - a cancel appearing in a restore would be a silent loss of something the teacher set on purpose.

howLateIsTooLate.rule: A run whose intended moment is further from now than the course's window stands down: it deploys nothing, clears the job away, records the outcome (scheduledPublishStopped.kinds.tooLateToRun) and leaves the trail line 'scheduled deploy turned off'.
howLateIsTooLate.compare: abs(now - intendedMoment) against the window, on ABSOLUTE instants. No calendar, no time zone, no daylight-saving arithmetic anywhere. Measured on the mac 2026-09-20: a 'same calendar day' rule REFUSES a 23:50 job on a Mac woken at 00:05 - the coalesced wake Apple's own launchd.plist page documents - turning a fifteen-minute delay into a silent non-deploy, which is the precise harm this exists to prevent. It also refuses a job set in Toronto firing at 06:30 local in Tokyo, which arrives BEFORE the recorded instant; abs is what allows that one.
howLateIsTooLate.failsOpen: A moment that is missing or unreadable means RUN. A deploy the teacher asked for beats a refusal nobody sees, and fail-closed would turn one unparseable stamp into every scheduled deploy silently not happening.
howLateIsTooLate.whereTheMomentComesFrom: The environment the scheduler hands the process, falling back to the job's own stored moment, which is still on disk at that instant.

cases.name: fifteen minutes late, across midnight
two and a half hours late, the same morning
twenty-six hours late - away sick, opened the laptop the next afternoon
thirteen hours EARLY, after a move to another time zone
eight days late
a year late - the fault itself
two days late, with one day chosen
two days late, with three days chosen
a year late, with two weeks chosen - the longest window still refuses it
the moment cannot be read

theSetting.where: Course Settings, under Deploying, beside the other deploying settings. NOT in the new-course wizard: a brand-new course cannot have anything scheduled, because a section that has never been deployed cannot be scheduled at all.
theSetting.whenItIsRead: At the moment the deploy fires, from the course's own settings file inside the working folder the job named - so changing the setting after scheduling changes what the job already on disk will do. The sweep asks the same question through the same function; two answers to 'how late is too late for this course' is one more than anybody can keep in step.
theSetting.whenTheJobsCourseCodeIsLOSSY: An agent written before the course code was recorded in the job itself carries it only in its own NAME, uppercased with every non-alphanumeric turned into a hyphen - so a course called "Chess Club" comes back "CHESS-CLUB" and is not found by name. The folder is matched by that sanitised form instead, and ONLY when exactly one folder matches: two codes that sanitise the same way are ambiguous, and guessing between them would read one course's setting for another's job. With no unique answer the default applies - the same answer a course that has gone gets. The folder is found by comparing the NAMES in courses/, never by asking the filesystem whether a built path exists: a teacher's volume is case-insensitive by default, so asking for CHESS-CLUB answers yes when the folder is really Chess-Club, and a lossy code would walk into a different course's settings and read its window. Measured on the mac 2026-09-20 against a folder pair one hyphen apart. Without this step such a course fell back to the default at sweep time although its teacher had chosen another window, and the direction of that mistake is a deploy DROPPED.
theSetting.whenItCannotBeRead: The default. A course that is gone, a file that cannot be read, a key that is not there - all of them mean the default rather than a refusal. A job whose course folder has gone is refused by the launcher anyway; the stand-down must still clear the job away, or the same job comes back next year, which is the whole fault.
theSetting.whyAShortList: A fixed list rather than a number a teacher types. The value is read at the scheduled moment with nobody there, so a 0 or a 365 typed into a field is a fault nobody meets until the morning it matters - and anything stored that is not one of the offered choices reads as the default rather than as itself, which is what the cases above pin.
theSetting.whyNoAlways: There is deliberately no 'always' and no 'never expires'. That is the annual repeat this whole rule exists to close, offered back as a setting.

wording.confirmationSectionRemoved: Section {section} is set to deploy on its own. Removing it turns that off.
wording.confirmationCourseRemovedOneSection: {sections} of {course} is set to deploy on its own. Removing {course} turns that off.
wording.confirmationCourseRemovedSeveralSections: {sections} of {course} are set to deploy on their own. Removing {course} turns that off.
wording.couldNotTurnItOffOneSection: {sections} of {course} is set to deploy on its own, and Plantoir could not turn that off — so nothing has been removed. Turn off the scheduled deploy from the section’s menu, then try again.
wording.couldNotTurnItOffSeveralSections: {sections} of {course} are set to deploy on their own, and Plantoir could not turn that off — so nothing has been removed. Turn off the scheduled deploys from the section’s menu, then try again.
wording.removalFailedAfterTurningItOffOneSection: {sections} of {course} will no longer deploy on its own — that was turned off first. Removing it then failed: {reason}
wording.removalFailedAfterTurningItOffSeveralSec: {sections} of {course} will no longer deploy on their own — that was turned off first. Removing it then failed: {reason}
wording.settingTitle: How late a scheduled deploy may still run
wording.settingCaption: A deploy set to happen on its own runs at the time you chose. If this Mac was off or asleep then, it runs the deploy the next time this computer wakes instead. This setting identifies how long after your chosen time the deploy is still worth doing. If your computer wakes after this time, Plantoir will cancel the scheduled deploy.
wording.rule: {sections} renders as 'Section 1' or 'Sections 1 and 2', the same listing a rename uses. The singular and the plural are separate strings rather than one string with a verb placeholder, for the reason assist-wording's linkedClassWasLeftAlone / linkedClassesWereLeftAlone are a pair: one rendering cannot show both branches, and a contract holding half a sentence is a contract the other platform has to finish by guessing. NOTHING is said after a cancel that WORKED - the confirmation already said it would happen, and a second alert saying it did is noise. A rename shows one because a rename's confirmation never mentions the schedule.
wording.machineryCheck: No 'job', 'agent', 'plist', 'launchd', 'task' or 'scheduler' in any sentence above. 'Scheduled deploy' is the teacher's name for it.

whatWasRejected.instead: Only the overdue sweep, which is provably harmless once the run's own check exists, plus the run's check, which reaches plists ALREADY ON DISK because every released plist's first program argument is the app's own binary - so an upgraded app runs the new check for an old job the moment it next tries to fire.
whatWasRejected.rejected: Sweeping a working folder for jobs whose COURSE no longer exists, at folder-open and at course creation
whatWasRejected.why: It is the only code here that DELETES something a teacher set on purpose, and every way it can be wrong is silent. An existing-but-empty courses/ reads as 'no courses' and would destroy every alarm naming that folder - a volume not mounted, a synced folder mid-materialisation - which is the same shape as the Docker check that read a daemon that did not answer as 'the machine is empty'. A course code recovered from a LABEL is sanitised and lossy, so a mismatch reads as 'this course does not exist'. And what it actually buys, once the run's own check exists, is one residue: a still-future job whose course was removed BEFORE the teacher upgraded and whose code is recreated before its date. That is not worth the family of ways it can delete a live deploy.

whatWasRejected.instead: Elapsed time between two absolute instants.
whatWasRejected.rejected: Deciding lateness by 'the same calendar day'
whatWasRejected.why: Measured: it refuses a 23:50 job on a Mac woken at 00:05, and it refuses a job that fires early after a time-zone move. It also drags a calendar, a locale and daylight saving into the one function that decides whether a teacher's site updates.

whatWasRejected.instead: A week, chosen per course from a short list.
whatWasRejected.rejected: A twenty-four hour window, fixed for everybody
whatWasRejected.why: A teacher away sick opens the laptop twenty-six hours late and still wants the site updated, and a laptop closed over a weekend is ordinary. The fault this closes is about eleven months late, so the window only has to sit far below that.

whatWasRejected.instead: The shortest window is one day and the longest is two weeks.
whatWasRejected.rejected: An 'always' or 'never expires' choice in the setting
whatWasRejected.why: That is the annual recurrence, offered back to the teacher as a preference.

whatWasRejected.instead: The orchestration lives in a model type the suite can drive, which takes the launchctl stand-in explicitly.
whatWasRejected.why: The archiver's own tests build an ICS3U fixture - a course a teacher plausibly has - and set no override for where agents live, so a cancel inside it with the real launchctl as its default would boot out and delete a real ICS3U schedule on the machine running the suite. Putting it in the sidebar view was rejected too, for the opposite reason: nothing in the suite constructs that view, so the wiring could not be pinned and a later edit that dropped the call would leave the suite green.

alsoSaid.note: Not a refusal - a teacher may be deploying deliberately without them - but the plan NAMES the section's unpublished class pages before the teacher agrees. A deploy that runs perfectly at half six and puts up a site missing tomorrow's class is the failure worth catching while somebody is awake.
alsoSaid.rule: list the class pages students cannot see yet, by name

cases.name: a time that has already passed
cases.why: First, because it is the one the teacher can fix without leaving the sheet.

cases.name: a folder deploy whose folder is not usable
Cloudflare with no Account ID
cases.why: A deliberate divergence, and the reason is worth keeping. The mac's plist carries --account, so the question is asked here and answered once. On Windows the scheduled task could not be handed one, which would make Cloudflare unschedulable - if that is still true, refuse it with a sentence that says so rather than scheduling something that will fail at 06:30.

cases.name: an ADDITIONAL folder destination whose folder is not usable
cases.why: Checked after the primary's own two checks, in the same order additional destinations are deployed to (primary first, then each additional one) - a redundancy target with no valid folder would otherwise sit silently broken until the scheduled moment, exactly what asking everything up front exists to prevent. hasDeployedBefore is true here so the PRIMARY's own checks pass first and this is genuinely the additional check firing.

cases.name: an ADDITIONAL Cloudflare destination with no Account ID
cases.why: cloudflareAccountID is the SAME key the primary's own Cloudflare check uses - it is one credential per teacher, not one per destination, so a missing Account ID refuses whichever destination (primary or additional) actually needs it.

cases.name: a section that has never been deployed
cases.why: The FIRST deploy of a section asks what to call the website. Nobody is there to answer at the scheduled time and it would simply wait. Deploy once by hand, then it can be scheduled - which is what the refusal says.

cases.name: the PRIMARY has deployed before, but an additional destination has not
cases.why: The same reasoning as the primary's own check, for whichever additional destination is new - a brand-new Netlify or Cloudflare destination also asks what to call the site; local_folder never does, so it can never trigger this one. A valid cloudflareAccountID is given so THAT check passes first and this is genuinely the never-deployed check firing.

cases.name: everything in order

scheduledDeployRefusals.note: Everything a deploy running at 06:30 would ASK is asked NOW instead, while somebody is awake to answer. A scheduled deploy that stops at a prompt in the dark is the worst outcome available: it reports nothing, changes nothing, and is discovered by a class looking at yesterday's site. Checked in this ORDER - the first match is what the teacher is told, so a time in the past is answered before a missing account.

cases.why: An empty filter shows everything.
Trimmed first.

Case-insensitive, and mid-word against the NAME as well as the code — so 'ics' finds ICS3U by its code AND SPH4U through 'Phys-ics'. That looks like a bug and is the rule working: a teacher hunting for a course types more letters, and one who typed 'ics' meaning Physics is served too. This case was written expecting ICS3U alone, and running it said otherwise.

One letter matches all three codes.
No match shows nothing - and the sidebar says so in words rather than showing an empty space.

sidebarFilter.note: What the sidebar's filter field shows. Case-insensitive, matched against the course CODE and the course NAME, and mid-word - a teacher typing 'comp' should find Introduction to Computer Science without knowing it starts with ICS. Matching is CONTAINS rather than prefix, deliberately: a teacher who knows their course as 'Calculus' should not have to know it is filed under MCV4U.

pagesDatedByTheBuild.note: How the build tells the app which of the teacher's pages it rewrote with their class's date (#275, #276), so the app can put their names on the activity trail. The rewriting rule itself is class-planning.json's; this is only the line that reports it.

marker.rule: One line on stdout, printed only when at least one page was rewritten: the prefix followed by a single-line JSON object carrying course (the course code), section (a number) and pages (each rewritten page's place in the course folder, without .md, e.g. "section1/index" or "Exercises/Using Aggregate Functions"). A plain sentence for a person reading the console is printed just before it. The apps keep the marker line itself out of the console a teacher reads, as they do PLANTOIR_HEALTH: lines - a line carrying it anywhere, hidden whole, including while it is still arriving, and read from the prefix onward (siteHealth.marker.rule).
marker.why: The same reasons as siteHealth.marker: a prefixed JSON line is unambiguous, survives interleaving with ordinary output, and carries structure a sentence cannot. Separate from PLANTOIR_HEALTH: because it is not a problem - an app that showed every health line in a dialog must not show this one.

trailLine.shape: the build gave N page(s) the date of their class: <names, comma-separated>
trailLine.why: Names only, and the count first, so a long list can be shortened without losing how many there were.
trailLine.readFrom: The console, as each line arrives, for a preview or a publish the app runs; the run's own log, from the size it had before the run, for a scheduled publish (the mac: ScheduledDeploy.recordFolderProblems, which reads that log for PLANTOIR_HEALTH: lines already). Both, or the scheduled build — the one likeliest to rewrite files — leaves no trace.

siteHealth.note: What the toolchain checks about a course's folders before it builds, and the WORDS a teacher reads when one of them is wrong. Certain folder and file names carry behaviour — the curriculum folder, the folder holding class pages, Media, a section's index — and nothing stopped a teacher deleting or renaming one in Obsidian. The features then failed SILENTLY: the Curriculum Coverage map in particular still rendered, still looked healthy, and was wrong.
siteHealth.whereItRuns: Inside build_site.py, after the shared and per-section folders have been merged into content/ and BEFORE Quartz builds or anything is uploaded. It has to run there rather than in the apps: every check is defined over the MERGED tree, which does not exist until the build makes it, and a check that only guarded the GUI button would be bypassed by the assistant, by `Plantoir --mcp-stdio`, by the launchers, and by the scheduled deploy — which runs from launchd or Task Scheduler with the app CLOSED, and is the case that matters most.
siteHealth.checksTheFeatureNotTheFolder: Every check asks whether the FEATURE produced anything, never whether a folder exists. Recreating an empty `Ontario Curriculum` folder does not restore a teacher's expectation pages, and `_find_curriculum_folder` requires a page named for an expectation code — so an existence check plus a Fix button would have silenced the warning AND left the map missing. A check that can be satisfied without fixing the problem is worse than no check.
siteHealth.scheduledDeployPublishesAnyway: A scheduled deploy NEVER refuses on a health finding. A slightly inaccurate curriculum map is a paper cut; a site update a teacher was counting on that silently did not happen is not. The finding is recorded and surfaced afterwards instead.

It could not find one, so the Curriculum Coverage page has been left out of this build. marker.rule: One line per finding on stdout, the prefix followed by a single-line JSON object carrying name, sentence, detail, fixable, course and section. The apps parse these lines out of the console transcript they are already reading; the teacher-facing SENTENCE travels in the line rather than being re-authored on each platform, so the two apps cannot word the same problem differently. A line CARRYING the prefix anywhere is machinery: it is kept out of the console a teacher reads WHOLE - what precedes a glued marker is half a line of progress chatter, not a sentence - including while it is still arriving, before its newline; and its finding is read from the prefix onward, so a marker glued to the tail of somebody else's half line is still found (#153: the mac had dropped it, finding and all, while showing the raw JSON). consoleCases below are the cases.
marker.why: A progress marker is matched loosely and getting one wrong is silent (see app-rules.json markerOrigins). A prefixed JSON line is unambiguous, survives being interleaved with ordinary build output, and carries structure a sentence cannot.

consoleCases.howToRunACase: Feed each case's chunks, in order, to ONE fresh console reader - the object that both reads findings out of arriving output and builds the transcript a teacher sees (the mac's ScriptRunner.receiveOutput) - exactly as a terminal would hand them over: a chunk is NOT a line, and a chunk boundary can fall anywhere. expectShown is the console's text once every chunk has arrived, as lines (joined with a newline, no trailing one). expectShownAfterEachChunk, where a case carries it, is the same thing read after EACH chunk, one entry per chunk - it is what pins a marker still arriving, which a check made only at the end cannot see. expectFindings is the names of the findings read, in order. The marker string is examples[1] verbatim, so the parse half is the toolchain's real output; 'a marker still arriving' cuts it after its first 60 characters, which ends in a colon.

repair.note: What Plantoir offers to put right, and what it says afterwards. Only two of the checks are repairable, and the line is the point: a fix must restore the FEATURE, not merely satisfy the check.

neverOffered.why: Recreating an empty curriculum folder would silence "the curriculum map could not be built" and leave the map missing, because the folder only counts once it holds a page named for an expectation code. A button that makes a warning go away without fixing anything is worse than no button: the teacher then believes it is dealt with. Decide from the check's NAME, not from the `fixable` flag alone — the flag means "this kind of thing is repairable", while what has to be true is that THIS app has a repair for it.

offered.rule: Create an empty Media folder, or a section index carrying only a title. Never overwrite: check first, so pressing twice — or pressing after fixing it in Obsidian — changes nothing.
offered.why: An empty folder and a bare front page are the correct starting state rather than a pretence. The pictures themselves are the teacher's and cannot be conjured back, and inventing content for a front page would put words in their mouth.

afterwards.rule: Say what was put back, offer to preview it again, and say what the preview does NOT cover. After a repair reported while PUBLISHING, the sentence must name who this does not reach yet (students) and what changes that (publishing again) — the preview is still offered, because that is how a teacher checks the repair worked. The preview is NOT offered in three cases: nothing needed repairing, the repair failed, and a publish is running just now. And the publish sentence must not assert a past publish: it is shown after a FAILED deploy too, and for a first publish nothing has ever gone out.
afterwards.why: The button is called "Preview Again", not "Build Again": the old label never said WHAT would be built, and the thing on offer already has a name the teacher knows. The preview was at first WITHHELD after a publish, reasoning that it does not change what students see — true, and beside the point: the teacher has just put a folder back and wants to SEE that it worked. Withholding it removed something useful to prevent a misunderstanding the words already prevent, so the words carry it instead. A repair whose outcome is invisible is one nobody trusts a second time, and the Media folder is somewhere a teacher cannot see from the app at all. A repair that FAILED must be reported too: both restores can fail on a read-only volume or a file sitting where the folder should be, and reporting only success made the two indistinguishable — silence on the failure path, in the feature written to end silence.

refusedWhenSomethingIsInTheWay.rule: A repair that cannot go ahead because something the TEACHER must move is sitting where it would write is refused, and reported as a failure — never as "already put right". Nothing is moved, renamed or deleted. The check that decides this asks whether the thing on disk is a file or a folder: a plain existence check is TRUE for a folder called index.md, and that is how a section with no front page came to be reported as already fine. The generic explanation offered for a repair that simply failed — the one that sends a teacher to check whether a folder is locked or read-only — is REPLACED by the sentence below, because permissions are not what is wrong. The preview is not offered. When BOTH kinds of failure happen at once, the generic explanation is said first and the sentence below last, so the paragraph ends on the step the teacher can actually take rather than on advice that does not apply to it.

cases.inTheWay: a folder named index.md, where the section's front page belongs
cases.sentence: There is a folder called index.md in the section{section} folder of your {course} course, where the front page should be. Plantoir has left it exactly as it is, in case your own pages are inside it. Move anything you want to keep somewhere else, then delete or rename that folder, and Plantoir can put the front page back.

refusedWhenSomethingIsInTheWay.namesTheCourse: The sentence names the course as well as the section folder. Every course has a section1, and the dialog it appears in shows a headline and this sentence and nothing else — so without the course code a teacher with two courses is told to go and look in a folder that exists twice.
refusedWhenSomethingIsInTheWay.why: "That is already put right. Nothing needed changing." was said about a section that still had no front page, so the build still produced no site and the publish still refused. The one dialog written to end silence was telling the teacher the problem was dealt with, which is the worst answer available: they stop looking. Answering "could not put that back" is at least honest, but the explanation that goes with it sends them to check permissions on a folder that is not locked.
refusedWhenSomethingIsInTheWay.rejected: Moving the folder aside and writing a proper front page in its place. It relocates a folder that may hold the teacher's own pages, without asking, and neither app can see what is inside it — a repair that moves a teacher's work to fix a warning is a worse outcome than the warning. Refusing costs one more step by hand and nothing else.
refusedWhenSomethingIsInTheWay.alsoRecorded: The refusal leaves a line on the trail — activityTrail "folder problem not repaired" — because the folder in the way is something the teacher will very likely have moved by the time they report it.

reportedOncePerFinding.rule: A repair reports one result per FINDING, never one per check NAME. Two sections each missing a front page are two findings with one name: both are repaired either way, but keyed by the name only the LAST result survives, so "section 1 restored, section 2 was already there" comes back as "That is already put right. Nothing needed changing." with no preview offered — for a repair that really did put a page back. The SENTENCE, on the other hand, names each thing ONCE however many findings produced it: "Put the front page and the front page back." is not a sentence.

cases.note: The case a name-keyed result gets wrong: the second answer overwrites the first, and the teacher is told nothing needed changing.
Two repairs, one sentence. The de-duplication that stops "the front page and the front page".

reportedOncePerFinding.howToRunACase: One finding per listed section, all of the named `check`, all `fixable: true`, for a course whose `section_numbers` are exactly the listed numbers. `frontPage` says what is on disk in that section before the repair: "missing" is nothing at all, "theTeachersOwn" is an index.md the teacher wrote, which must survive untouched. `expectResults` is one answer per finding IN THE ORDER GIVEN, drawn from restored | alreadyFine | failed | refused ("refused" is refusedWhenSomethingIsInTheWay, which BOTH platforms now have). `expectHeadline` and `expectCanRebuild` are what the report says; the occasion does not matter here, because it only changes the DETAIL. Ask for the report and the results on separate copies of the course: every repair runs as it goes, so anything a first pass RESTORED answers alreadyFine to a second. (Only that much — a repair that failed or was refused answers the same again, which is why the vocabulary above still has those two words in it.)
reportedOncePerFinding.reachability: Unreachable from either app's own front end today, and fixed anyway. A section window owns one runner and the checks announce per section, so the findings handed to a repair have always been one section's. The collapse is SILENT and the constraint was written down nowhere, so the next caller — the assistant, a second window, a whole-course fix — would have met it as a wrong report rather than as a compile error. Recorded as latent rather than as a shipped bug, so nobody later reads it as damage a teacher met.
reportedOncePerFinding.why: Windows found it by porting the mac's file line by line and shipped the per-finding shape first (reported from Windows, 2026-09-06); the mac followed on 2026-09-07. Both now return one entry per finding and de-duplicate the names when building the sentence.
reportedOncePerFinding.knownLimit: One name with TWO different outcomes — section 1 restored, section 2 failed — still reads "Put the front page back." followed by "Could not put the front page back.", because the sentence has no way to say which section is which. Left as it is on both platforms: it is as unreachable as the collapse was, and new wording nobody has weighed is harder to take back than a paragraph of explanation. The refusal case does not have the problem on either platform, because its own sentence names the section folder. Windows gained that case on 2026-09-07 (branch issue/33-repair-refused-folder-in-the-way): until then a blocked section there fell into `failed` with the generic explanation and the same nameless pairing, which is what this paragraph used to describe. That has stopped being a Windows limit; the limit above it is shared.

oneAlertAtATime.rule: The outcome is shown AFTER the dialog it was requested from has gone, never raised from inside that dialog's own button action.
oneAlertAtATime.why: A view presents one alert at a time; asking for a second while the first is dismissing loses one of them, and the one lost would be the report the teacher just asked for. It is worse than a lost alert: on 2026-09-05 doing exactly this CRASHED the shipping app (GUI-IMPROVEMENTS.md row 391) — EXC_BAD_ACCESS in AppKitDialogBridge.updateExistingAlert, because AppKit tears the sheet down inside a layout pass and spins a nested runloop from inside a display-cycle callback already running.

checks.name: curriculumCoverageFoundNothing
checks.sentence: The curriculum map for {course} Section {section} could not be built.
checks.detail: Plantoir looks for a folder whose name mentions the curriculum, holding one page per expectation. It could not find one, so the Curriculum Coverage page has been left out of this build. If you renamed or moved that folder, the map will come back as soon as it can find it again.
checks.why: The headline case. The map used to vanish with nothing said, and the page it would have linked from says nothing either — a teacher discovers it in May.

checks.name: courseTeachesNothing
checks.sentence: Plantoir could not find any class pages in {course} Section {section}.
checks.detail: The curriculum map counts an expectation as addressed when a page that a class links to mentions it. With no class pages to start from, it has counted every published page instead, so the map is more generous than it should be.
checks.why: This is the fallback that made a wrong map look healthy. Saying so is the entire fix: the fallback itself is deliberate, because a map that hid everything would be worse.

checks.name: mediaFolderMissing
checks.sentence: The Media folder for {course} is not there.
checks.detail: Images and files you have added to pages live in a folder called Media, beside your course. Plantoir could not find it, so anything on a page that points into it will be missing from the built site.
checks.why: Checks the TARGET, not the link: content/Media is recreated on every build, so checking the link itself always passes. What breaks is the course-level folder it points AT.

checks.name: sectionIndexMissing
checks.detail: Every section has a page called index.md that students land on first. This section's is missing. A preview will open on whatever page happens to come first, and publishing cannot go ahead at all until the front page is back.
checks.why: Restorable safely, unlike the curriculum folder — which is why this one may offer to fix itself and that one may not. The detail used to stop at "whatever page happens to come first", which is true of a PREVIEW and understates publishing by a mile: Quartz emits no root index.html without an index.md, so the build produces no site to publish and the deploy has nothing to upload. Naming both outcomes is what tells a teacher whether they can carry on for now or must fix it before they publish.

checks.name: handWrittenCoveragePage
checks.sentence: A page called Curriculum Coverage will be overwritten each time you build.
checks.detail: Plantoir writes the Curriculum Coverage page itself, every build. There is a page by that name in your own notes, and it is not the one being published — rename yours to keep it.
checks.why: The inverse of the other checks: not something missing, something PRESENT that gets clobbered. A name refusal in Settings cannot see this, because a teacher makes this page in Obsidian.

checks.name: noGradedFolders
checks.sentence: Nothing in {course} Section {section} currently counts for marks.
checks.detail: The curriculum map marks an expectation as evaluated when a page in your graded folders addresses it. None of those folders were found, so every expectation is shown as not yet evaluated. You can choose which folders count in Course Settings.
checks.why: When no folders count for marks or the configured folders are missing, the curriculum map shows zero evaluated expectations. Telling the teacher lets them choose which folders count in Course Settings rather than wondering why no expectations show as evaluated.

checks.name: pageSettingsUnreadable
checks.sentence: Plantoir could not read the settings of “{page}” in {course} Section {section}, so it is hidden from students until they are fixed.
checks.sentenceForSeveral: Plantoir could not read the settings of {count} pages in {course} Section {section}, so they are hidden from students until they are fixed.
checks.detail: A page whose settings cannot be read might be one you meant to keep from students, so Plantoir hides it rather than risk showing it. To show a page again, correct the lines at the top of it in Obsidian and build again: {pages}.
checks.frontPage: One of them is the front page of {course} Section {section}, so until it is fixed the website has no front page and cannot be published.
checks.fill: {page} is the page's place in the course folder without .md (section1/index for a section's front page), {line} the line of the PAGE the reader stopped near, counted from the opening --- as line 1, {count} how many. `sentence` when there is one page and `sentenceForSeveral` otherwise; `detail` names at most ten pages, each through `pageWithLine` or `pageWithoutLine`, joined with ", ", then `andMore` with the number left over; `frontPage` is added to the end of the detail, after a space, when the section's front page is one of them. Every value is filled in ONE pass, so a page a teacher named "{course} notes" is named as it is. ONE finding per section build, never one per page: both apps key a finding on name, course and section, so two per-page findings would collide.
checks.why: Russell, 2026-09-21 (#246, option B): a page that wrongly DISAPPEARS is noticed and harmless; one that wrongly APPEARS cannot be undone. Before, a page whose settings the build could not read was PUBLISHED whenever Quartz could read what PyYAML could not (a yes/no, number or date used as a key, U+2028, an impossible date) - even one hidden by publishForSection1: false, which is what the app writes - and for 14 of the 18 known shapes it STOPPED the whole build with a developer's error. The build now hides such a page in its own copy only, keeps its body, and names it here; the teacher's file is not touched. Not repairable: rewriting a teacher's settings means guessing what they meant. `contracts/shared-rules.json` -> `unreadablePageSettings` holds the cases, and documentation/05-build-pipeline.md the measurements and what was rejected.

unreadablePageSettings.note: What the build does with a page whose settings block it cannot read (#246). The words a teacher reads are siteHealth.checks[pageSettingsUnreadable]; these are the cases, run by scripts/test_unreadable_page_settings.py through the real build_site.process_frontmatter and by scripts/check_visibility_against_the_site.py down the rest of the chain to the site.
unreadablePageSettings.rule: A page whose settings block the build cannot read is treated as HIDDEN in every section, whatever it says, and named in ONE site-health finding per section build, with the line the reader stopped near where it can tell. Only the build's copy is changed - its settings become publish: false and its body is kept - and the teacher's file is never touched. A copy that cannot be rewritten is removed, and a build that can do neither stops rather than produce a site that might show it. An unreadable FRONT PAGE is hidden too, so the section has no website: the last built one is cleared, as for a missing front page, and a publish says why in its own words (app-rules.json -> failureExplanations) rather than the missing front page's. Nothing new goes on the trail: the finding reaches it through the existing `folder problem found` line, which carries the check's name and never a page's.
unreadablePageSettings.why: Russell, 2026-09-21, option B: a page that wrongly DISAPPEARS is noticed and harmless; one that wrongly APPEARS cannot be undone. Before, such a page was PUBLISHED whenever Quartz could read what the build could not - even one hidden by publishForSection1: false, which is what the app writes - and for most shapes the whole build STOPPED instead, withholding every other update including a scheduled publish a teacher was counting on.
unreadablePageSettings.measured: python-frontmatter 1.3.0 / PyYAML 6.0.3 / gray-matter with js-yaml JSON_SCHEMA, in the image, 2026-09-25. Of the shapes in copyingAPageBetweenCourses.builderAgreement, 18 are refused by the build's reader when it opens the page as a file: 14 of them Quartz could not read either, so the whole build stopped, and 4 (a date that cannot be, the 29th of February with a colon in its offset, `yes` as a key, U+2028) Quartz read, publishing the page unless it also carried a plain publish: false. A 19th, the lone carriage return, raises only when the block is handed over as text; the build opens pages with universal newlines and reads it (the case above). 0 of 14,699 real and shipped pages are refused today, so no existing site changes on the first build after the update. For the shapes that carry a position, the line is counted from it: of those, most point AT the wrong line and the rest one or two lines past it, so the words say NEAR line N.
rejected: Deleting the page from the build instead of hiding it: a missing front page is a different state, with a repair that would find the page and say it was already put right.
A rule in Quartz's publish filter: Quartz cannot read 14 of the 18 shapes at all.
Stopping the build, which is what happened before for most shapes: one typo withheld every other update, including a scheduled publish (siteHealth.scheduledDeployPublishesAnyway).
One finding per page: both apps key a finding on name, course and section, so they would collide.
Printing the reader's own message: it quotes the page's words into a console that goes into problem reports.

Making the apps' readers call such a page hidden: it would need a twin of the build's reader in Swift and C#, and the one direction left (the app says shown, the site hides it) is the mild one, and is announced by the finding.
unreadablePageSettings.notCoveredHere: A block whose END the build cannot find - a closing fence that is indented, or one never closed - is #188's. It cannot be told from a page that begins with a line across the page (the case above), and 0 of the 14,699 pages are either shape.
unreadablePageSettings.howToRunACase: Write `page` byte for byte as a page of the build's content, call process_frontmatter on it for `section`, and read what it became. expectHidden is what the site does with the result (build_site._is_draft over the processed text, which check_visibility_against_the_site.py holds to the site). expectReadable false means the page is recorded as unreadable with expectLine (null when the reader names none), its body below the settings is unchanged, and nothing printed carries the reader's message or the page's settings.

An OSC window-title sequence ends at BEL, not at a letter - a stripper that only knows CSI leaves the title text in the console.
Newline, tab and carriage return are KEPT. Stripping the carriage return breaks the progress lines the launchers redraw in place.

transcriptStripping.note: The launchers' output is written for a terminal: colour codes, cursor moves, window-title sequences. Both apps show that output to a teacher, so both must strip the same things - and KEEP the same things. Newlines, carriage returns and tabs survive; every other control character does not. Inputs below use \u001b for ESC and \u0007 for BEL.

wizard.note: What the New Course wizard says. AUTHORED rather than generated, and that is the whole point of the entry: a generated readout cannot fail when the code it reads changes, so a button label written by the generator would simply be rewritten to match whatever the button now says. Written by hand, each platform asserts its own constant against it and a drift goes red. Same reasoning as app-rules.json's split between milestones (a readout) and deployArguments (an expectation).
wizard.noExampleContentNote: Example content isn’t available for this course code yet, so the course will start with empty folders ready for your own pages.
wizard.noStartingContentNote: This course will start with empty folders ready for your own pages.
wizard.skeletonToggleLabelForAGeneralSkeleton: Start from a general course skeleton
wizard.skeletonToggleCaption: There is no ready-made course for this code, but there is a starting point shaped for the subject: folders that suit it, four units of class pages to rename, a page explaining what the site can do, and placeholders saying what belongs where.
wizard.skeletonToggleCaptionWhenExampleContentI: There is also a starting point shaped for the subject: folders that suit it, four units of class pages to rename, a page explaining what the site can do, and placeholders saying what belongs where.
wizard.structureFromExampleNote: The example content chooses the folders and files for this course, so every page lands where its links expect it. Turn off pre-populating to start from the subject’s own structure instead, and change it however you like.
wizard.whenTheNoteIsShown:
THREE situations under Starting Content, across TWO sentences. The course starts with empty folders in all three; what differs is whether example content exists for the typed code, because one of the sentences says something about that and must not say it when it is false.

(1) The typed code has neither ready-made pages nor a skeleton — in practice, no code typed yet — and (2) the typed code has a skeleton the teacher has turned DOWN: both read noExampleContentNote. These two are one situation for a teacher and neither platform invents a second sentence for them. (3) The typed code HAS ready-made pages, the teacher declined them, and then declined the skeleton those pages' absence revealed: this reads noStartingContentNote, which is the same sentence with its first clause removed. "Example content isn't available for this course code yet" is false to somebody who was offered it one question ago, and rewording the shipped sentence to cover all three would change what ~1,900 codes with no payload read, which nobody asked for.

The mac reads them from WizardWording.noExampleContentNote and WizardWording.noStartingContentNote, choosing between them in noteForACourseStartingEmpty; Windows from NewCourseDialog.NoExampleContentNote() and its sibling. (1) and (2) share the accessibility identifier noExampleContentNote, being branches of the same if and never on screen at once; (3) has its OWN, noStartingContentNote, because a test that found the shared one could no longer say WHICH sentence a teacher is reading. Windows has shown the note while the toggle is off since 2026-09-07; the mac showed it only for a code with no skeleton at all until 2026-09-18 (issue #77), which is the drift this key exists to stop. The third situation could not be reached at all until 2026-09-21 (issue #248), because a code with ready-made pages was never offered a skeleton.
wizard.whereTheStartingContentSentencesAreRende: All under the Starting Content section. skeletonToggleLabel is the toggle itself, with {subject} replaced by the family's label lowercased — the mac's WizardWording.skeletonToggleLabel(forFamilyNamed:label:), Windows' equivalent. skeletonToggleLabelForAGeneralSkeleton replaces it outright for the GENERAL family, whose own label is "This Course" (written for the skeleton's pages) and renders as "Start from a this course skeleton" through the template — which has been on screen for club and custom codes since the toggle existed, and which MCMPR11, the one British Columbia code with ready-made pages, now reaches too. The caption below the toggle is skeletonToggleCaption for a code with no ready-made pages and skeletonToggleCaptionWhenExampleContentIsDeclined for a code whose ready-made pages were declined, where the first one's opening clause is false. structureFromExampleNote stands in for the structure editor while the example content is choosing the folders; its second sentence changed with issue #248, since turning pre-populating off now leaves the SUBJECT's lists on screen rather than the school-neutral factory ones.
wizard.whereItIsRendered: The mac reads it from WizardWording.createCourseButton and renders it in NewCourseWizardView; Windows renders it in NewCourseDialog. Named in prose rather than as a structured key, the way buildOutputLocation names its sources, because nothing reads such a key and a rename would rot it silently.
wizard.whyThisOneString: It is the first thing a teacher presses in this app. Both platforms have said Create Course since the wizard existed and nothing pinned it until 2026-09-08 — Windows asserted it only in NewCourseWizardUiTests, which is opt-in behind PLANTOIR_UI_TESTS=1 and part of no gate, and the mac asserted it nowhere. Two apps agreeing by habit is not two apps agreeing on purpose; the first notice of a drift would have been a teacher reading a different button from the one in the other platform's screenshots.
wizard.gatedTests: Each platform's GATED test compares its constant to this key, which pins the constant rather than the rendered button. Only the UI suites see the button itself, and both are opt-in and part of no gate — QuartzTeachersUITests on the mac, [UiFact] under PLANTOIR_UI_TESTS=1 on Windows. Said plainly because the first version of this entry called Windows' arrangement the weakest place a shared sentence can live while the mac had the same arrangement and one fewer test.

skeletonToggle.rule:
A skeleton is OFFERED for a course code when a family exists for its prefix AND the teacher is not taking the example content written for that code. One question, in one function — SkeletonCatalog.hasSkeleton(forCode:takingExampleContent:) on the mac, SkeletonCatalog.HasSkeleton on Windows — because three surfaces ask it: the toggle's own visibility, what the structure editor adopts, and the use_skeleton key in course_config.json. A code with ready-made pages therefore has a skeleton too, and gets it the moment those pages are turned down.

And then: the structure editor must show what will actually be created, in BOTH directions. Turning "Start from a <subject> skeleton" ON adopts that subject's five lists. Turning it OFF puts the defaults back — the LCS variants for the two SHARED lists when the terminology switch is on, the plain defaults for the two per-section lists, which have no LCS variant — for each list still EQUAL to what the adoption put there, and leaves every other list exactly as the teacher left it. The marks pool is the one exception to that last clause, and why is in (4) below: a pool the teacher ticked is kept, but narrowed to the folders the course will actually have, since a pool naming a folder that has just left the editor is a silent loss of marks rather than a choice. With no adoption to compare against, nothing changes at all.

The example-content toggle moves the editor exactly as the skeleton toggle does, in both directions: turning example content OFF adopts (the skeleton it has just revealed), turning it back ON restores. A teacher who changes their mind must get the file they would have got without changing it.
skeletonToggle.why:
Russell's decision for Windows, 2026-09-06, copied to the mac 2026-09-18 (issue #77). A one-way adoption was this feature's bug in miniature: a teacher who typed SNC4M, watched Investigations and Concepts appear and then turned the toggle off was shown — and got — the science skeleton's folders with none of its pages, while the file said use_skeleton: false. A wizard that lies about what it is about to make is a worse product than one that never asked.

Four consequences, each deliberate. (1) A list is recognised as untouched by VALUE, not by a dirty flag: a list edited and then edited BACK to exactly what the adoption set is restored along with the untouched ones, and that is intended — a teacher cannot see the difference between a list they never touched and one they have put back, so neither can the rule. (2) The LCS switch REWRITES the two shared lists, so flipping it after an adoption leaves them unequal to the snapshot and they stay as the switch left them, while the per-section lists still go back. (3) With no snapshot — the toggle turned off before any code was typed, or on a code whose skeleton was never adopted — NOTHING changes, rather than the defaults being forced over lists the teacher may have edited first. (4) The marks pool can never name a folder that has just left the editor, and that takes TWO rules rather than one: a pool still equal to the adoption's is RE-INFERRED over the restored folders, and a pool the teacher has ticked themselves is kept but NARROWED to the folders the course will actually have. Miss the second and a teacher who adopted the mathematics skeleton, unticked Tasks and then declined the skeleton is shown a checklist with nothing ticked while the wizard writes graded_folders naming Thinking Tasks, a folder the course does not have — and the two apps then write DIFFERENT files for the same clicks, which is what this contract exists to stop. (The wizard's pool is the only net: since GitHub issue #192 setup_course.py writes a saved pool back as it was rather than reconciling it again — gradedFolders.rerunningSetup — so a wizard that wrote something untrue would leave it in the file.) The two apps reach the same answer from opposite ends: the mac narrows the pool inside the restore, Windows leaves it and narrows on every read (CurrentGradedFolders) and again when the file is written.

Rejected: tracking a dirty flag per list (a flag has to be got right in every editing path, and gets one wrong the first time a list is changed from somewhere new, where value equality cannot); and a further rule for the narrow hole value equality leaves, which would have made the two apps differ for a case no teacher can tell apart.

A fifth consequence, added 2026-09-21 with the first half of the rule above (GitHub issue #248). Both apps asked "is there example content for this code?" rather than "is the teacher taking it?", so for all 38 codes with a payload the toggle was never shown, nothing was ever adopted, and use_skeleton was written false whatever the teacher chose. MEASURED by driving the real scripts/setup_course.py through a pty: ICS4U created that way holds 18 .md files; the same code with use_skeleton true holds 47, and the tree and the config are byte-identical to what ICS2O — same family, no payload — has always got. The Python needed no change at all, find_skeleton_dir having never looked at payloads; the whole fault was the two apps, which is exactly the shape of drift this file exists to catch, and it stood for five weeks (091a23dc, 2026-08-13) because nothing here asked the question in the teacher's terms. REJECTED while fixing it: a third "empty folders" sentence covering all three situations at once, which would have reworded what ~1,900 codes read; and anything retroactive for courses already created this way — Russell's call, 2026-09-21, having deleted and remade the one course it affected.

A sixth consequence, 2026-09-22 (GitHub issue #251), and it REVERSES a rejection recorded here the day before. #248 also rejected a curriculum-pages toggle for a skeleton that ships a Curriculum folder, on the ground that the fixed and control runs produce identical trees, so adding one would make a payload code behave unlike its own family. Half of that is still right: for the ~1,900 codes with no payload there is nothing to include, and the toggle decides nothing. It was wrong for the 38 that HAVE one — the expectations written for their code exist, the teacher declined the lessons rather than the curriculum, and behaving like its own family is precisely what makes their course wrong. So a payload code that declines its ready-made pages now gets the subject's skeleton WITH the payload's curriculum expectations installed into it, and the three curriculum answers written as they are for a payload course. MEASURED: ICS4U went from 2 curriculum pages — a generic index and a placeholder expectation called A1.1 reading "DELETE THIS PAGE" — to 61, MCMPR11 to 59 British Columbia standards with no A1.1 among them, and ICS2O, which has no payload, stayed at 2. The key that says so is expectSavedIncludeCurriculumPages on the payload cases below.
skeletonToggle.whoRunsIt: The mac runs every case below in SharedRulesContractTests as of 2026-09-18; WizardStructureTests covers what the cases cannot reach — the pieces the rule is assembled from, and a scan proving the toggle is WIRED, since a control with no handler was the original bug and no test that calls the handler itself can see one. Nothing on Windows reads this key yet — their suite stays GREEN until it is wired in, and as of 2026-09-21 their behaviour is NO LONGER the one described here: SkeletonCatalog.HasSkeleton returns false for any code with example content, and their own SkeletonCatalogTests.HasSkeletonReturnsFalseWhenExampleContentExists asserts that against itself and passes. So what Windows owes is the behaviour AND the test, and the seam to run the cases against (their restore lives inside the private NewCourseDialog.RestoreGenericStructure). The line that WILL go red on their side is ContractTests.SharedRules_ActivityTrailEvents_Exist, over the "course created" event added to activityTrail.mustRecord in the same piece — deliberately, because an unrun case is a request nobody reads and a red suite naming the issue is one somebody answers.

lists.note: Two of the five slots cannot tell one answer from another for most codes, which is worth knowing before reading a green run as coverage: every bundled family ships per_section_folders of exactly ["All Classes"], which is also the factory default, so only perSectionFILES proves the per-section half of a restore; and every family declares graded_folders of ["Tasks"] except MATHEMATICS (["Thinking Tasks", "Tasks"]), so a marks-pool expectation means nothing unless its case uses a mathematics code. The cases below that carry courseCode MPM1D are there for exactly that reason. A third thing not to read as coverage: in a runner that resolves the skeleton symbol through the same catalog an adoption copies from, a turnOn case's four list expectations prove that the adoption FIRED rather than what it copied — which is why the MPM1D adoption case spells its marks pool out. The factory values of the five lists follow, so a case can say "the defaults" without either app retyping them. BOTH suites must assert these arrays EQUAL their own WizardDefaults constants — that is what stops the vocabulary drifting away from the thing it names, and without it a case could pass against a contract that no longer describes the product. The per-section lists have NO LCS variant, the terminology switch rewriting only the two shared ones, so "lcs" carries two arrays rather than four. scripts/setup_course.py keeps its own copies for the command-line wizard and they are deliberately NOT pinned here: the Python's shared-folder lists also carry "Media", which both apps leave out because the toolchain manages that folder itself, so an equality test would be asserting a difference that is correct.

symbols.note: What a list value in a case's given or expect means. A literal array means itself — used for a teacher's own edit, which belongs to nobody's constants.
symbols.factory: The lists.factory array for that slot.
symbols.lcs: The lists.lcs array for that slot. Valid for the two SHARED lists only.
symbols.skeleton: The family's own array for that slot, resolved through each app's SkeletonCatalog from support/skeletons/<family>/manifest.json for courseCode — NEVER a literal copy here, because the skeletons are GENERATED (.claude/skills/example-content/generate_skeletons.py writes ~1,950 pages across 50 families) and a copy would be a fixture nobody regenerates. In the gradedFolders slot it means what an adoption sets: the manifest's own graded_folders where it names any, and otherwise the historical rule over the family's own folders — SkeletonCatalog.adoptedGradedFolders on the mac, SkeletonCatalog.AdoptedGradedFolders on Windows.
symbols.skeletonReversed: The same family array, reversed. Stands for a list a teacher emptied and typed back in a different order: the same names, so a dirty flag would call it untouched, and a different value, so this rule leaves it alone.
symbols.lcsFlippedFromSkeleton: What the terminology switch leaves behind when it is flipped ON over the family's own list — switchingFactoryItems(in: skeleton, toFactory: lcs, fromFactory: factory) on the mac, SwitchingFactoryItems on Windows. Valid for the two SHARED lists only. Computed rather than written out, so a change to a generated skeleton cannot rot the case.

skeletonToggle.howToRunACase:
Start with given.lists, a snapshot of what an adoption of given.courseCode (or the courseCode above) would set when given.hasSnapshot is true and no snapshot otherwise, the terminology switch at given.usesLCSTerminology, and the toggle itself ON, which is where a new wizard opens. Apply each step in order, each step regardless of what the one before it left the toggle at — a case may open with turnOn on a fixture that has no snapshot, which is a state a real wizard reaches only by other means and is written this way to say what an adoption does from the factory defaults. turnOn adopts unless the teacher's shared folders say the list has been edited (SkeletonCatalog.structureToAdopt / StructureToAdopt, which is the rule that predates this one), recording a fresh snapshot when it does. turnOff restores as the rule above says and then forgets the snapshot. typeAnotherCode is the teacher editing the course-code field to otherCourseCode — a code in a different family — which adopts only while the toggle is ON: the guard in adoptSkeletonStructure / AdoptSkeletonStructure, without which a teacher who declined the skeleton and then corrected a typo in the code is given it back. Be honest about what that case proves: a runner implements the guard itself, so the case pins the RULE and not your app's wiring — deleting the guard from the product leaves it green. Each platform owes its own check that its real adopt entry point reads the toggle (the mac's is a source scan in WizardStructureTests). Compare all five lists with expect. Build each case's fixture on its own: a cache shared between cases would let one case's adoption answer another's.

given.takesExampleContent is where the example-content toggle starts, and ABSENT MEANS TRUE — which is where a new wizard opens and which leaves every case written before 2026-09-21 meaning exactly what it meant. A runner must tolerate its absence rather than require it. It is the second half of every adoption question: a case whose courseCode has ready-made pages still resolves a family by prefix, since the prefix map knows nothing about payloads, but nothing is adopted for it WHILE takesExampleContent is true — and everything is adopted for it once that is false, which is the whole of issue #248.

Two more steps, the two halves of the example-content toggle. declineExampleContent sets takesExampleContent to FALSE and then adopts for given.courseCode (not otherCourseCode — this is the same course, being offered its subject's shape instead of its ready-made pages) reading the same skeletonIsWanted guard turnOn and typeAnotherCode read: a teacher who declined the skeleton and then declined the example content must not have the skeleton handed back. takeExampleContent sets it to TRUE and then restores exactly as turnOff restores, forgetting the snapshot. Three states they reach together are worth saying out loud, because both apps must write the same file in each: a list the teacher EDITED after declining is left alone by the restore, so it travels into a course that is taking ready-made pages (harmless — setup_course.py's example branch overrides the structure and reconciles the marks pool, MEASURED — but the two apps must agree on it); flipping the terminology switch between the two leaves the two shared lists as the switch left them, by consequence (2) above; and a second decline after the skeleton was declined adopts NOTHING, the teacher's choice being remembered, with noStartingContentNote on screen.

expectSavedUseSkeleton, where a case carries it, is what course_config.json must say after the steps — the rule itself, hasSkeleton(courseCode, takingExampleContent) AND skeletonIsWanted. It is the assertion that fails against an app asking only whether example content EXISTS.

expectSavedIncludeCurriculumPages, where a case carries it, is what course_config.json must say about the curriculum pages — and ABSENT MEANS NOT ASSERTED, so a runner must tolerate its absence rather than require it, exactly as it does given.takesExampleContent. The rule behind it is curriculumPagesOffered: the code has a payload, that payload declares a curriculum folder, AND either the teacher is taking the payload or a skeleton is offered and wanted. It is written for issue #251, where a teacher who declined the ready-made pages and kept the subject's skeleton was given a Curriculum folder holding the skeleton's generic index and one placeholder expectation called A1.1 — so the curriculum coverage map, built from those pages, had one fake cell to colour. MEASURED by driving the real setup_course.py: ICS4U went from 2 curriculum pages to 61, MCMPR11 to 59 British Columbia standards with no A1.1 among them, and ICS2O — which has no payload — stayed at 2. An app that writes false here never runs the launcher's new branch, whatever its interface shows, and the course comes out exactly as broken with every gate green.

cases.name: off, with nothing touched since the adoption
cases.why: The plain case, and the one the bug got wrong. The marks pool is the historical rule read off the restored folders, which is what a brand-new course has always opened with. This is also the case a list edited and edited BACK exactly lands in — the data cannot carry that history, and that is the point: the rule asks what is on screen, not what happened to it.

cases.name: off, with the terminology switch on
cases.why: Restoring means restoring what a new course would have opened with NOW, which for a teacher who turned the terminology switch on before typing a code is the LCS set. The two per-section lists have no LCS variant and go back to the plain defaults, which is the half most easily missed.

cases.name: off, after the shared folders were edited
cases.why: List by list, not all-or-nothing. An earlier version of this on Windows asked one question of the shared folders and replaced all five lists on the answer, which discarded an edited file list. The marks pool is re-inferred over what the editor actually ends up with — the teacher's own folders plus the restored per-section ones — so it cannot name a folder that is no longer there.

cases.name: off, after the terminology switch was flipped
cases.why: The trap worth knowing: the switch rewrote the two shared lists, so they no longer equal the snapshot and the restore must leave them exactly as they are — including the skeleton's own folders that the switch carried across. The per-section lists it never touched still go back. An implementation that re-snapshotted on the terminology flip would silently restore these two as well, and the teacher would watch their College Board folder disappear.

cases.name: off, with a list put back in a different order
cases.why: Value equality compares ORDER too, and the order a teacher put their folders in is a choice — a course whose Tasks folder sits at the top of the sidebar was arranged that way on purpose. So the same names in a different order is an edit, and is left alone.

cases.name: off, with nothing ever adopted
cases.why: Nothing to recognise as untouched, so nothing is touched. A restore that ran anyway would overwrite the lists of a teacher who turned the toggle off before typing a code — work they did with no skeleton anywhere in sight.

cases.name: on, from the factory defaults
cases.why: The other direction, and the reason the marks pool is part of this rule rather than left to be worked out later: the mathematics family ships Thinking Tasks rather than Tasks, and a course that adopted its folders without its declared pool would lose those marks with nothing said.

cases.name: on, over lists the teacher has edited
cases.why: The adoption rule that predates this one still holds in both directions: a folder list the teacher has changed is never overwritten, whether the change comes from a new course code or from this toggle.

cases.name: off, then on, then off again
cases.why: A teacher changing their mind twice must end where they would have ended changing it once. This is the case that catches a snapshot forgotten on the way out or kept on the way back in: the second turnOn has to take a FRESH snapshot, or the last turnOff restores against a stale one and leaves the skeleton's folders on screen — the original bug, reached by a longer road.

cases.name: on, for a subject that names its own marks folders
cases.why: The only family whose marks pool is not ["Tasks"], and therefore the only code that can prove an adoption carries the pool at all. The wizard's own default is ["Tasks"]; a mathematics course that kept it would count nothing in Thinking Tasks, which is where its assessed work goes, and say nothing about it.

cases.name: off, after unticking one of a subject's own marks folders
cases.why: The pool is the teacher's — they unticked Tasks themselves — so it is not re-inferred; but Thinking Tasks has just left the editor with the rest of the skeleton, so what is left is nothing, and "asked, and nothing counts" is the honest answer. An implementation that only re-infers an UNTOUCHED pool writes graded_folders: ["Thinking Tasks"] here, against a course that has no such folder — a different file from the other app's for the same clicks. The expectation on this slot is written out as a LITERAL rather than as the skeleton symbol, which is the one place this list copies a generated value deliberately: the symbol would make the adoption case a tautology, so a change to support/skeletons/mathematics/manifest.json must be reflected here by hand.

cases.name: off, then a different course code typed
cases.why: The half of the fix that is not the toggle. Adoption runs on every change to the course code, so a teacher who declines the skeleton and then corrects a typo — or changes their mind about which course they are making — must not have it handed back to them. Both apps guard the adoption on the toggle for this; nothing else in this list reaches that guard.

cases.name: a course code with ready-made pages, being taken
cases.why: Example content beats a skeleton WHILE THE TEACHER IS TAKING IT, so this toggle is not even shown for such a code and neither direction may touch the lists. This is the case that proves the teacher who says yes to the ready-made pages is untouched by everything below: the four cases that follow it all begin by saying no.

cases.name: a course code with ready-made pages, declined
cases.why: Issue #248 itself, as data. A teacher who turns down the ready-made drama pages is offered the drama SHAPE, which is what the command-line wizard has always offered and what both apps refused to. Before the fix the lists stayed factory and the file said use_skeleton: false, so the course arrived with empty folders — 18 pages where the same code with the skeleton has 47.

cases.name: a course code with ready-made pages, declined, then the skeleton declined too
cases.why: Empty folders are still a choice, and a teacher may make it — twice over. What they read here is noStartingContentNote rather than noExampleContentNote, because example content plainly IS available for this code: they were offered it one question ago. This is also the state the fix must leave reachable: making the skeleton the default is not the same as making it compulsory.

cases.name: a course code with ready-made pages, declined and then taken again
cases.why: The thing that must not move, written as a round trip: a teacher who changes their mind gets the file they would have got without changing it. MCV4U is chosen because mathematics is the only family whose marks pool is not ["Tasks"] — an adoption that failed to come back would leave "Thinking Tasks" in the pool of a course taking ready-made drama-shaped-nothing, and no other code in this list can tell the difference. (MEASURED: the Python's example branch would override the structure and reconcile the pool anyway, so no teacher ends up with a broken course; what is at stake is the two apps writing the SAME file for the same clicks, which is what this contract is for.)

cases.name: a course code with ready-made pages, declined, for a subject that names its own marks folders
cases.why: The adoption a declined payload triggers carries the subject's marks pool, exactly as the toggle's own does — the same silent loss the MPM1D adoption case exists to stop, reached by the new road. Written as a LITERAL for the same reason that one is: the skeleton symbol would make it a tautology, so a change to support/skeletons/mathematics/manifest.json must be reflected here by hand.

clubToggle.note: “This is a club” in the New Course wizard (#267). Russell, 2026-09-24: a club starts with empty folders and a first “Week 1” page; it has NO curriculum coverage page and no Curriculum folder (coverage can be turned on later in Course Settings); its words are editable in the wizard and NOT switchable afterwards; the defaults are the `club` words below. The choice is shown for EVERY code and starts ticked for a code ClubCodeRule calls a club (course-management.json), until the teacher touches it. Nothing called is_club is written: the course is a club because of what IS written — class_page_scheme "numbered", unit_word, class_folder, front_page_heading and class_noun (file-formats.json) — plus use_skeleton and prepopulate_example_content false and the three curriculum keys false. A club takes no skeleton and no ready-made pages because both are Unit/Day pages, which a numbered course does not read as class pages; setup_course.py refuses to pour either into a numbered course as a second net. Mac: WizardWording, ClubVocabulary and ClubFill.applying (Models/ClubFill.swift); NewCourseWizardView.applyClubChoice.
clubToggle.label: This is a club
clubToggle.caption: A club meets rather than holds classes: its pages are numbered one after another, it has no curriculum, and it starts with a page for its first meeting. The words below can be changed now, but not once the course is made.
clubToggle.startingContentNote: A club starts with empty folders and one page for its first meeting — no ready-made pages, no subject skeleton and no curriculum coverage page. The coverage page can be turned on later in Course Settings.

rows.noun: The assistant calls a page a
rows.pageWordCaption: Pages will be named “{word} 1”, “{word} 2” and so on.

settingsRows.note: Course Settings shows the three new settings as LOCKED rows — a label and the value, no control — for every course, with one caption under them. The unit word keeps its own row, whose Rename… button is disabled for a numbered course (specialNames.renameUnitWord.renameLockedNumbered).
settingsRows.pageNamingValue: “{first page}” — the course's own first page name: “Unit 1, Day 1”, “Module 1, Day 1”, “Week 1”
settingsRows.frontPageHeadingValue: the course's recorded front_page_heading, exactly as stored — never a default
settingsRows.frontPageHeadingNotSet: Not recorded — the front page keeps the heading it already has
settingsRows.frontPageHeadingWhy: Shown for a course WITHOUT front_page_heading — every course made before #267, CODING included. The first version showed “Most Recent Class” there, and CODING's front page reads “## Most Recent Meeting”: a locked row stating something the page does not say (#267 implementation review, LOW). Nothing rewrites a heading after creation, so the row does not guess.
settingsRows.noun: The assistant calls a page a
settingsRows.lockedCaption: Chosen when the course was made. An existing course keeps these; they cannot be changed here.

clubToggle.fillRule: A field moves only while it still holds the value the OTHER choice would have put there — the words of `course` when ticking, of `club` when unticking — so a teacher's own typing survives the box going off and on. The class folder keeps its PLACE in the per-section list and `classFolder` follows it. Ticking removes every `curriculumFolders` name from the shared folders; unticking puts the terminology's factory curriculum folder back at its factory position. A skeleton's folders already adopted for the code are given up BEFORE the fill (the skeleton toggle's own restore rule), and adoption does nothing while the box is ticked.

cases.name: ticking the box fills a club's words and takes the curriculum folder out
unticking it puts a course's words and the curriculum folder back
a teacher's own words survive the box going off
cases.why: Typed words are the teacher's; only the untouched heading and noun follow the box.

cases.name: the class folder keeps its place in the list
cases.why: Measured for #267: the class-folder GUESS reads ["Resources", "All Meetings"] as "Resources". The folder is therefore recorded by name, and setup_course.py keeps the recorded name (classFolder.naming).

actions.means: Open the folder's PARENT with the folder selected.
actions.why: The same words and the same meaning this action has everywhere else in the app.

actions.gesture: double-click, and a second context-menu item
actions.means: Open the folder ITSELF in the file manager.
actions.why: Two different things, and a teacher wants both: revealing shows where a folder sits, opening shows what is in it. Finder's own path bar makes the same distinction, which is why the gestures match it — double-click opens, right-click reveals.

actions.means: The full path of that crumb.
actions.why: The crumbs show display names, which can be localised or truncated; the tooltip is how a teacher checks they are looking at the folder they think they are.
