ancestorPaths.note: Every ancestor from the volume root DOWN TO and including the folder itself. The root is included — a teacher scanning for where their folder lives reads the whole line.

windowsCases.why: A second drive is ordinary on a Windows machine and its root is 'D:\', not '/'. The rule is the same; only the spelling of a root is the platform's.

ancestorPaths.windowsEquivalent: Start at the drive rather than at '/': C:\\ , C:\\Users, C:\\Users\\teacher, … The RULE is 'every ancestor, root first, folder last'; the spelling of a root is the platform's. Added 2026-09-06: `windowsCases` above says the same thing as DATA, so the Windows suite runs the list rather than keeping its own hand-typed copy of it — proposed from the Windows side, and the mac needs nothing for it.

everyCrumbIsLive.rule: EVERY ancestor is clickable, not just the last one.
everyCrumbIsLive.why: It is how a teacher gets to the folder ABOVE their working folder — to make a sibling, or to see where things sit — without leaving the app to find it.

tooLongForTheSpace.rule: A path too long for the space it is given shows its END — the folder itself and its nearest ancestors — never its start. HOW room is made is the platform's own: the mac drops the ancestors' NAMES and keeps their icons and chevrons, which is what Finder does; Windows shows an ellipsis, which is what BreadcrumbBar does. Neither is drifting.
tooLongForTheSpace.why: The folder's own name is the part a teacher is looking for; 'Macintosh HD › Users › …' is the same for every folder they own. Found 2026-09-05 with an iCloud Drive folder, whose real path runs through ~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs and was cut off in the folder picker before reaching the folder's name. Wherever the bar appears — the window's own bar and the picker's — the same rule. THE MECHANISM WAS ADDED 2026-09-09 (issue #148), after Russell asked for Finder's answer rather than an ellipsis, and the two platforms deliberately differ the way specialNames.platformWording does: each app does what its own PLATFORM'S CONTROL does, because this bar exists to be RECOGNISED rather than learned (the mac's half was measured against the real Finder; the Windows half is BreadcrumbBar's documented behaviour, and File Explorer's address bar was NOT examined — the claim is about the control, not about Explorer). Windows' BreadcrumbBar “displays each node in a horizontal line” and, per Microsoft's page, “if the app is resized so that there is not enough space to show all the nodes, the breadcrumbs collapse and an ellipsis replaces the leftmost nodes” — right there, wrong on a Mac. Finder was MEASURED at five window widths before the mac's half was written, and two of the things it does are deliberately not copied: it shrinks the middle names before dropping them, which is per-crumb width negotiation for a state a teacher passes through rather than sits in; and at its narrowest it clips the TAIL, losing the folder's own name, which is precisely what the rule above forbids. So the mac collapses like Finder and, when even icons and chevrons do not fit, falls back to its own end-anchored scroll rather than to Finder's clipping. A hidden name is not a lost one: every crumb keeps its tooltip, its double-click and its context menu, so hovering an icon still says which folder it is.

fitsInTheSpace.rule: A path that FITS the space starts beside the label that introduces it, never at the far end of it. 'The space' is the room the window gives the bar: no fixed width narrower than that decides that a path does not fit.
fitsInTheSpace.why: The other half of tooLongForTheSpace, and it was missing for four days — the first rule BROKE it. Anchoring the crumbs at the trailing edge (2026-09-05) stopped a long path being cut off before the folder's own name; the mac's bar is a horizontal scroll view, a scroll view fills whatever width it is given, and with the content anchored trailing a two-crumb path then sat at the opposite end of the window from “Working folder:”, with the width of a window in between. Reported from a screenshot 2026-09-09 (issue #145). The two rules are one rule seen from each end: crumbs are read left to right FROM the label, and what is sacrificed when there is not enough room is the START of the path, never its end. **Windows' own control has both halves** — a BreadcrumbBar “displays each node in a horizontal line” and, in Microsoft's own words, “if the app is resized so that there is not enough space to show all the nodes, the breadcrumbs collapse and an ellipsis replaces the leftmost nodes” (learn.microsoft.com, BreadcrumbBar). That is the platform's control being right rather than a decision anyone made, so a surface that ever replaced it with a hand-rolled ScrollViewer of crumbs would meet exactly this. The mac's fix, the shape of the mistake it is an instance of, and the measurements pinning it are in documentation/10-local-ai-assistant.md. THE SECOND SENTENCE OF THE RULE WAS ADDED 2026-09-25 (issue #295), and it is what Windows now owes: the folder picker's bar, under a folder just chosen, was held to 520 points on BOTH platforms — on the mac by a limit added 2026-08-09, when the bar was a scroll view that filled any width and needed holding in, and left behind when #145 and #148 made it ask only for the room its crumbs need. So an ordinary Desktop path, which needs about 554 points, lost every ancestor's name at every window size, however much room the window had. The mac dropped the limit; Windows' picker carries the same one (MaxWidth="520" on its BreadcrumbBar), and there it ellipsises the leftmost crumbs at 520 whatever the window's width. The reasoning and the measurements are in documentation/09-mac-app.md.

icons.rule: Each crumb shows the folder's real icon from the host file manager.
icons.why: Not decoration: a teacher recognises their Desktop or their iCloud Drive by its icon before reading the word. Optional if the platform makes it expensive — say so rather than dropping it silently.

workingFolderPathBar.note: The 'Working folder:' bar under the sidebar. Modelled on the host file manager's own path bar — Finder's on the mac — because a teacher who has seen one knows what it does without being told. Reported missing on Windows 2026-08-16, in use: the context menu is not there. The LABELS are per platform ('Finder' against 'File Explorer'); the actions, the gestures and the crumb list are not.

workingFolderSelection.note: What a window lets go of when it is pointed at a DIFFERENT working folder. From GitHub issue #93, seen 2026-09-05: with a course selected, choosing another folder left the selection pointing at a course that folder had never had, so the detail pane greeted the teacher with 'Course Not Found' about a folder they had only just arrived in.
workingFolderSelection.rule: When a window changes working folder, it lets go of anything that names a course, an archive or a backup in the folder being left — and chooses nothing in its place. Re-choosing the folder the window already shows is not a change and costs the teacher nothing.
workingFolderSelection.why: Two failures, and one rule closes both. A selection carried across describes the OLD folder while the new one is on screen, which is the reported defect; and a pending confirmation carried across would ACT there — a restore or a delete still holding the file it was asked about, in a folder nobody is looking at any more. Nothing is chosen in the new folder to replace it, because the empty state already says what to do and picking for the teacher would be a guess.
workingFolderSelection.sameCodeIsADifferentCourse: A course in the new folder wearing the same code as the one that was selected is a DIFFERENT course, and the selection is cleared just the same. Landing on it would be a guess dressed up as a memory — and it is the case that separates this rule from the obvious alternative below, which cannot see it at all.
workingFolderSelection.alsoCleared: Everything else holding one of those things: the course whose code is being edited in place, every confirmation waiting on an answer about an archive, a backup or a rename, and the alerts describing what just happened in the folder being left. A sentence naming a course the window no longer shows is worse than no sentence, because it will be read as being about the folder now on screen.
workingFolderSelection.kept: The sidebar's filter text, and its disclosure state (which courses are unfolded, whether Archived and Backups are open). The filter is a way of LOOKING rather than a thing named — a teacher who typed '3U' to narrow one folder is usually after the same courses in the next. Disclosure state is the sidebar's SHAPE: a code left open that this folder does not have draws nothing at all, and no action hangs off a disclosure triangle for it to aim at the wrong folder.

rejected.instead: Check the selection against the courses just loaded, inside the reload that follows every folder change.
rejected.why: Rejected on three counts. It would erase the legitimately RIGHT 'Course Not Found' — the one a teacher sees after deleting a course in Finder while its window is open, where the sentence is true and useful. It would make what a teacher sees depend on when some unrelated reload next happened to run, since courses are reloaded after every rename, backup, restore and archive. And it would still land on the wrong course when the new folder has one wearing the same code, which is the case the rule above exists to answer.

rejected.instead: Clear the selection from a property observer on the folder itself.
rejected.why: Rejected: it fires for every write, including the one a window makes while restoring, and hides a rule a reader has to find. The clearing belongs to the one function BOTH ways of adopting a folder go through, so neither route can gain it while the other quietly keeps the old folder's selection.

workingFolderSelection.howToRunACase: Each case names the folders it needs by label; a suite materialises a real working folder for each. 'folderA' holds one course with two sections; 'folderBEmpty' is a working folder whose courses folder is empty; 'folderBSameCode' holds a course whose CODE is the same as folderA's and is otherwise a different folder. A selection is written structurally — its kind, the folder whose course it names, and a section number where one applies — rather than as any stored string, because the storage spelling is one platform's and this rule is not about it. Give each case its OWN folders rather than sharing them across the list: one case DELETES a course from the folder it starts in, and a shared fixture would hand the damaged folder to whatever ran next, making this list silently order-dependent. `then.pointAt` names the folder to point the window at next - the ordinary folder change. `then.removeTheSelectedCourseAndReload` instead deletes the selected course's folder from the working folder the window is ALREADY in and reloads the courses, which is a teacher deleting a course in the file manager with its window open: the folder has not changed, so nothing is let go of. `expect` is 'cleared' (no selection) or 'unchanged' (the same selection the case made). `expectNamesALoadedCourse`, present only where it matters, says whether that selection still names a course that LOADED - false is how the right 'Course Not Found' is pinned, and is what separates keeping a selection from keeping a working one.

cases.name: a different folder clears the selection
cases.why: The reported defect. The new folder has no courses at all, so the pane should show the empty state rather than a sentence about a course that was never here.

cases.name: the same folder chosen again keeps the selection
cases.why: The picker is reachable while a folder is open, and re-choosing what is already shown is not a change of folder. A teacher who does it must not lose their place.

cases.name: a different folder with the same course code clears it too
cases.why: A course wearing the same code is a different course. This is the case a selection validated against the loaded courses would get wrong, silently, by landing on it.

cases.name: a course that vanishes from the folder still in use keeps the selection
cases.why: 'Course Not Found' is the right answer here and must survive: the teacher deleted the course themselves, in the folder they are still working in, and the sentence tells them so. Nothing about the folder changed, so nothing is let go of.

buildOutputLocation.note: Where a section's BUILT WEBSITE is kept, and why it is not inside the working folder. Decided 2026-09-05; Windows had already done its half in row 290. The rule is implemented twice on the mac on purpose — in the app (BuildOutputLocation.swift, when a working folder's courses are read) and in the launchers (preview.sh and deploy.sh before they build, setup.sh for every course once the wizard has finished) — because a teacher at the command line and a publish scheduled with launchd have no app to do it for them, and if the two built into different places every build would read as stale.
buildOutputLocation.whyItMoves: A built site is DERIVED: every file in it comes from the teacher's notes and can be made again, which is why Plantoir's own backups already skipped it by name (CourseArchiver.excludedFromArchives, scripts/setup_course.py). Nothing OUTSIDE Plantoir knew that. A cloud-synced folder uploads every build and charges it against the teacher's quota; Time Machine backs it up; a zip, a Finder copy or a folder handed to a colleague carries it; Get Info counts it. Measured on this Mac on 2026-09-05, on the small EXC2O course the verification suite builds: 331 files and 9.8 MB for ONE section, and every build rewrites all of them (Quartz emits its output fresh, so rsync's mtime comparison copies every file), so the cost is paid again on every build rather than once. A real course with media is many times that.

appliesToEveryFolder.rule: The built site is kept outside the working folder for EVERY working folder, not only the ones Plantoir believes are synced.
appliesToEveryFolder.why: The benefit is not confined to syncing — a backup, a copy, a zip and a folder size are all smaller for it — and one code path is one code path: a rule that ran only for folders detected as synced would be a rule tested in one case and running in another, and cloud detection is deliberately not certain enough to hang behaviour on (see cloudSyncedFolders.neverRefused).

macLocation.folderId: The first 8 hex characters of SHA-256 over the working folder's PHYSICAL path plus a trailing newline — exactly `/bin/pwd -P | shasum -a 256 | cut -c1-8`, the same value the container name already uses, so a folder's container and its builds folder can never disagree about which folder they belong to. PHYSICAL means the disk's own spelling: links resolved, /private kept, the /System/Volumes/Data firmlink prefix dropped, and every name in the case and Unicode form the disk stored it in (GitHub #189). Each launcher moves into that spelling straight after its first cd — `cd "$(/bin/pwd -P)"` — so the id, the container's name, the builds folder and the courses folder the container mounts all come from one spelling however the launcher was reached; the app asks the same question with FolderIdentity.canonicalPath (fcntl F_GETPATH on the open folder), and uses the same answer for every comparison of two folder paths. Measured byte for byte the same as /bin/pwd -P on 17 spellings (wrong case, a link, /tmp for /private/tmp, the firmlink, iCloud Drive, Dropbox, an external disk, and both Unicode forms of an accented name). REJECTED: bash's built-in `pwd -P`, which the launchers used until #189 — it keeps the TYPED case and Unicode form, and the app hands a launcher an accented name as e + accent whatever the disk stores, so a folder with such a name (or reached in another case) had a second container and a second builds folder that cleared each other's builds; POSIX realpath, which the app used until #189 — it keeps the firmlink prefix /bin/pwd drops; Foundation's resolvingSymlinksInPath(), which strips the /private prefix and folds neither case nor form.
macLocation.underHomeWhy: The container VM (Colima) mounts only $HOME, so a builds folder anywhere else would appear EMPTY inside the container and every build would seem to vanish.
macLocation.workingFolderMarker: Each builds folder holds working-folder.txt naming the working folder it serves. The id is a hash and cannot be read backwards, so without it a builds folder left behind by a deleted working folder could never be recognised as abandoned.

windowsLocation.how: PLANTOIR_BUILD_ROOT, honoured by scripts/toolchain_paths.py -> merged_output_root(), which then does NOT nest a .merged_output level. Shipped in row 290 and unchanged by this piece.
windowsLocation.doNotChange: Windows keeps its environment variable and its flat layout. The symlink below is a MAC answer to a mac problem (a container that mounts only courses/, and three launchers plus three Swift readers that name the path), not a better idea Windows should copy.

theLink.rule: On the mac, courses/{COURSE}/.merged_output is a SYMLINK to the per-course builds folder, and the launchers bind-mount the builds root into the container at the SAME absolute path, unconditionally.
theLink.why: Every reader keeps working unchanged and they cannot disagree about where the build went: deploy.sh (MERGED_DIR_HOST, SECTION_DIR_IN_CONTAINER), preview.sh (OUTPUT_PATH, and stop mode), the Swift readers (BuildFreshness, ScheduledDeploy, SectionDetailView), the shell BuildFreshness that a launchd deploy writes out, verify.sh, verify-deploy.sh and the screenshot harness. Mounting the builds root anywhere ELSE in the container would leave the link dangling inside it, and every build would fail on a path a teacher can plainly see working in Finder.
rejected: One environment variable, as on Windows. The mac build runs in a container that mounts only courses/, so a build root outside the working folder is invisible in there until a second mount exists — and a launchd deploy and a teacher at the command line have no app to set a variable for them, so the app and the command line would build into different places and every build would read as stale.

Computing the path at every reader. Three launchers, three Swift readers, a generated launchd script and two verification scripts name it today; each one is a chance for two of them to disagree, and the failure mode of disagreeing is a publish that ships the wrong bytes.
A .nosync suffix. iCloud-only — Dropbox and OneDrive ignore it — and it moves the path just as much as this does.

aBuildWithNoLinkIsNotAdopted.rule: A per-course builds folder found with no link pointing at it is CLEARED, never reused.
aBuildWithNoLinkIsNotAdopted.why: Archiving a course, restoring one from a backup, and replacing a course's contents all remove the link along with everything else in the course folder — and each of them leaves content whose timestamps may be OLDER than the built site standing outside. Adopting that build would let a restored course publish last month's pages while every freshness check said it was up to date, which is the silent wrong answer this codebase refuses. Archiving a course or a section discards its build outright as well, so the clearing is a safety net rather than the only line of defence.
aBuildWithNoLinkIsNotAdopted.aSecondMacClearsRatherThanAdopts: A link left by a SECOND MAC sharing the folder clears this machine's build too, rather than adopting it. ADOPTING was proposed by one adversarial review and rejected by the next, and the reasoning is the point. Adopting looks strictly better: a teacher switching between two Macs would keep each machine's build instead of rebuilding after every switch. But the second Mac cannot tell 'the folder came back unchanged' from 'the folder was archived and restored while I was shut' — and in the second case the pages it would adopt a build for are OLDER than that build, so the freshness check says up to date and the teacher publishes what they undid. Clearing costs one rebuild, which is cheap and visible; adopting risks a wrong site nobody is told about. A generation stamp carried in the course folder (a UUID written beside the link and copied into the build, adopted only when the two match) would buy both, and was judged not worth a new synced file inside a teacher's vault for a case this rare. If two-Mac working ever becomes common, that is the design to build.
aBuildWithNoLinkIsNotAdopted.renameIsTheException: Renaming a course CARRIES its build across to the new code and re-points the link, because the built site used to travel with the folder and a rename should not silently cost a teacher their website.
aBuildWithNoLinkIsNotAdopted.restoringOneSection: Putting ONE section's pages back — from a backup, or by the assistant undoing what it just did — discards that section's built website too. The link is at COURSE level and survives, so the clearing rule above does not reach it. This staleness is OLDER than the move: it was equally true when .merged_output sat inside the course folder, because a section restore replaces section<N> and never touched the built tree beside it. Found and fixed on 2026-09-05 while moving the output; recorded as pre-existing so the fix is not read as repairing damage this piece did.

aSecondSpellingIsClearedAway.rule: A launcher handed a spelling of its folder that is not the disk's own clears away the second copy that spelling made before GitHub #189: the workspace teaching-quartz-{id of the spelling handed} if it is STOPPED (plain docker rm, never -f), and builds/{that id} if its working-folder.txt names THIS folder (an EMPTY note names no folder) and no workspace, running or stopped, still mounts it. A RUNNING one is left exactly as it is and named on the console. Nothing is removed when Docker cannot be asked, and the teacher's courses are never touched. It lives in the PREVIEW PORT BLOCK the three launchers share (clear_away_this_folders_other_spelling), called once by each just before it looks at its own workspace.
aSecondSpellingIsClearedAway.why: Until #189 the launchers named a folder by the spelling they were handed, the app by the disk's, so an accented folder name stored the Terminal or Windows way — or a folder reached in another case — had a second workspace and a second builds folder. Nothing makes them any more, and nothing else would ever remove them: the app's sweep keeps any builds folder whose folder still exists, and a stopped workspace keeps one of the forty preview blocks for as long as it exists (contracts/app-rules.json -> previewPorts). The builds folder is derived — the next build makes every file again — which is why removing it costs a teacher nothing but that one build.
aSecondSpellingIsClearedAway.sayWhenCleared: 🧹 Cleared away {what}, left behind under another spelling of the folder's name. Nothing in your courses was touched.

whatWasCleared.workspace: a second copy of this working folder's workspace
whatWasCleared.builtWebsites: a second copy of this working folder's built websites
whatWasCleared.both: a second copy of this working folder's workspace and built websites

aSecondSpellingIsClearedAway.whatWasClearedWhy: The sentence names only what was removed (review L3): the workspace alone when its builds folder is still mounted by another workspace or its note names another folder, the built websites alone when no workspace was left, both otherwise. The same {what} fills the console sentence and the trail line.
sayWhenStillRunning: ℹ️  A second copy of this folder's workspace, made under another spelling of the folder's name, is still running ({workspace}).
Plantoir is leaving it as it is, and will clear it away once it has stopped.
aSecondSpellingIsClearedAway.onTheTrail: activityTrail 'built site moved out of the working folder' -> launcherLineWhenASecondCopyIsClearedAway, written only when something WAS removed.
rejected: Sweeping at app launch, in Swift. A launchd publish still running the OLD deploy.sh at that moment builds into the old builds folder while the sweep deletes it; in the launcher, the one running is the new one, and an old one mid-publish has its workspace RUNNING, which this leaves alone.

Moving the old builds folder's content onto the new id. It is adoption under another name, for a build whose freshness nothing vouches for — the two copies had been clearing each other — which aBuildWithNoLinkIsNotAdopted already refuses.
docker rm -f of a running copy. It may be an older launcher's publish in the middle of its work; stopped, it is cleared on a later run.

Clearing every stale spelling at once. A launcher knows only the spelling it was handed, and the other spellings' ids cannot be worked out from the disk; each is cleared the next time it is used, which is how it was made.
aSecondSpellingIsClearedAway.knownLimits: A copy left RUNNING keeps `docker ps` from being empty, so quitting Plantoir leaves the virtual machine running until it stops (documentation/09-mac-app.md). A spelling that is never used again leaves its stopped copy behind. One narrow race is not closed: an OLD launcher (a launchd publish still running the deploy.sh from before the folder's launchers were refreshed) that has made its builds folder but not yet started its stopped workspace can have that builds folder removed under it by a new launcher handed the same old spelling at the same moment — its workspace is not yet RUNNING, so nothing marks it as in use. The loss is one derived build; that publish fails and the next one builds afresh. The app's own builds folder changes id only for a folder it was handed by the /System/Volumes/Data firmlink, whose old builds folder is then removed by the app's existing sweep only if the folder is gone — one leftover, derived, in a spelling nobody picks by accident. MAC ONLY: Windows has no container, and its folder id is already the disk's own spelling.

whatATeacherSees.inFinder: .merged_output is hidden, so it is invisible in Finder unless hidden files are shown — where it now appears as a shortcut rather than a folder. Their working folder gets markedly smaller, which is the point.
whatATeacherSees.atTheCommandLine: preview.sh --help says where built websites are kept and that the old path still works.
whatATeacherSees.onTheTrail: One line per course, the first time its built site moves — activityTrail 'built site moved out of the working folder'. Written by whichever of the two implementations does the move: the app when a folder is opened, and the LAUNCHERS when the move is done by a build at the command line or by a publish launchd ran at six in the morning. The launchers append it to the same file in the same shape, because a trail that recorded only the moves the GUI happened to make would be missing exactly the ones a teacher never watched happen.
whatATeacherSees.notesAreNeverMoved: Only the built site moves. Nothing a teacher wrote is touched, and the course folder keeps every one of its own files.

syncedFoldersFollowTheLink.measured: Tested on this Mac on 2026-09-05 against a real iCloud Drive folder and a real ~/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox, each given a throwaway course folder containing a real note and a .merged_output symlink to an outside folder holding a 3 MB file. BOTH kept it as a symlink and neither followed it: iCloud reported the link itself as uploaded at 82 bytes — the length of the target path — with isUbiquitousItem true and the 3 MB nowhere; Dropbox tagged the LINK with its own extended attributes and left the target folder outside Dropbox with none at all, so it had not reached through it. `du` of the synced folder counted 4 KB. OneDrive is not installed on this Mac and was not tested.
syncedFoldersFollowTheLink.consequence: The link is synced, which means a teacher with two Macs receives a link naming a path that may not exist there. On a Mac running THIS version that is handled before anything builds: a link naming another machine's builds folder is replaced, and this machine's own build under that course code is CLEARED with it — see aBuildWithNoLinkIsNotAdopted.aSecondMacClearsRatherThanAdopts for why the tempting alternative was rejected. scripts/build_site.py replaces a link it still finds dangling with a real folder and builds into the old place — deliberately NOT creating the target, which would answer the second-Mac case and silently ruin the other one it meets (a container made before the builds folder was mounted into it, where the folder would be created inside the container and the host would see an empty site with no error).
syncedFoldersFollowTheLink.aSecondMacMustBeUPDATED: The mac's OLD build_site.py fails outright on a link whose target is missing — mkdir raises 'File exists' — and no code shipped before 2026-09-05 can repair it. So a working folder synced between two Macs needs BOTH of them on this version or later. It is worse than one stale machine failing on its own: the launchers and .toolchain/ live inside the synced folder, so an older app refreshes them BACK to its own copies, and a scheduled publish on the up-to-date Mac then runs whatever deploy.sh is in the folder that morning. Before this change a version mismatch between two Macs was harmless. This belongs in the release notes, not only here.

upgradingAFolderThatAlreadyHasBuiltSites.rule: Everything an existing teacher already has survives the change, and nothing about it is one-way: the built site is MOVED (never rebuilt from scratch and never deleted), the site markers are untouched because they were never inside it, and if any step cannot be done the course is left exactly as it was and the build writes a real .merged_output folder — which is what it did before.
whatIsAlreadyThere: A real .merged_output folder holding built sites. Moved out on the first folder-open, or on the first build from the command line, and the same path still reads it.

.netlify_sites/ and .cloudflare_sites/ — the markers that say which published site a section belongs to. They live beside .merged_output in the course folder, NOT inside it, so nothing here touches them. Losing one silently creates a brand-new site on the next publish, which has happened on Windows before, so it is checked rather than assumed.
A container created without the builds mount. Recreated once, by whichever launcher runs first. A container is recreated on a toolchain change anyway, so this is not a new kind of interruption.
Scheduled publishes already written out to launchd. Their script names courses/<CODE>/.merged_output/section<N>/public/index.html and keeps working through the link, unchanged and unregenerated.

A course folder synced to a second Mac. The link is synced with it and names a home folder that is not there; it is replaced on that machine before anything builds — PROVIDED that Mac is also on this version. It must be: see syncedFoldersFollowTheLink.aSecondMacMustBeUPDATED.
upgradingAFolderThatAlreadyHasBuiltSites.neverWhileABuildIsRunning: A course being previewed IN THIS APP is left alone and picked up at the next reload. Moving the output from under a running build would break it on a path the teacher can see working. The qualifier is honest rather than cautious: preview leases are per-process, so the app cannot see a preview started at the command line, and the MCP server cannot see the app's. The window is small — a course is linked the first time its folder is opened, long before anything can be previewing it — and the cost if it is ever hit is a failed build, not a lost note.
upgradingAFolderThatAlreadyHasBuiltSites.whenItCannotBeDone: A read-only folder, a full disk or a permission the teacher has changed must never turn 'the built website could not be moved' into 'publishing is broken'. Every step is allowed to fail without stopping the run, and the fallback is the OLD behaviour rather than a broken one. The launchers run under `set -e`, which is what makes this a rule rather than a nicety. If the move succeeds and the link then fails, the move is put BACK — a course with its website in the old place still builds and still publishes, while a course with neither has lost it for nothing. The one case not covered is a DOUBLE fault, where putting it back fails too: then the built site stands outside with nothing pointing at it, and the next run clears it. That costs a rebuild and nothing else, and is not worth more machinery than saying so here.

containerRecreate.rule: A container that exists without the builds mount is recreated. All three launchers check, and all three create the container with the same mount set.
containerRecreate.why: A mount cannot be added to a container that already exists, so every teacher's existing container predates this and has to be replaced once. And if only SOME launchers created the mount, two of them would recreate the container away from each other on alternate runs.
containerRecreate.mountForm: MAC ONLY, and prose rather than a case because Windows has no container at all — there is no `docker` in setup.ps1, preview.ps1 or deploy.ps1, and a Windows path cannot hold a ':' anyway. The two mounts are named in the field-quoted `--mount` form, `type=bind,"source=<path>","target=<path>"` with any literal quote doubled, written by one shared helper the three launchers carry between CONTAINER MOUNT BLOCK markers. `-v A:B` splits its argument on ':', so a working folder called "Comm Tech 26:27" — which is what the disk holds after a teacher types "Comm Tech 26/27" in Finder — could not be named with it at all: the daemon read "/teaching/courses" as the MODE and refused with exit 125, after 147 seconds of first-run setup (GitHub issue #221, a real teacher, 2026-09-02). Measured 2026-09-19 on the pinned Docker CLI 29.7.2 and Homebrew's 29.7.1: a PLAIN `--mount` is strictly worse than `-v` rather than better, failing on ',' and on '"'; the quoted form mounts every name a teacher can type in Finder. The quote must open the FIELD (`"source=/x"`); `source="/x"` is refused for every path. The two forms produce identical `.Mounts`, so no container is recreated for this and an old launcher and a new one accept each other's containers — measured both ways. One name still fails and is written down rather than rounded off: a CR immediately followed by an LF, which Go's CSV parser rewrites to LF inside a quoted field, so the daemon looks for a path that does not exist. `-v` mounted that name, so it is a real regression, accepted because Finder's rename field will not accept a Return and because the failure is loud rather than silent. Reasoning and the full table: documentation/03-launcher-scripts.md.
containerRecreate.sourceMustExist: A bind mount whose source does not exist is REFUSED by this form, where `-v` silently created a folder at whatever path it was handed. That is the better answer and it is deliberate: a working folder renamed or deleted mid-run would otherwise be re-made, empty, at a path nobody is looking at any more. All three launchers check the courses folder first and say the sentence in app-rules.json -> failureExplanations for the case matched on "bind source path does not exist" — the same words the app says for the same trouble.

cloudSyncedFolders.note: A working folder that a cloud service keeps in sync — iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive, Box. Teachers keep their notes in such folders ON PURPOSE (it is how the notes reach an iPad and a second machine), so Plantoir never refuses one. It recognises the folder from markers the system exposes, says once and in plain words what a synced folder costs, lets the teacher decide, and leaves their content exactly where they put it. Decided 2026-09-05; both sides of the argument are in TODO.md under 'Should Plantoir refuse to work in a cloud-synced folder?'.

neverRefused.rule: A synced folder is never blocked, and detection is never treated as certain enough to block on.
neverRefused.why: A hard block is the one answer a teacher cannot opt out of, and it would mean telling them to give up reaching their own notes from other devices. Detection is also unreliable in both directions — a false refusal is unrecoverable for them, and a synced folder Plantoir cannot see still works. Refusing was rejected once already, on Windows, where the same problem was met and answered by moving the build output out of the folder rather than turning the folder away.

detection.rule: From markers the platform exposes, never from a folder's NAME. A teacher can have a folder literally called 'Dropbox' that is not one, and a wrong answer here is shown to them as fact.
macMarkers: Under ~/Library/Mobile Documents/ — iCloud Drive's real location; '~/iCloud Drive' in Finder is a view of it.

Under ~/Library/CloudStorage/<Service>-<Account>/ — where macOS 12.3+ keeps every File Provider service's folders: OneDrive-Personal, GoogleDrive-name@gmail.com, Dropbox, Box-Box. The service is the part of that folder's name before the first hyphen.

The item's own 'ubiquitous' flag (isUbiquitousItem), trusted ONLY under ~/Desktop and ~/Documents — the two folders 'Desktop & Documents Folders' syncs in place, which match no path rule. The flag is NOT iCloud-specific: it is set for any File Provider item, a Dropbox or OneDrive folder included (checked on a real ~/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox), so trusting it anywhere else would name the wrong service.

Symlinks are resolved before any rule runs. Dropbox and OneDrive both leave a link at the old place (~/Dropbox → ~/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox); a path arriving through it matches no rule while the folder behind it does. The resolved path is also the key the acknowledgement is remembered under, so one folder is one folder whichever spelling it arrives by.
windowsMarkers: The OneDrive roots the client publishes in the environment: %OneDrive%, %OneDriveConsumer%, %OneDriveCommercial%. A Desktop or Documents moved into OneDrive by 'Known Folder Move' physically lives under one of these, so the prefix rule catches it.
iCloud for Windows: %USERPROFILE%\iCloudDrive by default; the client's own setting if it can be read.
Google Drive for desktop and Box: their mount points, when the client publishes them; otherwise unrecognised, which is allowed — see neverRefused.

cases.why: The ordinary iCloud Drive folder.
The root itself counts.
The account is part of the folder name; the service is the part before the first hyphen.
No hyphen at all — the whole name is the service.
Recognisably synced — it is in the reserved location — but not a service Plantoir names. Say so honestly rather than guessing.
The reserved folder itself is nobody's.
A folder CALLED Dropbox proves nothing. The name rule that would catch it is the one that would also be wrong.
From the path alone, nothing — on a Mac with Desktop & Documents in iCloud, the live iCloud flag is what answers, and this rule must not pretend to.
Only the teacher's own home folder carries the markers; the same shape on another volume is a copy.

chosen.rule: A synced folder the teacher just CHOSE, or an empty synced folder about to be set up, stops at the folder picker: the folder's path bar FIRST, then the headline, the full explanation, and two buttons — go ahead, or choose a different folder. Setting up the empty folder IS going ahead. Neither button is the default action while the note is showing — including the set-up button, which is the default at every other time.
chosen.why: This is the one moment the choice is free — nothing has been written into the folder yet. A Return pressed out of habit must not decide it. The path bar comes first because the sentences say 'this folder', and a teacher reads that and looks for which folder.

notAskedAboutAFolderThatCannotBeUsed.rule: A synced folder the picker will not take anyway — neither a working folder nor empty — gets no note about syncing.
notAskedAboutAFolderThatCannotBeUsed.why: The teacher is about to choose again, and a note about a folder they cannot use is noise beside the guidance that says what to choose.

restored.rule: A synced folder the window RESTORED — opened on launch, or inherited by a new window — gets a quiet notice inside the window, above the working-folder bar: the headline, the one-line summary, a way to open the full explanation in place, and a button to dismiss it. Never a dialog, never a sheet.
restored.why: A folder can become synced AFTER it was set up (moved into iCloud, Desktop & Documents turned on) or have been set up before Plantoir could tell. But a folder that opens on every launch must not interrupt every launch, and the teacher did not choose anything just now.

rememberedPerFolder.rule: Going ahead — from either button — is remembered for THAT folder, keyed by its resolved path, and neither the choice nor the notice is shown for it again, in this window or any other window showing the same folder. A second synced folder gets its own note. The list is never pruned: a folder that is renamed or moved is a new key and is asked about again, and a deleted folder's key stays harmlessly.
rememberedPerFolder.why: Once is information; twice is nagging. And a teacher with two synced folders was told about one of them. Asking again after a rename is accepted: the folder may have moved INTO a synced location, which is exactly the case worth a note.

reChoosingTheOpenFolder.rule: Choosing, through the picker, the folder a window already shows counts as a restore, not a new choice: the notice form, never the picker's.
reChoosingTheOpenFolder.why: A teacher who re-picks their open folder while the notice is showing would otherwise find their courses hidden behind the picker, and read it as the app losing the folder.

checkedEveryOpen.rule: The check runs every time a working folder is adopted, not only the first time.
checkedEveryOpen.why: Folders move into cloud services after they are made, and the check costs nothing.

wording.rule: The sentences below, word for word, with the service's name where {service} is. They name EFFECTS a teacher can recognise — building can be slower, renaming a folder can take a while — and never machinery. No 'sync client', no 'file provider', no 'dataless file', no 'build root'.
wording.headline: This folder is kept in sync with {service}.
wording.summary: Plantoir works here, but building can be slower and renaming folders can take a while. Your notes stay where they are.
wording.notesStayPut: Your course notes stay exactly where they are. Plantoir never moves them.
wording.buildFilesAreCopiedRetired: RETIRED 2026-09-05, on BOTH platforms — do not show it, and do not add it back. It said: 'Building or previewing a website creates thousands of small files inside this folder, and {service} will copy every one of them to the cloud. That can make building slower and take up storage space.' It was true on the mac only, and only until the mac moved its build output out of the working folder as Windows had already done (see buildOutputLocation). Kept here rather than deleted because a sentence that once shipped gets re-proposed by whoever remembers it, and because the contract's own note said this sentence would leave when the mac moved its output — this is that.
wording.offloadedPagesAreSlow: If {service} has moved some of your pages off this computer to save space, Plantoir has to download each one before it can read it. Renaming a folder reads every page, so it can take a while.
wording.syncingCanInterruptAMove: If {service} is busy copying a file at the moment Plantoir needs to move or rename it, that step can fail. Plantoir checks before it moves anything, and you can try again once syncing has settled.
wording.whatToDo: To avoid all of this, keep your working folder somewhere that is not synced — a folder inside your home folder, for example. If reaching your notes from other devices matters more, carry on: Plantoir will work, just more slowly at times.
wording.whatToDoWhy: 'Your home folder', not 'your Desktop': on a Mac with Desktop & Documents in iCloud, the Desktop IS synced, and the advice would send them to the problem. The second sentence states the trade honestly and pushes neither way.
wording.explanationOrderWhy: Reassurance first — the words 'kept in sync' beside a warning read as 'your notes are at risk', and they are not. The choice last, once the reasons have been given.

specialFoldersHelp.note: The in-app answer to "What else does Plantoir use my folders for?" - a sheet reached from Course Settings that lists the folders and files THIS course has which the build treats specially. Shared because it is a rule with inputs and outputs wrapped around a set of sentences a teacher reads, and the two apps must give the same answers about the same course. Deliberately NOT here: the layout, and the MECHANISM of dismissal - a sheet on the mac, a dialog on Windows. The two button LABELS are here, because a label is a sentence a teacher reads and both apps already say the same words; only the thing the button is attached to differs.
specialFoldersHelp.openedBy: What else does Plantoir use my folders for?
specialFoldersHelp.title: Folders Plantoir uses
specialFoldersHelp.intro: Renaming or deleting one of these changes what appears on your site. Everything else in your course is yours to arrange however you like.

namesTheCoursesOwnFolders.rule: Every row that CAN be named from the course is named from the course, never from the rule that finds it. A row names a real folder, or it names nothing.
namesTheCoursesOwnFolders.why: Saying "any folder whose name mentions the curriculum" invites a teacher to get creative with it, and turns an implementation detail into a promise the product then has to keep. Saying "your expectations live in Ontario Curriculum" tells them the thing they can act on. It is also why the sheet is per-COURSE rather than one static help page: the answers genuinely differ. One course grades "Tasks", another "Tests" and "Thinking Tasks"; one calls its class folder "All Classes", another "Lessons".

rows.source: every per-section folder the build counts as a class folder
rows.why: Each day's class page lives here. Plantoir puts new classes in this folder, keeps them in date order, and uses them to work out which pages your course actually teaches.

rows.source: the curriculum folder the build resolves BY NAME for this course - the same first-the-recorded-name-then-the-scan order the build uses. Only the name half, and only among the SHARED folders: the build also wants an expectation page inside the folder, which neither app can see from configuration, so the sheet can name a folder the build passes over in favour of another - when the named folder holds no expectation page the build does not give up, it falls through to the same scan. The build's own scan walks the merged tree, so it would also find a per-section folder whose name mentions the curriculum, where both apps look at shared_folders alone - unreachable in practice, because every manifest declares this folder as shared, and named here rather than left to be rediscovered. Naming it is still righter than naming one that is not there.
rows.why: One page per expectation. The curriculum map is built from these — without them there is nothing to measure your lessons against, and the map is left out.
rows.whyPlaceholder: The NAME is the only thing that changes: "Your curriculum folder" is the single piece of text in the sheet allowed to describe rather than name, and only for a course that has no such folder at all. The explanation beside it does not change - a course with no expectations needs to hear the same thing about what they are for. The mac used to add a SECOND sentence here ("One page per expectation, in a folder whose name mentions the curriculum"), which this contract deliberately never carried: it publishes the matching rule in plain words, which is what saysNoMachinery exists to stop. Retired on the mac 2026-09-06, so both apps now say exactly what is above. It survived unnoticed for a fortnight because "mentions" is not a banned word and every fixture course had a curriculum folder, so the branch never ran in a test - which is why the case list below now includes a course that has none. The row check must run every one of those cases, so that the explanation beside the placeholder is compared with the one above it character for character: the case list on its own pins only the NAME, which is how a restored second sentence still passed every folders-help test on the mac as late as 2026-09-06, measured by putting it back. Both apps have done this since 2026-09-08 - the mac from 2026-09-06, Windows on closing item 40 in documentation/.

rows.source: the folders whose work counts for marks, including for a course never asked
rows.why: The curriculum map shows an expectation as evaluated when a page in one of these addresses it. You choose these above.

rows.name: Media
rows.what: Images and files you add to pages
rows.why: Plantoir looks after this one itself and keeps it out of your sidebar. If it goes missing, pictures stop appearing on your site.

rows.name: index.md
rows.what: The page a folder opens on
rows.why: Every section has one, and so does each folder. It is the way in, not a lesson.

rows.name: Key Links.md
rows.why: Plantoir adds the curriculum map to this list when it builds your site. Your own copy is left exactly as you wrote it.

rows.name: Curriculum Coverage
rows.what: Written for you, every time you build
rows.why: Do not write your own page with this name — it is replaced each time, so anything you put there would be lost.

rowsAreOrdered.rule: The rows appear in the order above, and no row is ever omitted - the curriculum row uses its placeholder rather than disappearing.
rowsAreOrdered.why: A row that vanishes when it has nothing to say is the case a teacher most needs to see: a course with no curriculum folder is exactly the course whose map is missing.

listing.rule: Several names are joined the way a person says them: "A", "A and B", "A, B and C". An empty list reads "None chosen".
listing.why: These lists are read aloud in a teacher's head. A bracketed, comma-separated list is a data structure showing through.

cases.why: An empty name is dropped before the joining, not rendered as a gap.

saysNoMachinery.rule: No text the PRODUCT writes - the title, the intro, and every row's what and why - may name the machinery or the matching rule. A folder's NAME is excluded: it is the teacher's own word shown back to them as they typed it, and a computer studies course with a folder called "Scripts" is not a wording bug.
saysNoMachinery.why: Rule one, plus the reason this sheet names configured folders in the first place. "Substring", "segment" and "case-insensitive" are banned alongside "container" and "script" because publishing the matching rule in words is the same mistake as printing it in a row, taken by another route.

cases.name: a course names its own folders, not the defaults
cases.why: The whole point. A course that renamed everything is told what ITS folders are called.

cases.name: never asked about marks: shown what the build counts today
cases.why: An absent pool is not an empty one - see gradedFolders.absentIsNotEmpty. The sheet shows what counts today rather than a blank list or a guess.

cases.name: asked and cleared: an empty pool is a real answer
cases.why: A teacher who cleared the pool is not shown "Tasks" as though they had never been asked, and a course with no curriculum folder gets the placeholder rather than losing the row.

cases.name: the curriculum folder is named even when the course never recorded one
cases.why: PROPOSED FROM WINDOWS, 2026-09-06; adopted by the mac the same day - see the ledger in documentation/. The build finds this course's curriculum folder perfectly well without the key being set, so the sheet must name it. Showing the placeholder here would tell a teacher to go and create a folder they already have, which is the one failure a sheet about folder names cannot afford.

cases.name: a recorded name the course no longer has is not shown
cases.why: PROPOSED FROM WINDOWS, 2026-09-06, adopted by the mac the same day - the second half of the case above and the sharper one. The course renamed its folder and the recorded name went stale; the build resolves past it to the folder that is really there. A sheet reading the raw name shows "Expectations", which the teacher does not have and cannot find - worse than the placeholder, because it looks like an answer.

cases.name: more than one class folder is listed, not just the first
cases.why: The build counts every class folder when working out what a course teaches, so the sheet names every one.

platformWording.note: These sentences name the machine — four since 2026-09-10, when renameUnitWord.explanation joined the three the rest of this note was written about — and the two apps deliberately say it differently — the same choice already recorded for the launcher markers in app-rules.json → markerOrigins.knownDivergence. The contract stores the MAC spelling because the contract is written here; Windows says 'on this PC' and is not drifting by doing so. There are THREE, and which record missed which is worth being exact about, because two passes at this paragraph got it wrong in opposite directions. Issue #102 named two of them — renameFolder.explanation and doneNothingWasThere — and not removeLeavesTheFolderOnDisk.message. The mac's OWN log had all three from 2026-09-01 (GUI-IMPROVEMENTS.md rows 388 and 389, which name explanation with removeLeavesTheFolderOnDisk and then doneNothingWasThere), six days before Windows' FolderRenameApplyTests began substituting on the third. So nothing here was behind the code: one Windows-authored issue body was incomplete, and this block is simply the first place all three are named together as a rule rather than as log entries.
platformWording.whyThisIsHere: Two failures, both already met elsewhere in these contracts — app-rules.json → markerOrigins.knownDivergence records exactly this kind of deliberate platform difference, and is READ by MilestoneContractTests on Windows rather than merely written down. Without a record, the next reader compares the two apps, finds a difference, concludes one of them drifted, and 'fixes' it. And a contract-driven test asserting the stored sentence verbatim would put the word Mac in front of a Windows teacher — a test enforcing a bug, which is the one outcome nobody wants. A suite asserting these keys must compare everything EXCEPT the platform word, or assert its own platform's spelling. That is a proven pattern rather than a proposal: SpecialFolderRenamerTests.TheTwoPlatformWordedSentencesSayThisPcRatherThanYourMac and FolderRenameApplyTests both do it on Windows, comparing against this file with .Replace("on your Mac", "on this PC"). On the mac, SharedRulesContractTests.testPlatformWordedKeysAreComplete pins the keys list itself: a fourth specialNames sentence containing the mac's platform word cannot be added without this record going red. It pins the RECORD rather than the behaviour. Windows has read the list since 2026-09-09 (SpecialFolderRenamerTests.EverySentenceTheContractCallsPlatformWordedSaysThisPc drives itself off `keys`), so a new key reds BOTH suites: the mac until the list names it, Windows until its substitution map carries it — which is what happened with renameUnitWord.explanation on 2026-09-10, and is the list being load-bearing rather than a fault. ONE SANCTIONED EXCEPTION to 'a new key reds BOTH suites until it is implemented', added 2026-09-18 and changing nothing in this file: when the feature a key belongs to is owned by an OPEN issue milestoned for a LATER release than the one being cut, the side that owes it may hold the key open in a NAMED GAP on its own side. windows-app/Plantoir.Tests/NamedGapLedger.cs does exactly that for renameUnitWord.explanation against GitHub issue #158 (v1.3.0), so the v1.2.0 gate is green with this list untouched and the mac still asserting all of it. It is not a softening: the ledger entry FAILS on Windows the moment the sentence starts existing there, and FAILS if this list stops naming it, so it cannot outlive either the fix or the requirement. What was REJECTED is doing it in this file — dropping the key from the list, or (for the matching activityTrail.mustRecord event) writing appliesOn: [mac] on it. Both would be false, since Windows owes both at v1.3.0, and appliesOn has no mend-check, so the day Windows built them both suites would have stayed green and nothing would have noticed. contracts/README.md, under 'Named gaps', says when a named gap is allowed and when it is not: never for a difference a teacher can see at the current milestone.

excludedFolderIndexNote.noteBody:
> [!NOTE]
> This folder was removed in Course Settings and is excluded from your website. Its pages will not appear in previews or on your published site. To include it again, add it back in Course Settings.
excludedFolderIndexNote.why: Explains why the folder is still present in Obsidian after being removed in Course Settings, and that it is ignored during build. Written into existing index.md files by preflight; stripped during merge so it never ships.

curriculumFolderBlockedByCoverageSetting.reason: The curriculum coverage map needs this folder to show your expectations. To remove it, turn off “Publish the curriculum coverage map” in Settings first.
curriculumFolderBlockedByCoverageSetting.why: Explains why the curriculum folder cannot be removed while the coverage map is enabled in Course Settings, naming the switch to turn off first.

curriculumFolderBlockedByCurriculumPages.reason: This folder holds your curriculum expectations. To remove it, turn off “Include {jurisdiction} curriculum pages” first.
curriculumFolderBlockedByCurriculumPages.why: Explains why the curriculum folder cannot be removed in the New Course Wizard while curriculum pages are enabled, naming the switch to turn off first.

curriculumFolderBlockedByCoverageMap.reason: This folder holds your curriculum expectations for the coverage map. To remove it, turn off “Include the curriculum coverage map” first.
curriculumFolderBlockedByCoverageMap.why: Explains why the curriculum folder cannot be removed in the New Course Wizard while the coverage map is enabled, naming the switch to turn off first.

lastGradedFolderBlocked.reason: At least one folder must count for marks while the curriculum coverage map is enabled. To remove or uncheck this folder, choose another graded folder under Marks first, or turn off “Publish the curriculum coverage map”.
lastGradedFolderBlocked.why: Explains why the last graded folder cannot be removed or un-ticked in Course Settings while the coverage map is enabled, preventing an empty marks pool.

lastGradedFolderBlockedWizard.reason: At least one folder must count for marks while the curriculum coverage map is enabled. To remove or uncheck this folder, choose another graded folder under Marks first, or turn off “Include the curriculum coverage map”.
lastGradedFolderBlockedWizard.why: Explains why the last graded folder cannot be removed or un-ticked in the New Course Wizard while the coverage map is enabled, preventing an empty marks pool.

classFolderBlocked.reason: “All Classes” holds your class pages and lessons — the pages the next-class button and the schedule write to. It cannot be removed; other per-section folders can.
classFolderBlocked.why: Explains why the folder named All Classes can never be removed, in Course Settings or the New Course Wizard. Russell's decision, 2026-08-24: exactly that folder is never removable; every other per-section folder can be added or removed as before. The name is compared case-insensitively and is ClassFolder.fallbackName.

lastPerSectionFolderBlocked.reason: Each section needs at least one folder for its class pages and lessons. Add another per-section folder first before removing this one.
lastPerSectionFolderBlocked.why: Explains why the last per-section folder cannot be removed, ensuring each section has a folder for its lessons.

sectionIndexFileBlocked.reason: Every section needs an index.md page for its home page. Without it, the section cannot be published.
sectionIndexFileBlocked.why: Explains why index.md cannot be removed from per-section files.

removeGradedFolderConfirmation.title: Remove “{name}”?
removeGradedFolderConfirmation.message: This folder holds work that counts for marks. Removing it will take it out of your course’s marks pool.
removeGradedFolderConfirmation.why: Prompts for confirmation when removing a graded folder when other graded folders exist.

removeCurriculumFolderConfirmation.title: Remove “{name}”?
removeCurriculumFolderConfirmation.message: This folder holds your curriculum expectations. Removing it means expectations will not be available if you later enable curriculum coverage.
removeCurriculumFolderConfirmation.why: Prompts for confirmation when removing a curriculum folder when curriculum coverage is off.

renameFolder.explanation: This renames the folder on your Mac — in every section that has one — and points your pages’ links at the new name. It happens straight away, so Cancel in Settings will not undo it.

problems.unchanged: That is already this folder’s name.
problems.hasSeparator: A folder’s name cannot contain “/” or “:”.
problems.isHidden: A name starting with a dot makes the folder hidden, and Plantoir would stop finding it.
problems.isMedia: Plantoir looks after the Media folder itself, so nothing else can be called Media.
problems.alreadyUsed: This course already has a folder called “{name}”.
problems.looksLikeASection: “{name}” is what Plantoir calls a section’s own folder, so it cannot be used here.
problems.destinationExists: There is already something called “{name}” beside it. Move or rename that first.

renameFolder.doneRelinkedOne: One page had links pointing into it, and they now point at the new name.
renameFolder.doneRelinkedMany: {count} pages had links pointing into it, and they now point at the new name.
renameFolder.doneRelinkedNone: No page linked into it by name, so nothing else needed changing.
renameFolder.doneNothingWasThere: There was no folder by that name on your Mac, so only this course’s settings changed. Make it in Obsidian when you need it.

interruptedRename.message: Plantoir started renaming “{old}” to “{new}” and did not finish — the folder has its new name, but this course’s settings still use the old one. Press Rename to finish.
interruptedRename.why: Proposed from Windows 2026-09-07. A rename interrupted after the folders moved is picked up the next time the sheet opens (the record under courses/.internal/renames names the target), and the field is filled in with that name so finishing is one keypress. The mac pre-fills silently; a filled-in field with nothing said leaves the teacher wondering why, and a modal on opening Course Settings would interrupt somebody who came for something else. One line, in the sheet, is the middle. The mac may adopt it or say why not.

renameFolder.hiddenIsTheDangerousOne: `hidden` holds the folders and files kept OUT of the built site. A rename that does not carry it across silently UN-HIDES the folder, and the next publish puts pages the teacher deliberately hid in front of students. Missed until the real app was driven on 2026-09-04, on a course whose `hidden` list named its Curriculum folder. `expandable` beside it is only cosmetic — the sidebar's expansion state — but is carried for the same reason: a key that names a folder and is not rewritten leaves the configuration describing a folder that no longer exists.

materialisesOnRename.rule: Renaming the folder a course currently RESOLVES to as its class folder or its curriculum folder writes that key, even on a course that never had one.
materialisesOnRename.why: Both are found by guessing at the name when the key is absent — 'class' in it, or 'curriculum' in it — and a course made from scratch has `curriculum_folder: null` and no `class_folder` at all. Rename `Curriculum` to `Expectations` without writing the key and the guess stops finding it: the map is built from nothing, and NOBODY IS TOLD, because from the coverage check's point of view the folder was never there. Carrying an existing key across is not enough; the key has to be created. A rename is the one moment Plantoir witnesses the change, which is the whole reason renaming belongs in the app rather than in Obsidian.

linkRewriting.note: How a folder’s new name is SPELLED inside the links a rename repoints. The rename itself is above; this is the half that decides whether the repointed link still resolves. The reference implementation is `FolderPathRewriter` on both sides.
linkRewriting.rule: In a MARKDOWN link, escape when the NEW name needs it, whatever the old segment looked like. In a WIKILINK, keep the plain spelling. A segment that ARRIVED percent-encoded goes back percent-encoded in either style, so a link a teacher already had keeps the shape it had.
linkRewriting.why: “Spell it the way the old segment was spelled” is the obvious rule and it is wrong. A Markdown destination ends at the first SPACE, so renaming Tasks to All Tasks turned `[q](Tasks/Quiz%201.md)` into `[q](All Tasks/Quiz%201.md)`, which neither Obsidian nor Quartz can follow. The old segment `Tasks` carries no `%`, so nothing escaped anything — the `%20` in that example belongs to the FILE name, which is what made it easy to miss by eye. Every Markdown-style link into the folder broke, in a teacher’s own pages, and nothing said so. Found on Windows by adversarial review 2026-09-06; the mac had the identical defect. Escaping a WIKILINK would be the mirror-image mistake: `[[All Tasks/Quiz 1]]` is exactly how Obsidian writes a wikilink whose folder has a space in it.

needsEscapingInAMarkdownLink.why: Whitespace and round brackets close a destination, and nothing else does. **A lone `%` was on this list for an afternoon and was taken back off.** The argument for it was that Quartz resolves an internal link with JavaScript’s `decodeURI` and `decodeURI("10%/Quiz.md")` throws — true of `decodeURI` on its own, and irrelevant here, because Quartz never sees a bare `%`: the Markdown parser normalises it to `%25` on the way to HTML, long before the link transformer runs. Measured in the running image 2026-09-06, `[b](Top10%/Quiz.md)` arrives as `Top10%25/Quiz.md`. A `%` is still ENCODED whenever escaping runs for another reason, which is what stops `Top 100%` becoming the half-escaped `Top%20100%`.

escapingSet.onceEscapingIsTriggeredEncodeEverythingE: Nothing is encoded unless a name needs it — see needsEscapingInAMarkdownLink — or the old segment arrived encoded. `Café` goes into a link as `Café`; `Café Notes` goes in as `Caf%C3%A9%20Notes`. Both resolve; the Markdown parser normalises the first to `Caf%C3%A9` itself. Reading this key as “always encode” is the way the two apps would drift, so there is a case for it below.
escapingSet.why: Neither macOS’s `urlPathAllowed` nor .NET’s `Uri.EscapeDataString` is right, and both were tried. Quartz v4.5.0 resolves an internal link with `decodeURI` (`quartz/util/path.ts`, `transformInternalLink`), and `decodeURI` deliberately leaves the reserved set `; / ? : @ & = + $ , #` still encoded. It then slugs what comes back, turning `&` into `-and-` and `%` into `-percent` (`sluggify`, same file). So a folder called “Tasks & Quizzes” written as `Tasks%20%26%20Quizzes` decodes to `Tasks %26 Quizzes` and slugs to `Tasks--percent26-Quizzes`, while the real folder slugs to `Tasks--and--Quizzes`: a 404 on the published site, and invisible in Obsidian, which decodes `%26` perfectly well. The set here is what JavaScript’s `encodeURI` leaves alone, minus three — `(` and `)` close a destination, `#` starts a heading — and minus `/` and `:`, which the rename sheet refuses anyway. **`?` was excluded at first and was put back**, on the reasoning that a bare `?` is a query delimiter to any other reader of the file. That was never a rule the code applied — `?` is not in needsEscapingInAMarkdownLink, so `Why?` always went in unescaped — and it was measurably wrong when escaping DID run: `sluggify` strips a `?`, so the real folder `Why Not?` slugs to `Why-Not`, an unescaped `Why%20Not?` slugs to the same and resolves, and the escaped `Why%20Not%3F` slugs to `Why-Not-percent3F` and 404s. Excluding it meant a folder resolved when it was called `Why?` and not when it was called `Why Not?`. Verified against the running image 2026-09-06: `decodeURI` turns `Work%28new%29` into `Work(new)`, `Top%2010%25` into “Top 10%”, `Caf%C3%A9%20Notes` into “Café Notes”, and leaves `C%2B%2B` alone.
escapingSet.windowsMustReplaceEscapeDataString: `Uri.EscapeDataString` keeps only `A-Za-z0-9-._~`, so it over-encodes `;`, `,`, `@`, `&`, `=`, `+`, `$`, `?`, `'`, `!` and `*`. **Only the first eight of those actually break a link**, and the distinction is worth keeping straight: `decodeURI` leaves exactly `; / ? : @ & = + $ , #` encoded, so those come back as `%XX` and `sluggify` turns each into `-percent…`, while `%27`, `%21` and `%2A` decode back to `'`, `!` and `*` and resolve fine — over-encoding them is noise rather than a 404. (An earlier draft of this note said all eleven broke. They do not, and the same encoder is still the right answer, because the eight that DO break include the two that will happen.) **Done on Windows 2026-09-07** (documentation/06-quartz-customizations.md): `Spelled` now calls a `PercentEncoded` driven by `leaveUnescaped`, in BOTH of its branches, and `FolderPathRewriterTests` deserialises every case below rather than retyping five of them. Three cases had been failing there — the ampersand, the comma and the question mark. The comma is the one that was going to bite: “Unit 1, Day 2” is this project’s own naming pattern, and Windows wrote `Unit%201%2C%20Day%202`, which slugs to `Unit-1-percent2C-Day-2` and 404s. The per-cent case passed there even before the fix — `Top 10%` triggers escaping on its space, and `EscapeDataString` encodes the `%` too — so do NOT add `%` to WouldBreakAMarkdownTarget. Kept here rather than deleted because the reasoning is what stops the encoder being “simplified” back to the framework call.

cases.why: The defect itself. The `%20` belongs to the FILE name, so the old folder segment looks unencoded and the new name used to go in plain.
Nothing in the link was ever encoded, and the new name still has to be.
A wikilink keeps the space: this is exactly how Obsidian writes one.
A round bracket ends a destination too, and `decodeURI` gives both back.
A name needing nothing is not escaped for the sake of it.
An embed is the same destination in the same shape, and a picture that stops appearing is as visible to a teacher as a dead link.

An ampersand is left as it stands. Encoding it to `%26` passes through `decodeURI` untouched and then slugs to `-percent26-` while the real folder slugs to `-and-`, so the page 404s for students while looking healthy in Obsidian. “Tests & Quizzes” and “Q&A” are ordinary folder names, so this is not a corner case.

A comma is left as it stands, for the same reason as the ampersand: `decodeURI` leaves `%2C` encoded and `sluggify` then makes it `-percent2C-`, so `Unit%201%2C%20Day%202` 404s while the folder itself slugs to `Unit-1,-Day-2`. This is the case most likely to bite a real teacher — “Unit 1, Day 2” is this project’s own naming pattern.

A question mark is left as it stands. `sluggify` STRIPS a `?` from the real folder’s name, so `Why Not?` slugs to `Why-Not` and the unescaped link slugs to the same thing, while `Why%20Not%3F` slugs to `Why-Not-percent3F` and 404s. Not reachable on Windows, where `?` cannot be in a folder name at all — but the encoder is a pure string transform, so the case still runs there.

A name outside plain ASCII is still left alone when nothing about it needs escaping. Reading `leaveUnescaped` as “encode everything else, always” would give `Caf%C3%A9` here and make the two apps write different text for the same rename, with no case to catch it.

The OTHER branch of the same rule, and the only case that reaches it. A segment that ARRIVED percent-encoded goes back percent-encoded even when the new name needs nothing — and it goes back through the SAME encoder, so an ampersand is left as it stands here too. Every other case that escapes at all is triggered by a space or a bracket, and the two that escape nothing (`Assignments`, `Café`) reach no encoder — so a `Uri.EscapeDataString` left behind in this branch alone would spell `Q%26A` and still pass all eleven of them. Proposed from Windows 2026-09-07 while replacing that encoder; both apps already behave this way — `spelled(_:likeThe:in:)` calls `percentEncoded` in both branches — so it should be green on the mac the day it is read.

Once escaping runs — here because of the space — a `%` is encoded with everything else outside `leaveUnescaped`. Half-escaping it to `Top%20100%` would be the failure this prevents. The `%` is NOT what triggers escaping; see needsEscapingInAMarkdownLink.

renameFolder.why: Renaming was the gap behind the whole special-names family: the list editors changed course_config.json and never touched disk, so Add wrote an entry pointing at no folder and Remove left a folder full of the teacher’s work unreferenced — and a rename was only possible in Obsidian, after which preflight discovered the new name and APPENDED it, leaving the config naming both. Renaming from inside Plantoir is the one place a rename can be WITNESSED, which is what lets every key that names the folder be carried across in the same breath. One constraint is not arbitrary and must not be relaxed without replacing what it protects: it commits to disk immediately rather than waiting for Save, because the folder really has moved and a Cancel that appeared to undo it would be a lie; only the keys in carriesAcross are written, so a teacher’s other unsaved edits stay unsaved. **A SECOND constraint was here for a day and is gone — do not put it back.** The class folder had to keep a name containing “class”, because ClassFolder found it by that substring. Russell, 2026-09-01: that is Plantoir’s vocabulary imposed on a teacher’s, and somebody whose units are Threads and whose classes are Days calls the folder “All Days”. The lookup was what was at fault. A recorded `class_folder` replaced the substring guess, and this rename MATERIALISES it — see materialisesOnRename. A rule enforced because a lookup was weak is a rule to delete once the lookup is fixed.

renameUnitWord.note: Renaming a course's word for a unit — “Unit” to “Module”, say — AFTER the course is in use. The sentences live here beside renameFolder's because they are the same kind: read in a sheet in Course Settings that commits to disk straight away. The RULES (which pages are renamed, what refuses it, how links follow) are in class-planning.json → renamingTheUnitWord, and the trail line is activityTrail.mustRecord → 'word for a unit renamed'. Mac: UnitWordRenameWording; the sheet is UnitWordRenameSheet, opened from a Rename… button beside the word under Settings — Overall. Added 2026-09-10 (issue #100).
renameUnitWord.fieldLabel: What do you call a unit?
renameUnitWord.rowCaptionWhy: In the course's CURRENT word, never the literal 'Unit': a literal would lie the moment a rename landed.
renameUnitWord.rowCaptionNumbered: Class pages are named “{word} 1”, “{word} 2” and so on.
renameUnitWord.renameLockedNumbered: This course numbers its pages one after another, so its word was chosen when the course was made and cannot be renamed here.
renameUnitWord.renameLockedNumberedWhy: A numbered course (class_page_scheme "numbered" — a club's “Week 1”, #267) shows the word but its Rename… button is DISABLED, with this sentence under it. Russell, 2026-09-24: a club's settings are chosen in the wizard and are not switchable afterwards. The rename itself is not the danger — the renamer reads pages through the course's scheme, so “Week 3” would become “Meeting 3” — but a club's page word, class folder, front-page heading and assistant noun are one choice, and renaming one of the four afterwards leaves a course none of the settings describes. The caption says the numbered shape, never “{word} 1, Day 1”, which no page in such a course is called. Proposed from the mac 2026-09-24; Windows owes both sentences and the disabled button.
renameUnitWord.explanation: This renames every class page on your Mac, in every section, and points your pages’ links at the new names. It happens straight away, so Cancel in Settings will not undo it. To change it back, rename it again; a backup of the whole course is saved first, as a last resort.
renameUnitWord.proseIsLeftAlone: Pages and sentences that mention a unit by number, other than the class pages themselves, are left as they are.
renameUnitWord.proseIsLeftAloneWhy: The 2026-09-01 decision, restated for a course already in use: the payload rewrite that pours 'by the end of Unit 3' as 'by the end of Module 3' runs only over content Plantoir ships, never over a teacher's own writing, where 'Unit 3 of the textbook' would be a false positive nobody could undo. So a course poured as Unit and renamed to Module keeps its prose — around 574 payload files carry such a sentence — and a shared task called 'Unit 2 Test' keeps its name. Said in the sheet, because otherwise the first teacher who compares the two would report it as a defect.

problems.empty: Type the word this course uses for a unit.
problems.unchanged: That is already this course’s word.
problems.mustFinishFirst: Plantoir is part way through renaming to “{target}”. Finish that first — press Rename with “{target}” — and then rename again.
problems.mustFinishFirstWhy: While a record of a stopped rename is on disk, only its target word is accepted. Any other word would plan from the old word alone, leave the pages already moved matching neither, clear the record, and end with three words in one course — the two-numbering-schemes state everything else here refuses. Found by the implementation review, 2026-09-10.
problems.unchangedWhy: Only the IDENTICAL word is unchanged. A change of capitalisation alone is a real rename — the configured spelling is what every new class page is written in, so a course whose word is 'module' would get a 'module 3, Day 1' next-class page beside 'Module 2, Day 9' — and it is safe because a page is MOVED, never copied and deleted, so a case-insensitive volume cannot lose one.
problems.pageInTheWay: {code} Section {n} already has a page called “{name}”, so the pages cannot be renamed. Move or rename that page first.
problems.pageInTheWayWhy: Refuses the WHOLE rename, not the one page. Skipping it would leave two numbering schemes in one section — 'Unit 2, Day 3' beside 'Module 2, Day 3' — which every feature that counts class pages would then read as two classes.
problems.pageUnreadable: “{name}” in {code} Section {n} could not be read, so nothing was renamed. If the course is kept in iCloud Drive, wait for it to finish downloading and try again.
problems.pageUnreadableWhy: Every planned page is read into memory BEFORE anything moves, and one that cannot be read refuses everything. Skipping it — the insertion planner's habit — would write unit_word: Module while that page still said Unit, recognised by nothing: the exact silent failure unit_word exists to prevent.
problems.recordNotWritten: Plantoir could not write its note of the rename under way ({reason}), so nothing was renamed. Check that the working folder can be written to, then try again.
