problems.recordNotWrittenWhy: The note under courses/.internal/renames/ is written after the backup and before the first page moves, and a failure to write it is a refusal with its own sentence — a rename with no note cannot be recognised if it stops, and 'renamed 0 of 3 and could not rename Unit 1, Day 1' would blame a page nothing had touched.
problems.busy: {code} is previewing or deploying right now. Stop that first, then rename.
problems.busyWhy: The same sentence shape restoring a backup uses, for the same reason: a build copies the course's pages, and copying half of a rename builds a site with two numbering schemes. Checked against the preview and deploy leases before anything is touched.
problems.digitAndComma: Not here: the two refusals for a word containing a digit or a comma are the wizard's own, ClassPageTerm.problem(with:), and the sheet reuses them.

preview.note: Shown in the sheet BEFORE the teacher agrees, worked out once when it opens. The counts do not depend on the word typed; the destination check does, and is redone when Rename is pressed.
preview.pagesNone: No class page in {code} is named “{old} N, Day N”, so only this course’s settings would change: new class pages will be named “{new} 1, Day 1” and so on.
preview.pagesOne: One class page, in {sections}, would be renamed — “{old} 1, Day 1” becomes “{new} 1, Day 1”, and so on.
preview.pagesMany: {pages} class pages in {sections} would be renamed — “{old} 1, Day 1” becomes “{new} 1, Day 1”, and so on.
preview.linksNone: No links point at those names, so nothing else needs changing.
preview.linksOne: One link points at those names and would be updated to match.
preview.linksMany: {count} links point at those names and would be updated to match.

renameUnitWord.donePagesNone: No class page needed renaming, so only this course’s settings changed.
renameUnitWord.doneLinksOne: One link was updated to match.
renameUnitWord.doneLinksNotWrittenOne: One page could not be written, so its links still use the old names.
renameUnitWord.doneLinksNotWrittenMany: {pages} pages could not be written, so their links still use the old names.
renameUnitWord.doneLinksNotWrittenWhy: A page whose links could not be written back is skipped rather than stopping the rename — the pages have already moved, so stopping would leave MORE links broken — but the teacher was shown a count and would otherwise be told a smaller one with no explanation. Said after the links sentence, and recorded on the trail.
renameUnitWord.donePublish: Publish each section for its website to use the new names.
renameUnitWord.donePublishWhy: The fact a teacher would otherwise report as a bug: every section reads as Edited at once and the built site keeps the old names until each section is rebuilt. That is correct — the build copies content/ afresh and the freshness check sees the new timestamps — so it needs saying, not fixing.
renameUnitWord.doneBackup: A backup of the whole course was saved first, and is listed under Backups.
renameUnitWord.doneOrder: done, then the pages sentence, then — when a page was renamed, any link was touched, or a page could not be written (finishing a rename that stopped during its link pass moves nothing and rewrites plenty) — the links sentence, the not-written sentence when there is one, and the publish sentence, then the backup sentence.

interruptedRename.message: Plantoir started renaming “{old}” to “{new}” and did not finish — some class pages have the new word, and this course’s settings still use the old one. Press Rename to finish.
interruptedRename.why: A record is written under courses/.internal/renames/<CODE>.unit-word.json before the first page moves and cleared after the configuration is written. It is believed only when BOTH the configuration and the disk agree: a record whose 'from' is no longer the course's word is stale (the configuration landed and only the clearing failed, or the word was edited by hand), and one with no class page SPELLED its 'to' way — parsing under the new word AND beginning with it, case-sensitively; parsing alone is not enough because the parser ignores case, and 'does not begin with the old word' is wrong because 'Units 1, Day 1' begins with 'Unit' — describes a rename that moved nothing — or one a restored backup has undone, which also clears the records itself. Either is cleared rather than believed. Finishing is running the same rename again with the same word (any other is refused — see problems.mustFinishFirst): pages already moved come out of the plan with nothing to move, and the link map carries their old names anyway.

renameUnitWord.halfDone: Plantoir renamed {renamed} of {total} class pages and then could not rename “{name}”: {reason}. Press Rename to finish the rest.
renameUnitWord.settingsNotWritten: Every class page now says “{new}”, but Plantoir could not write the change to this course’s settings: {reason}. Press Rename to finish.

addCreatesTheFolder.message: Plantoir made the folder “{name}” for you. Open it in Obsidian to put pages in it.
addCreatesTheFolder.why: Adding a name used to write a config entry pointing at nothing: the folder had to be created in Obsidian afterwards or the entry named a folder that did not exist. Creating it is what makes the list mean what it appears to mean. Nothing is put INSIDE it — an empty folder is the honest starting state, and inventing a page would put words in the teacher’s mouth.

removeLeavesTheFolderOnDisk.message: “{name}” and everything in it stays on your Mac — this only takes it off your website. Add it back here to include it again.
removeLeavesTheFolderOnDisk.why: Removal excludes; it has never deleted anything, and teachers could not tell. Saying so is what makes the button safe to press, and it is also the sentence that explains why a folder they “removed” is still sitting in Obsidian. Deleting the folder was rejected outright: it holds the teacher’s work, and no button in Settings should be able to destroy it.

contentStructureTip.message: Tip: you can also simply create new folders and files in Obsidian — they’re added to your site automatically the next time you preview. The exception is anything you remove here: it stays off your site, even if you make it again in Obsidian, until you add it back here.
contentStructureTip.why: The caption under the four Content Structure lists in Course Settings. Proposed from Windows 2026-09-07, resolving a divergence: the two apps had worded the same rule differently since the day it was written (the mac in row 375, 2026-08-24; Windows a day later in its parity pass, because row 375’s Windows-notes cell never mentioned the callout), and neither sentence was pinned. Both halves matter. The FIRST is the promise that a teacher need not come here at all — preflight discovery appends anything new it finds at the top level. The SECOND is the one rule a teacher cannot infer and is not told anywhere else on this page: an exclusion is name-based and does not expire, so a folder removed here stays off the site even if it is deleted and made again in Obsidian, and only this page can undo it. That became more consequential, not less, after excluded_items was made authoritative at build time (GUI-IMPROVEMENTS row 377, the same day): preflight now DROPS an excluded name it finds back in a copy list. The mac’s wording said the exception in a six-word bracket — “(unless you have removed them here)” — and named no remedy; that was rejected as under-weight for a permanent, silent rule with a single escape. Windows’ wording was adopted with two changes. “on this page” became “here”, because the sibling sentence removeLeavesTheFolderOnDisk already says “Add it back here to include it again” and Windows was using two names for one place in one sentence; “in these lists” was rejected as more precise but breaking that parallel, and because no Plantoir sentence calls a mac Form a page. And “folders” became “folders and files”, because the caption sits under FOUR lists of which two are file lists, and the behaviour is identical for files — discovery appends top-level files (discover_shared_items / discover_section_items) and exclusion skips and drops them (build_site.py). Both apps had promised only the folder half, so a teacher who removed a file got the permanent, silent behaviour with nothing anywhere warning them. “pages” was rejected for the widened clause: discovery is not limited to .md, and “files” is the word the four list labels above the caption already use. ONE KNOWN EDGE, named here rather than papered over: “even if you make it again in Obsidian” is true when the name is remade as it was, which is the realistic case, and not when it is remade with different capitalisation. That is not a defect in the matching — exact, case-included matching is the RULE, stated in this same file at gradedFolders.choices.walk.excludedItems (“the same way preflight matches”) and reasoned in GUI-IMPROVEMENTS row 412: a case-insensitive answer would have the app believe a folder is excluded while the build published it. So a teacher who removes “Old Tests” and later makes “old tests” does get it published. What IS inconsistent is that _dropping_excluded_items lowercases both sides while every other consumer matches exactly, so build_site.py gives two answers in one file. Tracked in TODO.md (“_dropping_excluded_items matches excluded names case-insensitively…”) and as issue #99, with the warning that case-folding the live path would break walk.excludedItems and re-introduce what row 412 rejected. Not resolved here: it is a build-behaviour decision wanting its own piece, its own contract case and a verify.sh run.

settingsSavedWhilePreviewing.message: A preview of this course is still showing the settings it started with. Press Preview Again to see what you just saved.
settingsSavedWhilePreviewing.why: Shown beside the Save confirmation in Course Settings when a preview of the course is open, with a Preview Again button that builds that preview afresh (issue #265, Russell's choice 2026-09-24). A preview bakes every setting in when its build starts - measured: 20 s after a save the served sidebar filter was unchanged - so a Save 'did nothing' to the page the teacher was looking at, and stopping and restarting showed the latest, one or more steps behind, which reads as random. About EVERY setting, not only the sidebar, so it names none. A caption, not a removal-blocked sentence: no `reason` key (Windows' NoBlockedSentenceInTheContractIsUnusedHere sweeps those). Rejected: rebuilding the preview automatically on every Save - it kills a page the teacher may be reading, for a Save that may have changed only the footer, and the preview can belong to another window.

settingsSavedWhilePublishing.message: This course is being published right now, and that publish uses the settings from before this save. Publish again once it has finished to send what you just saved.
settingsSavedWhilePublishing.why: Shown instead of settingsSavedWhilePreviewing when a publish of the course is running (the plan review's A3). The publish read the settings when its build began, so it sends the earlier ones. 'Publish again' is advice that WORKS only because of app-rules.json -> buildFreshness's rule about something saved after the build started: until that rule (issue #265 fix round, 2026-09-24) the next Publish compared the course with the time the built page was WRITTEN, found this Save older, called the site up to date and sent the same old build while reporting success — the review's H1, a sentence promising the opposite of what happened. Said rather than blocked: the Save is right. No Preview Again button beside it, because a preview is refused while that course publishes.

previewUsesSavedSettings.message: Course Settings has changes you have not saved, so this preview uses the settings as they were last saved.
previewUsesSavedSettings.why: Shown where a preview's progress appears when the preview starts while Course Settings holds unsaved changes — in ANY window open on that folder, not only the one previewing (issue #265; the review's L1: with two windows the unsaved switches can be in the other one, and asking only the previewing window's copy said nothing). Unsaved edits live in memory and survive leaving the form, so the switches can say one thing and the preview another with nothing on screen explaining it. Rejected: saving automatically (a half-typed setting would be written without a Save) and refusing the preview (previewing the saved settings may be the point).

settingsSaveReplacedSidebarChange.message: Which items the sidebar hides had also been changed somewhere else since this window read them — most likely in another Plantoir window. This save replaced that change with the switches shown here.
settingsSaveReplacedSidebarChange.why: Shown after a Save in Course Settings, first among the after-Save sentences and with or without a preview or publish running, when the Save found that the sidebar list (`hidden`) in the file had been changed since this window read it AND this window had changed it too — savingSettings' replacedChangesFromElsewhere naming `hidden`. The last Save wins for the whole list (savingSettings' case 'both windows changed the same list'); the review's M2 found that was told to nobody but the trail. Ruled by the director for Russell, 2026-09-24: last Save wins, but SAID; no merge of the two lists (rejected for the reason savingSettings gives: rules for order and for an item removed on one side and added on the other, which nothing reported needs). Only the sidebar list, because it is the one a teacher reads back as 'the switches do nothing'; another setting replaced this way is on the trail only. 'Most likely another window' rather than 'another window' because a hand edit of the file reaches the same branch, and the build no longer writes `hidden` at all (sidebarHiding.buildKeepsHidden). Stays on screen after Preview Again is pressed, which answers only the preview sentence. A caption: `message`, never `reason`.

settingsPreviewAgainNothingOpen.message: That preview has stopped since, so there is nothing to preview again. Open the section and press Preview to see what you saved.
settingsPreviewAgainNothingOpen.why: Shown in place of an enabled Preview Again (the button stays, disabled) when every preview the after-Save notice offered has since stopped: its lease released, its section window gone, or the window still there with its preview no longer running. The notice is worked out at the Save and stays up until the next Save or leaving the course, so this is an ordinary sequence — save, then close the other window, then look back — and before the review's L2 the button stayed enabled and did nothing, with no trail line. Measured from the code rather than driven: an in-app preview lease is taken only in the section view's startPreview and released in the same synchronous onDisappear that unregisters its window, so a lease with no window does not persist; what does is the notice outliving its preview. Re-evaluated whenever PreviewLeases changes, which is observable. A caption: `message`, never `reason`.

cases.why: Configured name wins.
Configured name wins even when it does not mention the word curriculum.
Unconfigured: alphabetically first folder containing 'curriculum' wins.
Unconfigured single curriculum folder.
No curriculum folder present.

curriculumFolderResolution.note: Which folder the GUI protects as the curriculum folder, computed from the config's shared_folders list: if `curriculum_folder` is configured and in the list, it is used; otherwise the alphabetically first name containing 'curriculum' (case-insensitive). This is the NAME half of build_site.py:_find_curriculum_folder, which additionally scans the vault on disk and accepts a folder only if it holds a page whose title is an expectation code — a check the apps cannot make from the config alone. So the GUI may protect a folder the build would skip (one with no expectation pages yet). It may ALSO name a DIFFERENT folder than the build picks, which this note used to deny: when a course has two folders mentioning the curriculum and only the second holds expectation pages, this rule takes the alphabetically first and the build takes the other. Measured on a real machine 2026-09-06 - two courses keeping both an "Ontario Curriculum" and a "College Board Curriculum" folder, the latter’s pages named "1.A" rather than in expectation-code form. Both apps agree with each other, so this is a shared limit rather than drift; whether to break the tie by reading the vault is an open question in TODO.md.

stopPreview.note: Which processes belong to a section's preview, and must therefore be stopped. This was answered THREE times before it was written down here - `preview.sh --stop` swept working directories inside the container, `preview.ps1 --stop` matched command lines natively, and `build_site.py` matched command lines again from inside the container because it cannot call either host script (both are HOST scripts; it is not). The reason for the third copy is sound and has not gone away. What went wrong is what always goes wrong: they drifted, and by the time anyone looked, only one of the three walked the process tree and one had a prefix bug that stopped the wrong section.
stopPreview.whatWasNotObvious: The three were not three copies of one rule - they were three PARTIAL rules, and picking any one of them as 'the' implementation would have shipped that one's blind spot everywhere. A working directory catches what a command line cannot (a child launched by a relative path carries no directory: `npm install` runs exactly that way). A command line catches what a working directory cannot: the Python driver itself, which never calls os.chdir and so sits in the container's own folder for the whole build. So the shared rule is a DISJUNCTION of evidences plus a walk down the process tree, and it stops strictly more than any of the three did on its own.

modes.everything: The launcher's `--stop`. The teacher, or the app, has ended a preview and the container-side work must be reclaimed: the server, the build, the driver, and every child of them. A mid-flight build is most of the point - ending the host-side script leaves it burning CPU for a preview nobody is waiting for any more.
modes.servingOnly: `build_site.py --build-only`. A build for PUBLISHING is about to start and the only thing that must go is the preview SERVER, which would otherwise overwrite what was just built about a second later through its own host mirror. A build must never be stopped here, because the build being protected is itself a build of this section. Implemented by `build_site.py` on BOTH platforms: inside the container on the mac, and natively on Windows since 2026-09-05, when `stop_preview.read_snapshot()` became a dispatcher and gained a `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` reader beside the `/proc` one. Before that there was no dispatcher, `/proc` was the only reader, and a native Windows run of this mode always came back with an empty process list — so the overwrite race this mode exists to prevent was live there, with nothing anywhere saying so. That is why the dispatcher is ONE function rather than a branch at each caller: a platform that keeps its process list somewhere else is then a change in one place, instead of a rule that quietly does nothing. See documentation/03-launcher-scripts.md.

evidences.rule: The process's working directory IS the section's build directory, or is inside it.
evidences.catches: Children launched with cwd= and no directory on their command line - `npm install`, and the esbuild workers under it.

evidences.rule: The command line contains the section's build directory, ending at a path separator, a quote, whitespace, or the end of the line - NEVER as a bare substring.
evidences.catches: The serving node, which the launcher runs by absolute path precisely so that this works.

evidences.rule: The command line names `build_site.py` and carries `--course` and `--section` whose VALUES, read as arguments rather than as substrings, are this course and this section.
evidences.catches: The build driver itself, during every phase it does in its own process - which is the only thing running for much of a build.

identity.descendants: Every descendant of a matched process is matched too, repeatedly until no new child appears - the chain is driver -> npm -> node -> esbuild, so one pass is not enough. This is the half Windows had and the mac did not, and it is what catches a child spawned by a relative path that no evidence above can see.
identity.boundaries: Every path and argument comparison ends at a boundary. `.../section1` is a prefix of `.../section10` and `--section=1` is a prefix of `--section=10`; both have already stopped the wrong section on one platform. A boundary is a path separator, a quote, whitespace, or the end of the string - and allowing the end of the string is safe precisely because what follows `section1` in `section10` is `0`, which is not one.
identity.separators: Both `/` and `\` count, on both platforms. The container never sees a backslash and a native Windows run passes POSIX spellings around in places; accepting either costs nothing.
identity.caseInsensitive: Every comparison is case-insensitive, on BOTH platforms. Windows filesystems are case-insensitive but case-preserving, so a folder stored as `Ada1o` against a command line saying `ADA1O` is an ordinary Windows state. Making the rule case-sensitive on POSIX only would mean a case here could have two different right answers depending on which suite ran it, and then it is not one rule.
identity.spellings: A caller passes EVERY spelling of the directory it knows, because `courses/<CODE>/.merged_output/section<N>` is a symlink to the builds folder outside the working folder and a working directory is always the resolved path. When the built site moved, a sweep that knew only the symlinked spelling matched nothing and reported success while the build ran on.
identity.neverStop: Never the calling process, and never pid 1 - in this image pid 1's working directory can be inside a section's folder, and stopping it takes the container down with every other section's work in it.
identity.evidenceAPlatformMayNotHave: A case carries `needsEvidence` when it can only be decided by evidence some platform cannot see — today that means `workingDirectory`, which `Win32_Process` does not expose. A runner that has the evidence MUST run the case; a runner that does not MUST skip it and say which evidence was missing, rather than recording a pass. Cases without the key are every platform's to answer.
identity.repeatedFlags: A repeated `--section` or `--course` is read as the FIRST occurrence, while `build_site.py`'s own argparse would take the LAST. Nothing produces a repeated flag today — every caller builds the argument list itself — so this is recorded rather than fixed, and is the thing to change if a caller ever starts appending.

notShared.thing: How the process list is obtained
notShared.mac: `/proc`, read inside the container, which is where both of the mac's paths run.
notShared.windows: `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`, natively. It exposes no working directory at all. Where a process can be reached another way — its command line, or the descendant walk from a parent that WAS matched — a platform without that evidence still reaches the same verdict, and proving that is most of what these cases are for. Where it cannot, the case says so in `needsEvidence` and a runner without that evidence SKIPS it, naming the reason. A skip is honest; a case quietly passing because nothing ran it is not.

notShared.mac: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL a second later - ask, then insist. A node server closes its sockets and a Python driver runs its own cleanup.
notShared.windows: `Stop-Process -Force` in `preview.ps1`, and `os.kill` — reached indirectly, through `stop_preview.stop_one`, from `build_site.py`'s `servingOnly` sweep, which runs natively there too since 2026-09-05. The indirection is deliberate, and the reason lives in `build_site.py`'s own comment above the call rather than being copied here. On Windows `os.kill` is `TerminateProcess` whatever signal number it is handed, so both spellings end the process outright and there is nothing to ask with. Said precisely, because the short version is wrong: `signal.SIGTERM` DOES exist on Windows and `build_site.py` hands it to `os.kill` as the fallback where `SIGKILL` is absent — what Windows has no is SIGTERM's SEMANTICS, a signal a process can catch and shut down cleanly on. Deliberately not shared rather than papered over: the rule is WHICH processes, not how they end.

notShared.mac: Every process in the list. The evidences below are the whole filter.
notShared.windows: Every process in the list, the same as the mac, since 2026-09-05. Until then `preview.ps1` narrowed DIRECT evidence to `node.exe` and `python.exe` — a pre-existing narrowing recorded here rather than left to be discovered, and then removed once it had been: it refused most of this contract's own fixtures (`python3`, `npm`, `esbuild`, `sh`), which is a filter failing its own test suite rather than a defensible difference. The judgement this entry used to leave open has been made, and it went the mac's way: a process carrying this section's build directory on its command line IS this section's process, whatever its executable is called.

notShared.thing: How hard a publish build insists
notShared.mac: `servingOnly` sends SIGKILL at once rather than asking first. The preview server has to be gone BEFORE the build writes anything, and a second spent waiting politely is a second in which its host mirror can overwrite the build — which is the whole failure being prevented. `everything` asks first, because there a build's own cleanup is worth having.
notShared.windows: `Stop-Process -Force` in `preview.ps1`, and `os.kill` from `build_site.py`'s own native sweep; both end the process outright, because there is nothing to ask with. The question of how hard to insist does not arise on that platform — the first ask is already final.

cases.name: the preview serving this section is stopped
cases.why: The ordinary case, and the one both older rules already agreed on.

cases.name: a build for publishing stops the preview that would overwrite it
cases.why: Serve mode keeps mirroring its own build to the host every second, so a publish build that leaves the server running has its output replaced by the preview - live-reload client and all - about a second after it lands.

cases.name: another section's preview is left alone
cases.why: The regression that caused this rule to be written down. Stopping by PORT killed whatever held the default 8081, which is the first section to have previewed in the folder rather than the one being published: previewing section 1 while publishing section 2 took section 1 down.

cases.name: section 1 is not section 10
cases.why: A LIVE BUG when this was written, on the platform that matched with a bare substring test: `.../section1` is a prefix of `.../section10`, so stopping section 1 stopped section 10's preview. Needs ten sections in one course to bite, which nothing refuses.

cases.name: section 10 is stopped when section 10 is what was asked about
cases.why: The other half of the boundary: refusing the prefix must not refuse the real thing.

cases.name: a publish build is never mistaken for a preview server
cases.why: `--serve` is the only honest separator between the two. Without it a build for publishing would stop ITSELF, since the build it is protecting is also a build of this section.

cases.name: the launcher's stop DOES end a build
cases.why: The two questions differ here and this is the case that shows it. A mid-flight build is most of what `--stop` exists to reclaim: ending the host-side script leaves it running, burning real CPU for nothing.

cases.name: the build driver is found although it sits in the container's own folder
cases.why: The mac's blind spot for as long as `--stop` existed. `build_site.py` never calls os.chdir - it passes cwd= to its CHILDREN - so the driver stays in /teaching. During every in-process phase (copying the scaffold, copying content, social cards, the rsync mirror) it is the ONLY process there is to find, and a sweep by working directory found nothing and said so.

cases.name: --section=1 is not --section=10
cases.why: The same prefix bug by a second route, and live on the same platform: the driver is recognised by its arguments, and `--section=1` is a prefix of `--section=10`. Read the value as an ARGUMENT, never as a substring.

cases.name: another course's build is left alone
cases.why: Two courses can build at once in one working folder; a section number on its own means nothing without the code beside it.

cases.name: a child launched by a relative path goes with its parent
cases.why: The reason the rule is a walk down the process tree rather than a question about one process. `npm` and the esbuild workers under it carry no directory on their command lines at all, and esbuild does not even sit in the section's folder - it is reachable only through its parent. Windows found this first and had walked descendants for months while both of the mac's copies did not.

cases.name: a child of a process that does not belong is left alone
cases.why: The walk must start from a real match. A descendant rule that runs from an unmatched root reaches every process on the machine.

cases.name: a process is caught by its working directory alone
cases.why: What a command line cannot see. `npm install` runs with cwd= the section's folder and names no directory at all, so a rule that reads only command lines leaves it running.

cases.name: a build for publishing does not stop a build by working directory
cases.why: The same process, the other question. `servingOnly` must ignore the working directory entirely: the build being protected is itself sitting in that folder, and so is every child it has already started. Answerable on every platform despite the working directory in it: the verdict is 'nothing', which a runner that cannot see a working directory also reaches — checked, rather than assumed, by the test that blinds each case and compares.

cases.name: a publish build does not stop itself
cases.why: `build_site.py --build-only` calls this rule from inside the very process the driver evidence describes. Driver evidence is not consulted in `servingOnly` for exactly this reason - and the caller excludes its own process id besides, because one guarantee that matters this much is worth having twice.

cases.name: the resolved spelling and the symlinked spelling are one section
cases.why: `courses/<CODE>/.merged_output/section<N>` is a SYMLINK to the builds folder outside the working folder, and a process's working directory is always the resolved path - never the spelling used to get there. When the built site moved out of the working folder, a sweep that knew only the symlinked spelling matched nothing at all and reported success while the build kept running. Every caller passes every spelling it knows.

cases.name: the init process is never stopped
cases.why: A container's pid 1 is its own entry point, and in this image its working directory is /teaching. Killing it takes the container down with every other section's work inside it.

cases.name: a blank build directory is not a match for everything
cases.why: An empty string is a prefix of every path, so a caller that loses track of which section it is asking about would sweep the whole container rather than fail. Found by review, and it is the prefix bug one level up: the same mistake about where a path ENDS, made about where it begins.

cases.name: a Windows path is matched with backslashes, quotes and any casing
cases.why: The port sees only this shape, and until this case existed nothing in the contract did — the separators-and-casing rules were claimed in prose and pinned only by the mac's own unit tests. The space in the folder name is deliberate: it is why the path is quoted, and a rule that reads a command line as whitespace-separated tokens would get this wrong.

cases.name: a Windows path for section 1 is not section 10
cases.why: The live bug, in the shape the platform that had it actually sees.

cases.name: the space-separated spelling of an argument is read too
cases.why: `build_site.py`'s argparse accepts `--section 1` as well as `--section=1`. The launchers use the `=` form today, so a rule that only understood that one would look correct indefinitely and fail the day a caller changed.

cases.name: cancelling a publish stops the build it started
cases.why: A deploy runs `build_site.py --build-only` as a child, and Cancel calls the launcher's stop. Before the driver became evidence, the mac's sweep could not see that process at all — so Cancel ended the host script and left the build running inside the container. Pinned because the fix is easy to lose: it is a consequence of the driver evidence rather than anything named after cancelling.

cases.name: a publish build takes the server's own children with it
cases.why: The descendant walk applies in `servingOnly` too, and nothing said so. A serving node's esbuild workers are not stopped by anything else — the node is what is matched, and the workers hang off it.

quittingWhileWorkIsUnderWay.rule: Quitting asks the teacher to confirm when THIS app is in the middle of publishing or of building a preview, and never asks when the Mac itself is logging out, restarting or shutting down.
quittingWhileWorkIsUnderWay.why: Quitting used to be free, because it could not reach anything: the path that stops a working folder's website builder looked for programs it had never told itself where to find, so on an ordinary teacher's Mac it did nothing at all and there was nothing to interrupt (issue #220, 2026-09-19). Making it work means a quit can now genuinely land on work in flight, and the one case where that hurts is the one the teacher cannot see happening.
quittingWhileWorkIsUnderWay.whatCountsAsUnderWay: A publish this app started - in any of its windows, or by its own assistant. Counted from the app's own record of active publishes, which lasts exactly as long as the publish does. And, since issue #232 (2026-09-23), a preview being BUILT - from the moment it is asked for until its page first answers, or the run ends - whether a section window started it or the app's own assistant rebuilt it with no window open. Counted from a second record of the same kind, of preview builds. A publish's own build is NOT counted as a preview build: it is part of the publish, which is already counted. When both are under way the question names the publish, whose loss reaches the class website.
quittingWhileWorkIsUnderWay.whatDoesNotCount: A preview that is merely OPEN. A preview is known by the port it holds, and that is held for as long as the preview is OPEN - it cannot tell a section still building from one that finished twenty minutes ago and is being read. Asking on every open preview would mean asking almost every quit, which teaches a teacher to dismiss the question unread, and the question exists for work that can still be lost. Previews are not abandoned either: quitting stops this app's own previews deliberately, the way the Stop button does, before anything else is asked to rest. The record of a preview BUILD is a different fact from the port, and it is the one that counts: it ends when the page first answers, so a preview being read is never asked about. It is NOT the preview's address either - the launcher prints the address before it starts building, so the address is known for almost the whole build.
quittingWhileWorkIsUnderWay.whatIsNeverAskedAbout: Work belonging to another process - a publish set to happen on its own, an assistant driving the app over a connection, or a teacher's own command line. None of them is visible from here, so none of them is asked about; they are protected instead by the quit path refusing to stop anything while a launcher for that folder is running on the machine.
quittingWhileWorkIsUnderWay.neverAskWhen: The quit came from the system rather than from the teacher: log out, restart, shut down, and the 'are you sure?' forms of each. A question raised there blocks the log out until the Mac gives up on the app and names it as the one that would not quit. Everything is left running instead, which is the same answer the quit path reaches on its own when it finds work in flight.

buttons.defaultWhy: The safe answer is the default answer: a teacher who presses Return without reading keeps their work. Quitting anyway is the deliberate one.
buttons.keepWorking: the app stays open and nothing is stopped or released
buttons.quitAnyway: the app goes, and it does not END the publish: that is a separate program and the app deliberately passes it over rather than being the thing that kills a teacher's publish. It will very likely stop on its own anyway, which is why the sentence the teacher reads says quitting COULD leave the publish unfinished and promises neither outcome - on the mac the launcher runs under `set -euo pipefail` and writes to a terminal the app owned, so when the app goes its next line of output fails. Measured 2026-09-19, twice independently: two orphaned children of identical shape, the plain one ran to the end and the `set -e` one died at its next line of output. Whatever is left, the quit path then handles safely - a builder still working is left running and said so on the trail, an idle one is stopped. For a preview being built, quitting ends a section window's preview the way the Stop button does; the assistant's own rebuild with no window is passed over like a publish and may run to its end, since the preview launcher does not stop at its first failed line of output - which is why that sentence says COULD as well. Nothing a student can see is touched either way.

cases.name: nothing is happening
cases.why: The ordinary quit, and it must stay silent. A confirmation a teacher meets every time is one they stop reading.

cases.name: one section is publishing
cases.why: The case this exists for.

cases.name: several sections are publishing
a preview is open and nothing is publishing
cases.why: The decision this case exists to pin. A preview that is merely open is not work under way, and an app that cannot tell a building preview from a finished one must not guess. Still true after issue #232: what counts is a preview being BUILT, which is its own record, and an open preview whose build has finished is not one.

cases.name: the Mac is logging out while a section is publishing
cases.why: The rule that must never bend. A modal here holds up the log out, and a teacher whose Mac will not log out has a worse problem than a publish that did not finish.

cases.name: a preview is being built and nothing is publishing
cases.why: The case issue #232 exists for. Russell's ruling on 2026-09-20 named a publish OR a preview; a first build can spend minutes fetching what it needs, and a teacher who quits through it deserves to be told.

cases.name: a preview is open and another is being built
cases.why: The open preview adds nothing and takes nothing away: the build is what is asked about.

cases.name: a preview is being built while the Mac logs out
cases.why: The rule that must never bend bends for a preview no more than for a publish.

quittingWhileWorkIsUnderWay.appliesOnWhy: Written on the mac 2026-09-19 with the quit-path fix it belongs to. An acknowledged EXCEPTION, not a permanent difference: Windows could ask the same question, and contracts/README.md's "Four ways out" passage rejects softening a contract this way. Taken here because the alternative reddens a suite nobody is watching with a failure only Windows can mend, and recorded in the README's Named gaps section so the file does not argue both sides. Two honest costs: appliesOn has no mend-check, so nothing will go red when Windows adopts this; and the block-level appliesOn KEY ITSELF is read by no test on either platform, so that key is documentation rather than a gate. The block's own cases are run on the mac (QuitConfirmationTests) and by nothing on Windows. The SHAPE is portable - what counts as under way, what never counts, and when never to ask are all platform-neutral; only the signal that says the system is logging out differs (kAEQuitReason here, WM_QUERYENDSESSION there). Adopt this and the "quit asked about work under way" trail line together, or neither, and delete both appliesOn keys when you do.

referenceCourses.note: A REFERENCE COURSE is last year's course — or a course full of example content — kept in this year's sidebar so a teacher can read it, and which Plantoir never deploys. It is FROZEN: its pages are locked on disk, and every action that would change a page, a setting or the shape of the course is withheld. This block is the whole rule as data: how one is marked, how the school years are named and offered, when a code may not join the shelf, and what is done to the course's deploying settings so that an OLDER copy of either app — one that has never heard of the marker — refuses it too.

identity.folderName: The folder under courses/ — ICS3U-2025. It is IDENTITY: the launcher argument, the built-site folder, the preview lease, the backup zip's name and the scheduled-deploy identifier are all built from it, so two ICS3Us never collide.
identity.courseCode: course_code stays the REAL code — ICS3U, unchanged from the course it was copied from. That is also what keeps the preview's site title, grade label and social card right, and it is why the folder and the key are allowed to disagree here and nowhere else.
identity.displayedToTheTeacher: The real code. A teacher reads ICS3U in the sidebar, the window title, every alert and every sentence; the folder name appears only where a folder name is the fact — Obsidian's own vault switcher, for one, which opens the course folder AS the vault and shows its name.
identity.why: A separate display_code key was REJECTED: it would be a third spelling of the same fact, and it would leave the site builder putting ICS3U-2025 in the site title of a course whose preview the teacher is reading.

schoolYearLabel.rule: A school year is named for the calendar year it STARTS in and is stored as that integer. The label is derived: the starting year, an EN DASH (U+2013), and the last two digits of the following year.
schoolYearLabel.why: Storing the integer keeps the dash out of the file format entirely, and one rule in one place means the two apps cannot render the same year two ways.

cases.why: The century rolls; the label is the last two digits of the following year and nothing more. Pinned so neither app invents a four-digit second half.

schoolYearsOffered.rule: Newest first, from the school year containing today down to the floor. A new school year appears on 1 AUGUST — the year containing today is today.month >= 8 ? today.year : today.year - 1. The current school year IS offered, and is first. 'No year' is offered too, and is always last; it is an absence rather than a year, so it is not in this list.
schoolYearsOffered.why: The rule is INHERITED rather than invented: Windows already ships Timetable.AcademicYearStarting with exactly this shape, documented as 'a school year is named for the calendar year it starts in, and starts in the late summer'. Ontario and BC both start in September, so 1 August leaves a month of headroom for a teacher setting up over the summer. The top end is derived from the day and never written down, so the list grows by itself; the floor is Russell's and does not move. Every function takes the DAY rather than reading the clock, or none of these cases could be run at all.

cases.why: The day before the rollover: 2026–27 is not offered yet.
The rollover day itself, and the first day 2026–27 appears.
Nine years, grown by itself, with nothing hard-coded at the top.

schoolYearRead.rule: A stored reference_school_year reads as the year when it is a whole number within the offered list for today, and as 'Other' otherwise.
schoolYearRead.why: Anything else — a missing key, a null, a hand-edited 2019, a 2031 written on a Mac with a wrong clock, a word, a true — lands in 'Other', which a teacher can see and can change. The alternative is a group labelled 0000–01 built out of a value that coerced to zero. A year ABOVE the range today joins its own group on the day that year arrives, because the range only grows at the top. A JSON true needs no case of its own in the code: true and 1 are indistinguishable without CFGetTypeID, and both read as the year 1, which is out of range either way.

cases.name: the ordinary case
no key at all
an explicit null
below the floor

cases.why: A teacher may keep a copy of a course they are teaching this year — the other semester's, or one they will not run again in this order.

codeUniqueWithinAGroup.rule: Within one school-year group — including 'Other' — no two reference courses may share a course code. Refused with a sentence when a course is put on the shelf and again when its year is changed. The courses a teacher TEACHES are in no group at all and are never consulted.
codeUniqueWithinAGroup.why: Three rows all saying ICS3U under one year is a teacher's mistake made permanent; the same three under 2024–25, 2025–26 and 'Other' is exactly what they meant. It is also what makes 'take a fresh copy' an ordered act — delete the reference copy first, then copy again — rather than a way to end up with two of the same thing.

cases.name: the same code in the same year
the same code in different years
one with a year and one without
two with no year at all
cases.why: 'Other' is a group like any other. Two ADA1Os of example content with nothing to tell them apart is the row a teacher cannot read.

cases.name: a different code in the same year
beside the LIVE course of the same code
cases.why: The ordinary case, not an exception: a teacher keeps last year's ICS3U while teaching this year's. The rule never looks at the courses being taught.

cases.name: re-filing a course into the year it is already in
cases.why: Changing a course's school year must not find the course itself sitting where it is about to move from.

neutralises.rule: Whatever makes a course a reference course writes these settings in the same act, so the course has nowhere to deploy to whatever is reading it.
neutralises.why: The marker is what THIS version reads. This is what every other version reads — including an older Plantoir on a second Mac sharing the folder over iCloud Drive. Every shipped version refuses a folder deploy with no folder, with sentences it already has. Measured: a real previous-generation working folder carries no deploy_target at all, and an absent deploy_target reads as 'netlify', so a plain copy would have arrived with a working Deploy button aimed at last year's live class site.

keys.why: A reference course must never claim last year's domain — the live course that replaced it may be using it.

neutralises.alsoRenamedAside: .netlify_sites/section<N>.json and .cloudflare_sites/section<N>.json become the frozen previous-marker name (file-formats.json → firstDeployMarkers). Renamed rather than deleted: the file holds the site id and the admin address, which a teacher may still want. Two fail-safes fall out of one rename — a deploy that somehow ran would make a NEW site rather than overwrite last year's live one, and a section that has never deployed cannot be scheduled.
neutralises.kept: Per-page visibility frontmatter is KEPT exactly as it is: it is last year's record of what students actually saw, and it is what makes a preview of a reference course show a sensible site rather than everything. That holds for a course made from a MODERN course. It does not hold for one imported from the older folder-per-class layout (#254): its pages carry Obsidian Digital Garden's dg-* keys, which the build does not read, and its shared pages carry none at all, so its preview shows every page except draft: true ones - more than students saw. Accepted by Russell for v1.3.0; see importing.olderLayout.whatThePreviewShows. One imported from the 2024-25 website-folder-per-class layout (#256) is section 1 only, and there it DOES hold: its pages were hidden by draft:, which the build reads, so its preview matches section 1's own site (280 of 324 and 213 of 220 pages visible, 0 disagreements, measured); see importing.quartzCheckoutLayout.whatThePreviewShows.

markerAgreement.rule: FOUR implementations answer 'is this course kept for reference?' - the APP itself, scripts/reference_course.py, deploy.sh and deploy.ps1 - and two of them are plain shell with no JSON parser. So the question is one regular expression, run over the WHOLE settings file as a single string: the quoted key, a colon with any whitespace (newlines included) on either side, and the word true in any case, unquoted. Every row below carries the deploy outcome all four must produce, and what the APP reads the row as.
markerAgreement.theAppIsTheFourthReader: Added after the app was measured reading `"kept_for_reference": 1` as TRUE while all three launchers read it as an ordinary course and deployed it - JSONSerialization hands back an NSNumber and NSNumber conditionally bridges to Bool for 0 and 1, so `as? Bool` said true. Both directions of the fault at once: the app FREEZES AND LOCKS a course, with no way back to live, that the launchers then publish. CourseConfiguration now reads this one key through CFBooleanGetTypeID - a real JSON boolean and nothing else - and every row states appReadsAsReference so the four can never silently disagree again.
markerAgreement.theInvariant: Wherever the APP reads a course as kept for reference, every launcher must REFUSE. The reverse is allowed: a launcher may refuse something the app calls ordinary (that is the 'cannot tell' rule below), because refusing publishes nothing and freezes nothing. A test asserts the implication on every row.
markerAgreement.cannotTell: A marker that is THERE with a value that is neither true nor false - `1`, `"true"`, `True`, a key written with backslash-u escapes - is something a person plainly MEANT. The launchers refuse it with a sentence of its own ('cannot tell whether this course is kept for reference ... its settings say something other than true or false'), which deploys nothing and freezes nothing; the app treats such a course as ordinary, so the launcher's refusal is what the teacher meets. Leniency in the APP was considered and REJECTED: the app's reading does two things rather than one - it refuses a deploy AND it locks every file, with no way back - so a false positive there is not loud and harmless, it is a live course the teacher cannot edit and cannot un-reference.
markerAgreement.whyItMatters: The one door the shared Python never reaches is deploy.sh's folder publish: it copies host-side with rsync and exits 0 before the container is started. So a disagreement between the shell and the Python IS a deploy of a frozen course. Measured on 2026-09-20, before this table existed: a config whose key and colon sat on different lines was a reference course to the Python and an ordinary one to the launcher, because grep works a LINE AT A TIME - and the launcher published it, exit 0, saying 'Published: 1 file(s) updated.'

pattern.whyEscapedKey: An object KEY written with a backslash-u escape - ANY key, not just this one - makes the text readers say 'cannot tell'. A key escaped ALL the way through is decoded by the app and by the Python's parsed half, which both call it a reference course and FREEZE it, while a text reader sees nothing and the folder publish goes through at exit 0. Measured: it deployed. Every key Plantoir and the shared Python write is plain ASCII, so an escaped key is never ours. KEYS ONLY: json.dump escapes non-ASCII in VALUES by default, so a course name with an accent and every emojis value legitimately carry backslash-u - the [{,] anchor is what tells a key from a value, since a key follows an opening brace or a comma and a value never does. Proven against copies of the four real previous-generation configs, all 38 example-content payloads, the app's own writer with accents and emoji, and hand-made values containing escaped quotes and colons: no false refusal.
pattern.whyPresent: The PRESENCE test, and the false test beside it. A marker that is there with a value that is neither reads as 'cannot tell' and the launchers refuse. `[^"]*ept_for_reference` also catches a key written with backslash-u escapes in its first characters, and cannot match an ordinary key.
pattern.why: Three dialects of one rule, and each line of it is load-bearing. The POSIX form is run by grep, which reads a line at a time, so deploy.sh flattens the file with `tr '\n' ' '` FIRST - without that, [[:space:]] cannot span a newline. The .NET form needs no flattening, because backslash-s matches a newline there. All three spell the VALUE's case out and are matched CASE-SENSITIVELY: deploy.ps1 used -match, which is case-insensitive in PowerShell and applied that to the KEY as well - so `KEPT_FOR_REFERENCE` refused there while the mac and the Python allowed it, stranding a Windows teacher with a live course whose Deploy button could never work. JSON keys are case-sensitive; -cmatch, and the value's case written out. Python's re.search is given the whole file as read.

markerAgreement.whenInDoubtRefuse: The two directions are not comparable. A live course wrongly refused is loud and harmless - the teacher sees a refusal and says so. A reference course wrongly deployed REPORTS SUCCESS and nobody finds out. So every ambiguity here is resolved by refusing: a marker nested inside another OBJECT is refused, because plain shell cannot tell it from the real key and one answer shared by three implementations beats three answers that are each right about something different. The marker's own text inside a string VALUE is a narrower case than it looks, and the exact rule is worth stating because it is not the flat 'no pattern matches a value': a config is refused when it carries a QUOTED TOKEN - key or value - whose text ends in the key's tail and is not followed by true or false. The marker's text written plainly inside a value therefore DOES read as 'cannot tell' (measured), while the only way that text legitimately reaches a value is through escaped quotes, which never match. No realistic config was found that is refused by this: it would need a course name, folder name or path that literally ends in the key's tail.
markerAgreement.whatIsDeliberatelyNotRefused: A malformed config with NO marker in it: a course nobody can open must not become undeployable by accident. A malformed config that DOES carry the marker is refused, because there is nothing accidental about it. (This key used to say the opposite about `"true"` and `1` - that both read FALSE in CourseConfiguration on both platforms and so should deploy. The mac half of that was measured FALSE on 2026-09-20 and both rows are now 'cannot tell'.)

the marker set to false
